en: Now begins the third chapter. *Then,
upon entering into another state, he departs enveloped [by subtle elements], according to the question and its determination.* (BS 3.1.1)

Demonstrating the relationship characterized by the state of being the "possessor of the reason" (hetumat) between the second and third chapters, he states a summary of the subject matter for the sake of easy comprehension, beginning with the words "In the second chapter":

For, by removing contradictions with Smṛti, Nyāya, and Śruti, the lack of authority characterized by indecisiveness (anadhyavasāya) has been removed; and thus, when its authority has been rendered firm, the investigation of the third chapter proceeds, whereas otherwise it would not be established due to a lack of foundation.
To show the intermediate connection (*avāntarasaṃgati*), it was stated therein that the principles distinct from the individual soul (*jīva*) are the instruments (*upakaraṇa*) of the soul.
Having stated the summary of the meaning of the chapter, he states the summary of the meaning of the section (*pāda*): "In that regard, first, in the first section.
He states its purpose: "For the sake of dispassion (*vairāgya*)."
He prepares the ground for the subsequent and prior purification [of the subject] with the statement: "The individual soul has the chief vital breath as its minister.
This is because, unlike the case of the instruments (the senses), there is no scriptural mention of the elements as the material cause [of the body].

Here, since the instruments are composed of the elements, their elemental nature is established by the very scriptural mention of the instruments as the material cause; therefore, this section is commenced with the intention of discussing the elements that are distinct from the material cause of the sense organs.
If it were to come having taken up the elements (*bhūta*), then that too would have been heard of, just as the instruments (*karaṇa*) are mentioned as being taken up.
But it is not so heard; therefore, the soul does not depart enveloped by the elements, but rather enveloped by the instruments alone.
For in a matter that is known solely through scripture (*āgama*), the absence of such a scriptural statement cannot be held to determine the non-existence of the object of knowledge.

Nor is it correct to assume that the soul moves enveloped by the elements merely because the commencement of another body would otherwise be inexplicable; thus he says: "And the elemental constituents (bhūtamātrā) are easily obtained everywhere.

Regarding the passage beginning with "the sky, the rain-cloud," etc., for here, in the commencement of the body, the *apūrva* (unseen force) resulting from the *agnihotra* sacrifice is divided fivefold as faith (*śraddhā*) and so forth.

The Śruti, intending to describe the worship of the fires beginning with *dyu* (heaven) as the means for attaining the northern path (*uttaramārga*) by way of their being the objects of oblation, says: "That world indeed, O Gautama, is the fire," and so forth.
Herein, [it refers to] the two oblations of the Agnihotra performed in the evening and in the morning.

When the means of accomplishment, such as milk and so forth, have been offered with faith into the Āhavanīya fire— thereby becoming permeated by the states of the fuel, smoke, flame, embers, and sparks,

and further permeated by the causal factors (kārakas) such as the agent— the two subtle elements, which are liquid substances like milk and the like and are designated by the word "water" (ap) due to their connection with water, ascend successively through the intermediate space (antarikṣa) and enter the heavenly world (dyuloka).
And because they have faith as their cause, they are denoted by the word "faith.
The fire that is the locus of those two oblations, as well as the fuel, smoke, flame, embers, and sparks, are indicated by way of metaphorical representation.
"That world of heaven, O Gautama, is indeed the fire."

Just as the Āhavanīya fire is the locus for the Agnihotra, so too the celestial world is the locus for those subtle waters—which are the transformed state of the Agnihotra oblation denoted by the word "faith" (śraddhā) and permeated by faith. The sun is its fuel, for it is by being kindled by that [sun] that the celestial world shines; thus, it is called "fuel" (samit) because of this kindling. The rays of that sun are its smoke, because the rays rise up from the sun just as smoke rises from burning fuel.
The sun is the seeker of food,
because of its commonality with light and because it is the effect of the sun;
the moon is the charcoal.
Because they are manifested upon the subsiding of the flames;
the stars are its sparks, like the scattered fragments of the embers of the moon, being called "sparks" due to the common quality of being dispersed.
In this fire, the gods—the vital breaths of the sacrificer in the form of Agni and the other deities—reside as the divine aspect (adhideva).
They offer faith, and faith is said [to be the oblation]. Parjanya, O Gautama, is indeed the fire; Parjanya is a specific deity presiding over the instruments of rain.
Of that [fire], the wind itself is the fuel.
For by means of the wind the rain-cloud is kindled as fire,
since rain is observed when the east wind and other winds are strong;
the smoke is the cloud.
Because it is an effect of smoke and because of its similarity to smoke; lightning is like fire,
due to the commonality of luminosity.
The thunderbolt consists of embers because of its hardness and its connection with lightning;
the roar is the sparks because of their common quality of being scattered.
In that [cloud], the gods—whose nature is fire and who are the vital breaths of the sacrificer—offer King Soma as an oblation; from that offering of Soma, rain comes into being.

This is what is meant: the waters called "faith," having entered the heavenly world as an oblation, are transformed into the form of the moon; then, in the second stage, being offered into the fire of Parjanya, they transform into rain.
"The earth, O Gautama, is indeed the fire"—for that fire called the earth, the year itself is the fuel.
For after a period of one year, the earth, fully kindled, becomes fit for the production of rice and other crops.

Smoke is the sky; just as smoke rises from fire on the earth, the sky appears like smoke. Night is the flame; corresponding to the darkness of the dark earth, night is like a flame corresponding to fire.
The quarters are the coals, because they are seen as tranquil and serene when the flames of night have subsided at dawn.
The intermediate directions are the sparks, due to their similarity in minuteness.

Into that fire, the gods offer the waters—which have arrived through the process of the transformation of faith and Soma and have been transformed into the form of rain; from that oblation, food such as rice and barley comes into being.
Man, indeed, O Gautama, is the fire. His speech is the fuel;

for by means of speech—which resides in the eight locations beginning with the palate—this [fire] is kindled through the sequence of manifesting sounds, words, and sentences, thereby illuminating the multitude of objects.
His breath is the smoke.
The mouth is like smoke because it issues forth from the face; the tongue is like a flame due to the similarity of its redness;
and the eyes are like embers because they are the locus of radiance.
The ear is the sparks, because of its scattered nature.

Those very waters, having arrived through the sequence of transformations beginning with faith, and having been transformed into the form of rice and other grains, are offered as an oblation into the fire that is the person; their transformation results in the production of semen.
Woman indeed, O Gautama, is the fire; her lap is the fuel.
Therefore, she is kindled for the production of sons and so forth; that which is the whispering [of love] is the smoke.
Because the whispering arises from the woman, the hair is the smoke, and the womb is the flame because of its redness.
That which he performs within—the sexual union—is the embers.
Delights are mere fragments of pleasure, like sparks, because of their insignificance.
Into this very fire, the gods offer semen; from that oblation, the embryo comes into being.
Thus, through the sequence of offerings consisting of faith, soma, rain, food, and semen, having reached the fire that is the woman, the waters come to be known as the embryo.
Because they are composed primarily of water, those waters come to be called "man" at the fifth oblation.
Since the waters come to be called "man" at the fifth oblation, it is understood from this that the living self (jīva) departs enveloped by the waters.

This is what is meant: as will be stated later, water is denoted by the word "faith" (śraddhā); because these [elements] have been made tripartite (trivṛtkṛta), there is an inclusion of both fire and food through the mention of water due to their inseparable connection with it—this too will be stated.

Even so, the departure of the individual soul (jīva) enveloped by the elements is not understood from this much alone, because the scriptures merely state that fire, water, and food attain the state of being called "man" (puruṣavacastva) at the fifth oblation.

Nevertheless, it is understood that the soul departs enveloped by the elements, because of the authority of the scriptural passage, "They offer faith as an oblation; from that oblation King Soma arises," which is consistent with the scripture stating that those who perform sacrifices for desired objects attain the world of the moon by the path of the fathers via smoke and so forth, namely, "From space [it goes] to the moon; he is Soma, the King."

For instance: those very waters which, having been offered in the second oblation, have attained the state of Soma—it is with these that this living being (jīva), the performer of sacrifices and other rites, is enveloped when it has reached the state of the moon and arrived at the lunar world.

Now, one might object: let the waters themselves, independently, attain the state of Soma through the sequence beginning with faith; meanwhile, let the living being go, unenveloped by them, as a mere possessor of the senses, and experience the state of Soma.
What is the harm in that?
This is the objection:
namely, that it would involve overstepping the commonality of the scriptural statement.

For the commonality of the scriptural statement would be maintained only if the soul's transformation into Soma occurred in the same form and by the same sequence as the transformation of water into Soma.
Otherwise, however, there would be no commonality of scriptural statement (*śrutisāmānya*).

Therefore, regarding the question of whether the deceased is carried while embraced or unembraced, it is determined—on account of the commonality of the scriptural statement—that he is carried while embraced.
Consequently, because of their preponderance of fluidity, the substances such as curd and milk, once offered as oblations, become subtle and adhere to the performer of sacrifices and other rites.

"When the body is being offered as an oblation according to the method of fuel, those who have performed sacrifices such as the *iṣṭi*—being themselves of the nature of oblations when offered—are enveloped by the fires and lead the sacrificer to the heavenly world.
[The opponent] objects: "But surely there is another scriptural passage?"
This is the meaning: for [the soul] would indeed travel enveloped by the subtle body only if it did not possess a gross body while traveling;
however, there exists for it a connection with a present gross body until the attainment of another body, as demonstrated by the illustration of the caterpillar (*tṛṇajalāyuka*).
Therefore, because this contradicts the scriptural illustration, the soul does not travel enveloped by the subtle body.
He refutes this with the words "even there":
first of all, the possibility of transmigrating does not exist for the supreme self (*paramātman*),
because its intrinsic nature is eternally pure, awakened, and liberated.
However, regarding living beings:
the Supreme Self itself, when its limitation is conceived through adjuncts (upādhi), is designated as the "living being" (jīva).
Since its adjuncts—such as the body and the senses—are localized, the [Self], while residing therein, cannot go to another body.

Therefore, it should be understood that [the soul], enveloped by the subtle body and impelled by karma, moves toward the body that is to be attained; the mere prolongation of the cultivation directed toward that body is compared to a leech.
He states the Sāṃkhya position: "of the pervasive organs.
Since the organs are derived from the *ahaṃkāra* (ego-sense), and since the *ahaṃkāra* pervades the entire circle of the world, the meaning is that the organs are also pervasive.
He states the conception of the Buddhists: "Of the self alone.
Here, the "self" is the continuum of the *ālayavijñāna* (storehouse consciousness), and its "activity" consists of the six *pravṛttivijñānas* (evolving consciousnesses).
As for the five sense organs, such as the eye and so forth, they are produced anew.
He states the doctrine of Kaṇabhuj (the Vaiśeṣika): "The mind alone," and so forth;
that is to say, the body is the locus of experience, the abode of experience, meaning it is newly produced.
He states the doctrine of the Digambara (Jaina): "The soul itself, having leaped up," and so forth.
By the inclusion of the word "etcetera" (ādi), he includes the conceptualization of the Lokāyatikas;
for they are proponents of the doctrine that the self is the body, and they assert that the self becomes reduced to ashes and that there is no going anywhere for anyone. //1//
START BsVBh_3,1.1.2 He objects:
"But surely [it was said], 'by the two examples cited'..."
Regarding this, he provides the answer by means of a sutra:
"But because it consists of three elements and because of their predominance.
The function of fire is the digestion of food that has been eaten and drunk.
The function of water consists of lubrication, perspiration, and so forth;
the function of earth consists of odor and so forth.

However, one who—observing the presence of odor, perspiration, digestion, vital breath, and the provision of space—perceives the body as being composed of all five elements, is not satisfied with the view that it consists of only three elements, namely fire, water, and food.
He replies to that: "Furthermore, it consists of three constituents. This is because the body consists of the three elements—wind, bile, and phlegm—which have the nature of sustaining the body;
therefore, that body cannot be produced by water alone, setting aside the other elements.
If it is asked, "Then why is there a restriction regarding the non-inclusion [of water]? he says: "Therefore, it is with regard to abundance.

Excluding the earth element, because the effect—the body—has an abundance of liquid substances such as blood in comparison to fire and the others, and because its two causes—the material cause (*upādāna*) and the instrumental cause (*nimitta*)—also have an abundance of liquidity, the statement that "water is man-like" is made; it does not, however, intend to exclude the other elements. //2//

And because of the departure of the vital breaths (prāṇa). It is understood that the vital breaths have a substratum in the living body; it is observed that when the living body moves, the vital breaths, which conform to it, also move.
Therefore, when departing from the body composed of the six sheaths (ṣāṭkauśika), they depart as that [subtle body] departs;
and it is understood that this subtle body which governs them consists of the elements (bhūta) and the sense organs (indriya).
For it is not observed that their support consists of the sense organs alone, such that their movement would be possible if they were supported by those alone. //3//
"Because of the scriptural statement regarding the movement toward fire and so forth— if this is argued, we say no, because it is figurative.

(BS 3.1.4) Even though the departure of the individual soul together with the vital breaths has been clearly stated, the doubt concerning its movement toward fire and so forth is raised for the purpose of demonstrating an apparent contradiction with scripture.
For here, since the transition of body hair and head hair to plants and trees contradicts what is perceived by the senses, it must first be accepted as figurative (*bhākta*).
And so, because they fall in between those two categories, it is likewise appropriate that their transition is also figurative due to contradiction with scripture.
Furthermore, "figurative" has been explained as the cessation of assistance. //4//
START BsVBh_3,1.1.5:
If it is argued that [the water] is not mentioned in the first [libation], we say no, for it is precisely those [waters] that are established by logical consistency.

When the manner in which the waters come to be called "man" at the fifth libation is questioned, it would be both irrelevant and illogical to state that something other than water—namely, faith (*śraddhā*)—is to be offered in the first libation.

For it is not the case that faith— characterized by clarity of intellect— can be extracted or offered in the same manner as the heart and other organs are cut out and extracted from animals and so forth for sacrifice;
nor is such a deviation from the general rule of the effect conforming to its cause logically tenable.
Therefore, the word "faith" (śraddhā) is applied to water because of its similarity [to faith].
For this very reason, the Śruti says: "Water, indeed, is the self. //5//
"If it be argued that [they do not go] because they are not mentioned in scripture, we say no, because those who perform sacrifices such as the *iṣṭi* are known [to go].
The meaning of this has already been explained previously.

In the context of the Agnihotra, there are six questions concerning the departure, the path, the support, the satisfaction, the return, and the rising toward the world—pertaining respectively to fire, fuel, smoke, flame, embers, and sparks.
The collection of these six is the "Six Questions" (ṣaṭpraśnī); its detailed exposition is the "Answer" (prativacana). //6//
In order to introduce another sūtra, [the author] raises an objection with "But how? [The response is:
"They consume them there, saying, 'O King Soma, swell! Wane! and so forth.
The meaning is that, through the intensification of the action, they cause the worlds consisting of Soma to swell and diminish, just as [the cups] do with the Soma;
therefore, he recites the following:
"Or it is figurative, because there is no selfhood; for thus the scripture shows. (BBs 3.1.7)

For one who is entitled [to the ritual] is the agent who experiences the fruits produced by karma, not the object of experience; therefore, since those who have attained co-residence with the Moon would otherwise be food for the gods and others, this would contradict the scriptural injunction regarding the ritual process of sacrifice—which states, "One desiring heaven should sacrifice"—in that it prescribes the means required by the agent. Consequently, the word "food" (anna) must be understood as figurative, referring merely to the fact that they are sustained by the gods while remaining as enjoyers, and not in its primary sense of being chewed and swallowed.
Regarding this very point, he states that another scriptural passage is consistent: "For thus the scripture shows.

Scripture demonstrates that one who does not know the Self, by virtue of being ignorant of the Self, is an object of enjoyment for the gods like an animal, but not because of being something to be chewed.
For just as oxen and the like, even while eating their own fodder, are objects of enjoyment because they benefit their masters by pulling plows and so forth; [so too is the ignorant person].

Thus, the meaning of the Śruti is that those who perform sacrifices and the like, being ignorant of the supreme reality (*paramatattva*), become objects of enjoyment for the gods in this world and in the next through the offering of curds, milk, sacrificial cakes (*puroḍāśa*), and so forth, by serving them.
Alternatively, there is another interpretation of the phrase "because they are not knowers of the Self" (*anātmavittvāt tathā hi darśayati*).
One who knows the Self is one who possesses the knowledge of the five fires (*pañcāgnividyā*); one who does not know the Self is an "ignorant of the Self" (*anātmavit*).
For it is said that "the gods devour him who does not know the knowledge of the five fires" (pañcāgnividyā) in order to praise that very knowledge, since it is the subject under discussion;

by this, the purpose of the figurative expression (upacāra) has been stated. He states the impossibility [of the literal sense] which serves as the ground for the figurative expression: "For thus [scripture] shows."
The scripture [indicates] the state of being an enjoyer:
"He experiences power in the world of Soma.
The remainder has a meaning that is not obscure. //7//
Upon the exhaustion of what has been performed, one possessing residual karma [returns], according to what is seen and remembered; as it went, and not so;
having dwelt there until the exhaustion of its momentum.
Because of the connection [of the text],
as it says, "Whatever he does here," and because of the scriptural statement, "having reached the end of whatever karma has been performed here."

Furthermore, because death (prāyaṇa) manifests all karma through a single impulse, it is not logical that there should be a restriction regarding manifestation when the cause of manifestation is common to all. Moreover, manifestation consists in making [the karma] ready to yield its fruit; therefore, every action has had its fruit fully experienced.
And action is opposed to its own fruit;
therefore, on the basis of both scripture and logical reasoning, the descent occurs solely from conduct—that is, from behavior—and not from [ritual] action.
Furthermore, conduct and action are well-known to be distinct according to scripture.
"As one acts, as one behaves, so does one become.
Thus, by stating "those of pleasant conduct" and "those of foul conduct," the text teaches that conduct alone is the cause for the womb of rebirth, and not mere ritual action (*karman*).

Or, even if both action and character were equally intended as residual impressions (*anuśaya*), nevertheless, although this person has performed sacrifices and works of public utility (*iṣṭāpūrta*) himself—

Although he is free from latent dispositions (*anushaya*) because he has already experienced his [karmic] enjoyments, nevertheless, due to the force of the latent dispositions belonging to his father and others, he will descend from the world of the moon and experience their ripened results—namely, birth, lifespan, and enjoyments.

For it is recorded in tradition that one person may partake of the fruit of the good or evil deeds of another who is related to them, as in the passage: "If a wife drinks liquor, half her body falls [upon her husband]," and so forth.
Likewise, there are scriptural declarations regarding the fruits of rites such as the *shraddha* and the *Vaisvanari-isti*, which accrue to the father, son, and others.

Therefore, because of the introductory statement "as far as the completion [of their works]" (Chāndogya Up. 5.10.5) and in accordance with another scriptural passage, "whatever he does here" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Up. 4.4.6), the quality of having "pleasant conduct" must be understood figuratively as residing in another relative—the performer of sacrifices and charitable works.

Thus, it might be concluded that those who have descended are indeed devoid of residual karma (niranuśaya), having already experienced their enjoyment. To this, it is replied: even when that aggregate of karma by which the fruit was enjoyed has passed away, they descend from the lunar orb still possessing residual karma (sānuśaya).
Why? Because of perception and recollection.
"Perception" refers to what is expressed by the word *dṛṣṭa*, namely Śruti perceived through direct experience;
and *Smṛti* has also been presented.
Alternatively, by the word "seen" (dṛṣṭa), enjoyment in its various forms is expressed.
This is the intended meaning: the qualifiers "those of foul conduct" and "those of beautiful conduct" refer to those who have descended [to earth].
And when the primary sense is possible, it is not logical to assume a figurative sense based merely on a relationship [with the primary object].
Nor is it correct to argue that the primary meaning [of the text] is impossible due to contradiction with the commencement [of the ritual] and contradiction with other scriptural passages;
for the words "as long as" (*yāvat*) and "whatever" (*yatkiñcit*) are compatible even when referring to those works of merit, such as *iṣṭāpūrta*, whose fruits have already been exhausted.

Indeed, the injunction "one should perform the Agnihotra as long as one lives" does not prescribe the offering at times such as eating or walking throughout one's entire life, nor even at midday and so forth, but rather in reference to the specific times of evening and morning.

If it is argued that this is so because of the force of the injunction regarding the times of morning and evening, and since time—though not a subsidiary element (*aṅga*) because it cannot be taken up as an objective—is nonetheless included as a causal condition (*nimitta*), [we reply: no;
for here too, this is possible in accordance with the primary sense of the passage beginning with "those of pleasant conduct" (*ramaṇīyacaraṇāḥ*).
In that case, should the initial statement now be restricted in accordance with the concluding summary?
No, it is said in reply; for even in accordance with the concluding summary, it is not possible for that [initial statement] to maintain an unrestricted application.
For it is not the case that all *saṃpātas*— or rather, the *saṃpātas* of all persons— are brought to exhaustion there by the experience [of results] for one who performs sacrifices and other rites;
because if the *karmāśayas* residing in other persons were exhausted by his experience, it would lead to an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*),
and because those *karmāśayas* that have long been experienced and are no longer present are removed by the experience on the lunar orb.
And thus, the Śruti itself, contracting of its own accord, even allows for that contraction which results from the requirement of systematic consistency (upasaṃhāra).
By this, the passage "whatever one does here" is also explained.

Furthermore, the performer of *iṣṭāpūrta* did not merely perform that much in this birth; rather, by fetching water with the *godohana* vessel, he also accumulated a new unseen merit (*apūrva*) resulting in cattle.

Thus, for one who has accumulated merit and demerit through the activities of speech, mind, and body day and night—destined to be experienced here or in the hereafter—it is not possible for that which is to be experienced in the world of mortals and so forth to instead be experienced in the world of the Moon.

Furthermore, unless there is a rite of expiation (*prāyaścitta*) or the knowledge of the Self (*ātmajñāna*), the destruction of residual karma (*anuśaya*) whose fruit has not yet been given is impossible, as it would contradict its own inherent result.
Therefore, it is logical that this person, possessing such residual karma, returns because of that *anuśaya*.

Furthermore, the author of the Commentary (Bhāṣyakṛt) will state later that the latent deposit of karma (*karmāśaya*) does not pertain to a single lifetime alone. Others, however, considering the apprehension of a total transformation (*parāvṛtti*) upon the exhaustion of all karma to be groundless, have described the section (*adhikaraṇa*) differently; thus he says: "Some, first of all, say... Here, "residual tendency" (*anuśaya*) refers to the remainder of karma that has already yielded its fruit.

In this regard, the following is investigated here: Do those who have returned [to earth] do so due to the remainder of their *iṣṭāpūrta* (sacrificial and charitable) works whose fruits have already been enjoyed, or do they return here on account of unenjoyed karma after having exhausted those [works] entirely through experience?

On this point, since the *iṣṭāpūrta* works have been eradicated root and branch by experience, it follows that they return as "without remainder" (*niranuśaya*) solely on account of unenjoyed karma; to this, it is replied: they return indeed "with remainder" (*sānuśaya*).
Why? Because it follows from what is observed.

Just as it is observed that when honey or ghee is contained in a vessel, even though the vessel has been washed, the residue of the coating or the remaining honey or ghee cannot be washed away; in accordance with that observation, this too should be understood.

Nor can one who is about to dwell in the lunar disk remain there merely because a remnant remains; just as it is observed that a servant, though attending upon a great king while surrounded by a multitude of elephants, cavalry, and infantry, is no longer fit to serve when, by the power of time, only the royal umbrella and sandals remain— and since worldly tradition is rooted in such observation, it follows from both observation and tradition that those who return do so still possessed of latent dispositions (*sānuśaya*).
He refutes this with the words "And this is not so.
While the particle *eva* ought to have been used, the particle *iva* was employed as a mere sweetener (*guḍajihvikā*).
The meaning is that when an object is accessible solely through verbal testimony (*śabda*), there is no occasion for inference based on general observation (*sāmānyatodṛṣṭa*).
The remainder has its meaning unobscured.
He restates the reason for the prima facie position—that which was said regarding "departure"—and refutes it with the words:
"That too [is explained] by the existence of residual karma (*anuśaya*)."
The meaning is that this contradicts such scriptural passages as "those of pleasant conduct" and "those of foul conduct," which are intended to establish the existence of residual karma (*anuśaya*).
Furthermore, etc.: for in this present life, pleasure and pain are indeed seen to be experienced in alternation.
If, through a single impulse at the time of death, all karmas that have pleasure and pain as their fruits were manifested simultaneously,
then their fruits would be experienced all at once. Therefore, because we observe a succession in experience, one must conclude that the stronger karma overcomes the weaker.
The same should be understood regarding actions that have results consisting of the experience of contradictory types of birth (*jāti*).
Furthermore, it is not possible for an action that has become manifest (*abhivyakta*) not to have yielded its fruit;
for the manifestation of actions consists precisely in their being oriented toward the production of a result.

Furthermore, if the vital breath (*prāṇa*) were the manifestor [of karma], then for beings born in the realms of heaven, hell, or as animals, there would be no production of new karma in that lifetime because they lack the qualification for ritual actions.

Since the residue of previously performed karma would be exhausted through the experience of its fruits— manifested at the time of death (*prāyaṇa*)— they would have no remaining karmic residue and thus would not transmigrate.
Furthermore, they would not be liberated due to the absence of self-knowledge; alas, what a wretched and defiled state!

Moreover, it is only that which inheres in oneself (*svasamaveta*) that is manifested by death, and not that which inheres in another (*parasamaveta*), such that one could be affected by the karma residing in a father or other relative.
The remainder is easy to understand. //8//
"Because of their conduct," if it be argued thus, [the Sūtra] refutes this by stating: "It is for the purpose of indication, so says Kārṣṇājini" (BSBh 3.1.9).
By this, he uncovers and discards the hidden seed of the prima facie argument—that those who descend are indeed devoid of residual karma (*niranuśaya*).
"Though it may be said: 'Absence of anger toward all beings through deed, mind, and speech, as well as benevolence and knowledge—this, the wise know, is moral conduct (śīla).'"

According to this Smṛti, conduct (*śīla*) or behavior (*ācāra*) is distinct from latent disposition (*anuśaya*); nevertheless, the teacher Kārṣṇājini maintained that it serves as an indicator (*upalakṣaṇa*) of the latent disposition by virtue of being an auxiliary to it.

Thus, since the phrases "those of pleasant conduct" (*ramaṇīyacaraṇāḥ*) and "those of foul conduct" (*kapūyacaraṇāḥ*) indicate the latent dispositions, it is established that the descent occurs only for those who possess such latent dispositions. //9//

"If it is argued that [conduct] is purposeless, we say no, because it is dependent on that.

For the Smṛti statement, 'The Vedas do not purify one who is devoid of conduct,' by using the word 'Veda' as an indicator (*upalakṣaṇa*) for the meaning of the Veda, declares that conduct is a subsidiary element (*śeṣa*) to the performance of the Vedic meaning; it does not mean that conduct is independent [of the Veda] with respect to its result."
Therefore, because it assists in the performance of the meaning of the Vedas, there is no pointlessness for conduct that serves the purpose of the sacrifice (*kratvartha*).
By this, it has been stated that conduct, like the *samidh* offerings and so forth, serves the purpose of the sacrifice.

Now, he says—"Even if conduct serves the purpose of the person"—to show that there is no fault even if it serves the purpose of the person (*puruṣārtha*) as a refinement of the person (*puruṣasaṃskāra*), just like bathing and other such acts.
Thus, it has been stated that by the word *caraṇa*, which denotes conduct (*ācāra*), all latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) are indicated. //10//
But Bādari says that the word "conduct" (caraṇa) refers primarily to action itself—namely, good and evil deeds—as follows: "But Bādari [holds] that they are indeed good and evil deeds. (BS 3.1.11)
The principle of the Brahmin and the wandering mendicant (brahmaṇaparivrājaka-nyāya) and the principle of the cow and the bull (gobalīvarda-nyāya). The remainder has its meaning not obscure. //11//

Because it is heard that those of foul conduct go to their own source even if it is non-human,
and because only the two paths of the gods and the fathers are traditionally taught for going and returning, while no other path is mentioned.

Because the statement, "Be born and die—this is the third station," indicates merely the status of being a station and does not suggest it is a path; because even those who have descended from the world of the moon can have that as their station; because, due to the non-completion [of the journey] and the absence of any other path, it is possible for those devoid of enjoyment there to go to the world of the moon for the sake of falling under Yama's control at places such as Saṃyamana—just as one going to a village passes by the roots of trees;
and because the phrase "not by either" is intended to demonstrate the non-completion [of the journey] and does not intend to prohibit both paths.
Since it might be argued that even those who perform undesirable acts (aniṣṭādikārin) reach the world of the moon, it is replied: It is true that what is understood as a "place" cannot be a "path";

If, however, one were to return by that very same path and occupy a station characterized by the continuity of birth and death, this would not constitute a third station.
For those who perform sacrifices and other meritorious deeds, descending from the lunar orb and entering a pleasant or contemptible womb, do not enter a third station.
Why is that?
Because [the soul] descends by way of the path of the ancestors (pitṛyāṇa).
For if even small creatures were to descend by this very same path,
this third station would not be characterized by a continuous succession of birth and death for them.
From this we understand that those who perform undesirable deeds, having entered the realm of Yama and the seven regions of torment under his control, do not descend from the lunar orb.
Therefore, the phrase "whoever they may be" refers specifically to those who perform desirable deeds and is not universal in scope.
Furthermore, the statement "in the fifth oblation" is intended to enjoin its own specific meaning, rather than being intended as a prohibition against any oblation other than the fifth.
Because it would result in a split of the sentence (*vākyabheda*).

And thus, this is indeed a sūtra of the established conclusion (*siddhānta*).
If, however, this is a sūtra presenting the prima facie view (pūrvapakṣa), it must somehow be interpreted by supplying an additional doubt:
"born from a living being" means born from a womb;

START BsVBh_3,1.4.22:
Attainment of similarity [of nature] [is meant], because that is logical.

(BBs_3,1.22) Although identity is not clearly understood from the passage "having returned as it came, [it goes] to space, from space to air," nevertheless, because identity is more clearly understood from such statements as "having become air," the phrase "to space as it came" also [refers to attainment of similarity].
It remains in a state of identity;
nor is it impossible for one thing to become another,

as is evidenced by the traditional accounts of Nandikeśvara’s transformation of his human body into the form of a divine body, and of Nahuṣa’s transformation of his divine body into that of an animal.
Therefore, one should not resort to a figurative application (*gauṇī vṛtti*) by abandoning the primary meaning;
and the term *lakṣaṇā* is employed in the context of figurative application because secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*) is possible within it.
As they say: "The figurative mode of application is indeed desired because of its connection with qualities that are being indicated."
This being the case, we reply: it is the attainment of similarity.

"Sabhāva" refers to those things whose nature (*bhāva*) or form (*rūpa*) is the same; their state is "sābhāvya," which means having the same form or similarity. Why? Because it is logically consistent (*upapatti*).
He explains this very point by way of negative concomitance (*vyatireka*): "For the primary existence of one thing as another is not logically possible.
It is reasonable that the body of a god transforms into the state of a python, because at the time of the god's body, the body of the python is non-existent."
If, however, the body of a god and the body of a python were to exist simultaneously, the body of a god could not be made into the body of a python even by a hundred craftsmen.
For curd and milk cannot be transformed into each other's nature at the same time;
likewise here, because the subtle body and space exist simultaneously, they cannot possess the nature of one another.
The same should be applied to air and the other elements as well.

Thus, their existence [in those elements] is to be explained as metaphorical, based on similarity to them. Now, one might object: "Let mere conjunction with space be indicated by the term 'being space'; what is the use of similarity? To this, he says: "And because of its all-pervasiveness (vibhutva), it is like space. (22)

"Before long, because of the distinction" (BSBh 3.1.5.23). The proponent of the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣin*) maintains that the expression "more difficult to emerge from" (*durniṣprapataram*) denotes an emergence with difficulty, but not a delay.
The established conclusion (rāddhānta) is that, since one cannot experience suffering in the subtle body without the gross body, the phrase "it is more difficult to emerge" indicates a delay. //23//
"In the case of those presided over by others, as before, because of the statement.

It was previously stated that the latent dispositions (*anuśayins*) attain a similarity to space and come into contact with wind, smoke, and so forth; now, it is heard in scripture that they are born as rice, barley, herbs, trees, sesame, and beans.

In this regard, there is a doubt: do the beings with residual karma (*anuśayin*) become stationary entities such as rice and barley as the substratum for their experience, or do they merely undergo contact while these entities are presided over by other conscious subjects (*kṣetrajña*)?

Since in such usages as "a human is born" or "a god is born," the verb *jan* (to be born) is well-known to mean the assumption of a body, here too the word "birth" must be taken in its primary sense as the assumption of a body consisting of rice and so forth.
It is logical that those possessing residual karma (*anuśayin*) are indeed embodied as rice and so forth.

Nor is it correct to argue that, because specific actions are not mentioned— as they are in the cases of "those of pleasant conduct" and "those of foul conduct"— and because rice and the like lack a body in their absence, [the soul] merely comes into contact with them while being presided over by another knower of the field (*kṣetrajña*).

It is not correct to argue that because the performers of sacrifices (iṣṭādikārins) are mentioned in connection with their sacrificial rites, and because those rites— such as the *iṣṭi*— are tainted by the fault of violence (*hiṃsā*) and thus have blameworthy results, it follows that after the enjoyment of the lunar world, there must also be the result of suffering in the form of a stationary body;
nor is it right to claim that the general rule "one should not harm any living beings" is sublated by the specific rule concerning the killing of the animal for Agni-Soma,

on the grounds that the general rule is weaker because it applies to the particular case only through the mediation of the general category of violence, and thus its application is delayed compared to the specific rule which directly touches upon the particular act and operates more swiftly.
For it is not the case that the strong necessarily sublates the weak; rather, this occurs only when there is a contradiction.
And here there is no contradiction, because they operate within different spheres of application.

For the injunction "One should sacrifice an animal dedicated to Agni-Soma," recited within the context of a ritual (*kratu-prakaraṇa*), establishes its purpose for the ritual; it does not, however, remove the fact that it is a cause of harm to the person, which is brought about by the prohibition.
Therefore, let there be its status as a cause of harm to the person due to the prohibition, and its status as being for the sake of the ritual due to the injunction—what contradiction is there?
As they say: "If someone, while standing in the midst of a ritual, were to eat *kalañja* and other such forbidden foods..."
"There is no deficiency in the ritual there, because it is accomplished exactly as prescribed.

Therefore, since the term "birth" (janman) is used in its primary sense, it follows that those with residual karma (anuśayin) are born with bodies consisting of rice and other grains; this being the prima facie view, the following is stated:

This would indeed be so if a specific karma of those possessing residual karma were mentioned in relation to rice and the like, as is done in the cases of "those of pleasant conduct" and "those of foul conduct," but such is not the case here.
It is not possible for an action such as ritual effort (*iṣṭādi*) to be the cause that produces the fruit of suffering to be experienced by the body of a stationary being (*sthāvara*),
because such an action is of the nature of merit (*dharma*) and thus has pleasure alone as its cause.

Nor is it possible for the injury to animals involved in that [ritual]— even though it is for the sake of the sacrifice— to result in the fruit of suffering, because of the prohibition "one shall not injure" (*na hiṃsyāt*).

[The prohibition] "one should not harm" is indeed for the sake of human purpose (*puruṣārtha*). For instance, since the determination of a prohibition such as "one should not harm" is dependent upon that which is prohibited, the prohibition is understood to be for the very same purpose as that which is prohibited. Furthermore, this [prohibition] is not recited within the context (*prakaraṇa*) of any specific ritual—unlike [the rules] "one should not speak untruth" or "one does not perform those two on the sacrificial animal"—by virtue of which the prohibition of speaking untruth might be for the sake of the sacrifice (*kratvartha*); rather, the prohibition itself...
It would be for the sake of the sacrifice (*kratvartha*).
Since the two *ājyabhāga* offerings are prohibited in the animal sacrifice (*paśu*), the prohibition itself must also be for the sake of the sacrifice.

For if this were the case, it would be understood that the sacrificial benefit (*kratūpakāra*) accomplished by the *ājyabhāga* offerings is still achieved through other auxiliary elements (*aṅga*), even though they are devoid of the *ājyabhāga* offerings.

Therefore, because there is a contradiction with the injunctive suffix regarding the human activity— constrained by an injunction and expressed by the rule "one should not harm" (*na hiṃsyāt*) which is taught as an independent statement (*anārabhyādhīta*)— the state of being the result (*bhāvya*) must remain as a human goal alone, by abandoning the state of being the result consisting of the act of harming (the meaning of the verbal root) which is the object of the injunction.
This is because the person, even though not explicitly denoted by the verb ending (*ākhyāta*), is presented through the medium of the expression of the agent's activity.

Since that [killing] is obtained solely through passion (*rāga*), the injunction approaches the meaning of the negative particle by way of restating it; thus, the human goal (*puruṣārtha*) is what is to be prohibited, and since its determination is dependent upon that [human goal], the prohibition itself also becomes a human goal.
Consequently, this is the resulting meaning: "One should not perform that killing which is a human goal."
Furthermore, even if injury were prohibited for the sake of the ritual (*kratvartha*), its status as a contributor to the ritual would still have to be assumed.
However, when the visible benefit to the person (*puruṣārtha*) stands as an opposing factor, there is no basis for such an assumption.

Moreover, independence and dependence cannot coexist in a single instance through the principle of "separateness of connection" (*saṃyogapṛthaktva*), as is the case with the use of *khadira* wood and other such examples.

Therefore, since the prohibition of human effort does not extend even to that which is for the sake of the sacrifice, sacrifices such as the *iṣṭi* have only pure happiness as their fruit, and do not have suffering experienced in a stationary body as their fruit;
for, as in the case of [the descent into] space and so forth, this occurs through mere verbal expression without the operation of karma.
For those possessing residual karma (*anuśayin*), there is merely a conjunction with rice and other grains, but not the state of being a body.
This very point is indicated by the statement regarding general rules (*utsarga*) and exceptions (*apavāda*).
Furthermore, it concerns the primary case of those possessing latent dispositions (*anuśayin*) being born as rice and so forth;

for it is heard in scripture that those possessing latent dispositions, having attained the state of rice and so forth, are consumed by persons and subsequently experience the state of being seed-sprinklers (*retaḥ-sic*).
This [process] is not possible for those possessing residual karma (*anuśayin*) when they have rice and other grains as their bodies.

For if rice and other grains were their bodies, then when the rice is cut and threshed, and when it is husked, the bodies of the rice would perish; consequently, those possessing residual karma would depart [from them].

How then could there be the state of being a "seeder" (*retaḥsigbhāva*) for those possessing residual karma? However, in the case of mere contact, when the rice and other grains—which are the objects of contact—[perish], [the souls do not perish].

Even when [the ancestors] have perished, those who are associated with them and possess latent dispositions (anuśayin) do not depart [from the sacrifice]; thus, the status of being the "procreator" (retaḥsigbhāva) is established.
The rest has been explained. //24//
If it is argued that [the world] is impure, we say no, because of the Word (Śabda). 3.1.25.25.

Now, regarding the connection with the seed-sower (retas-sig-yoga):
for a child who is born immediately does not become a seed-sower; rather, it is one who has been born for a long time and has reached full maturity [who becomes so]. BBs_3,1.26.
Therefore, it is understood that this too is merely a conjunction. //26//

Now, does this mean that in all cases there is merely contact with those possessing latent dispositions (*anuśaya*), such that a similar state would result even in the case of those "of pleasant conduct" (*ramaṇīyacaraṇa*) and so forth? No, he says:
