START BsVBh_3.2.1.1:
"In the intermediate state there is creation, for so [the scripture] says.

Now, however, the different states of that very *jīva* are being elaborated in order to establish its self-luminosity—namely, whether the creation in dream is as real as in the waking state, or whether it consists of illusion (*māyā*).

Although both creations occurring in the states of waking and dreaming are illusory in nature because nothing other than Brahman can be described as real, there remains the point of inquiry: just as the waking creation persists until the direct realization of one's identity with Brahman and ceases upon that realization, does the dream creation likewise persist, or does it cease every single day? This is the purpose of the investigation.
It pertains to the two states of being in this world and the next world. It is "intermediate" (*saṃdhya*) because it exists at the junction (*saṃdhi*).

It is not of this world, because the direct perception of forms and so forth arises without the operation of the eyes and other faculties belonging to this world; nor is it of the next world, because the operation of the sense faculties and so forth belonging to the next world has not yet arisen, being something that will occur in the future.
Furthermore, it is not the case that there is no direct perception of forms and so forth for one who sees a dream;
therefore, because this state lies between the two worlds, the creation must indeed be real in form prior to the direct realization of the nature of Brahman as the Self.
This is the intended meaning: here, all false cognitions are cited as examples, yet their reality is asserted.
However, dream-cognition has been cited here for its relevance to the present topic.
It is logical that an object which a cognition makes known exists exactly as it is presented,
because its existence in that manner has ascended into the cognition.

If it is argued that because non-reality (*atathātva*) is not perceived, its status as an object of cognition (*prameya*)—insofar as it contradicts reality—is merely a basis for conceptual construction, and therefore non-reality follows from a subverting cognition (*bādhaka-pratyaya*); we say no, because the subverting nature of such a cognition is unestablished.
For two cognitions are contradictory only when they bring forward opposing objects within the same cognitive domain.
Furthermore, the relationship of the sublated and the sublator is established through the determination of relative strength and weakness;
however, there is no identity of object here, since the arrangement is justified by the difference in time.
For just as milk, when seen, becomes curd after some time, so too silver, when seen, might become mother-of-pearl after some time;
or else, that object would possess various forms.
If one's eye is affected by exhaustion from intense heat, it perceives that object as having the form of silver; however, if one's eye is assisted by mere light alone,
it perceives that very same object as having the form of mother-of-pearl.
In this way, even a blue-lotus flower, when manifested by the sun's rays during the day, is perceived as blue;
but when manifested by the light of a lamp at night, it is perceived as red.

Similarly, one does not perceive existing objects such as chariots while awake, yet one perceives them while asleep; thus, there is no contradiction because of the difference in causal conditions (*sāmagrī*) or the difference in time.
Nor can there be a determination of the relative strength or weakness of the preceding and succeeding [texts],
because both are equal in their operation within their own respective domains, and thus there is no reason for a decisive preference.
Therefore, for this reason as well, non-contradiction must necessarily be established.
Thus, this is established: the conditions under dispute are correct.
Because it is a cognition, like the cognition of a pillar and so forth during the waking state;
the Śruti also demonstrates this point: "Then he creates chariots, horses for the chariots, and paths."

Nor should the scriptural statement "There are no chariots there, no draft animals, no paths" be interpreted as having a figurative meaning due to contradiction with the statement "He creates. For the statement "He creates" is more authoritative because it is corroborated by many other scriptural passages and by other means of valid cognition; thus, the statement "There are no chariots there" must be explained as being figurative, meaning that chariots suitable for perception in the waking state do not exist there, but it does not mean that chariots do not exist at all.
For this very reason, the scriptural mention of an agent from another recension has been cited;
and because its creation has the Wise One (prājña) as its agent, it possesses ultimate reality, just like the creation of ether and the other elements.
Nor is it correct to argue that because the individual soul (jīva) is the agent, it does not have the Wise One as its agent.

Because it is the Wise One (prājña) who is the subject under discussion in the phrase "other than dharma and other than adharma"; and because even if the individual soul (jīva) were the agent, the soul is essentially the Wise One due to its non-difference from Him;
furthermore, some dream-cognitions are observed to correspond with waking cognitions.

For example, in a dream, a Brahmin youth wearing white garments, adorned with white garlands and unguents, says to Priyavrata: "Priyavrata, on the fifth day at dawn, a king will honor you by granting you land consisting mostly of fertile soil. While awake, having experienced that honor for himself, he considers the dream-cognition to be true.
Therefore, the creation during the intermediate state (saṃdhyā) is ultimately real. //1//
And some [maintain that the self] is the creator of sons and so forth. (3.2.2)
When this [objection] has been raised, it is said:
"But it is mere illusion, because its true nature is not manifested in its entirety. (BSBh 3.2.3)
This is the intended meaning here:
first of all, it is not possible for mother-of-pearl to be a transformation (*pariṇāma*) of silver, in the same way that curd is a transformation of milk;
for even silver vessels that have remained for a long time in the house of a lord are never seen to undergo the state of being mother-of-pearl.
It is not the case that at the time of another person’s experience of silver, someone else with unimpaired senses does not experience and recognize its state as mother-of-pearl;
nor is it that the object possesses both forms.
Rather, due to the difference in causal complexes (*sāmagrī*), at one time its state as water is experienced by this person, and at another time its state as rays of light. This is the correct view.

For if its nature as water were ultimate, it would perform the causal function (arthakriyā) to be accomplished by it—namely, the cessation of thirst—even though that [function] is actually accomplished by a mirage, which is characterized by the manifestation of form.
Yet, no one’s thirst-born parching is ever quenched by mirages.
Nor is it logical to claim that water itself is of two kinds: that which quells parching and that which does not.
The nature of water (*toyatva*) is pervaded by the capacity for that [specific] causal efficiency; therefore, if it did not perform even a fraction of that [efficiency], it would not be water at all.
Furthermore, its twofold nature is accepted in order to account for the validity of the cognition "this is water"; yet even if such an acceptance were made, it could not be established.

For instance, one who considers this water to be included within the category of the "inefficacious" would not, even out of thirst, run toward the water of a mirage, just as one does when perceiving the mirage-rays themselves.
Now, [the opponent] runs toward [the object], imagining it to be capable [of producing cognition].
But what offense has been committed by the universal human error of perceiving water in mirages, such that this error is bypassed and another distinct error is postulated?

Furthermore, the cognitions of water and mirage do not involve a simultaneous apprehension—as in the case of the notions of milk and curd, or of a teacher, a maternal uncle, and a Brahmin—since, according to one's own experience, these two mutually contradictory cognitions manifest in the relationship of the sublated and the sublator (*bādhyabādhakabhāva*).

In that case as well, the prior cognition of silver is the sublated (bādhyam), while the subsequent cognition of mother-of-pearl is the sublator (bādhakam), because negation is preceded by attainment. Since there was no means of attainment prior to the cognition of silver, it is impossible to negate the mother-of-pearl when it has not been attained; however, the cognition of mother-of-pearl is able to sublate the silver that was attained by the prior cognition. And this nature of sublation is determined from one's own experience.
As they have said: "Because it is yet to come, the later [cognition] arises without subverting the earlier;
however, the earlier [cognition], in turn, never arises without having subverted the later.

Furthermore, a cognition manifesting present silver is not subverted by a subsequent cognition that takes as its object the mother-of-pearl existing at its own time, because the former does not take the future state of that [mother-of-pearl] as its object.

It is logical [to say] that there is no contradiction because of the difference in time. Let it be that perception does not know its future state; however, the inference following upon it perceives stability—just as it perceives the cause of a functional relationship—in the absence of the occurrence of a cognition of destruction. In the absence of the occurrence of a cognition of destruction, one thinks: "This silver is stable, because it possesses the nature of silver (rajatatva), like silver previously experienced and now recognized."
And thus, a perception whose object is silver would, in reality, have as its object a silver that is indeed stable;

and consequently, it would pervade the silver even at the time of the future cognition of the mother-of-pearl. Therefore, due to this contradiction, the [erroneous] cognition is sublated by the cognition of the mother-of-pearl.
As they have said: "For silver, when being perceived, is perceived as enduring;
it pervades the future time of the cognition of the mother-of-pearl, and therefore it is so."
Thus,
some explain that it is apprehended by direct perception as being long-lasting;
that is incorrect.
If fitness (*yogyatā*) consists in lasting for a long time, it is not within the range of perception, because power (*śakti*) is supersensible (*atīndriya*).
If, on the other hand, it consists in pervading another time, that too is untenable.
Because there can be no conjunction with a sense faculty that will exist at a later time, and because the all-pervasiveness delimited by that [faculty] is beyond the senses;

furthermore, unlike in the case of the cognition of recognition (*pratyabhijñā*), there is no mental impression (*saṃskāra*) acting as a cooperative factor here by which one could perceive what is not currently present.

Therefore, it should be understood that due to the force of extreme habituation, immediately after perception, the object is grasped as "long-lasting" through a perception that arises even more rapidly than the preceding one, accompanied by an inference in its state of perishing.
For this very reason, not discerning this extremely subtle temporal interval, the Buddhists (Saugatas) have said:
"The object of perception is twofold: the apprehended (*grāhya*) and the determined (*adhyavaseya*).
The apprehended is a single moment, the particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*); and [the determined is] the [conceptualized object]."
Regarding the term "continuum" (*saṃtāna*):
by this, the dream-cognition is explained as being false.
As for that which was stated to be a true dream-vision, even there, because there is no correspondence with what was related by the Brahmin narrator, it is likewise false.

The conversation reported by Priyavrata is merely a coincidence, like "the crow and the palm fruit" (kākatālīya); it cannot serve as a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) for dream-cognition, because such [cognitions] are frequently seen to be inconsistent.
And this inconsistency has been demonstrated by the author of the Bhāṣya while explaining that [dreams] lack complete manifestation.
Regarding the phrase "asleep at night": for even during the time of night, there is daylight in other regions such as Ketumāla and others; therefore, it is specified as "in the land of Bhārata. //3//
For it is indicated by scripture, and those who know it declare so;
that perception is indicative, and it exists in its own essential nature.
The visible object is unreal; for this very reason, the emission of the final element and so forth, which are to be accomplished by the nature of seeing a woman, persist during the waking state,
whereas those things accomplished by a woman such as garlands, ointments, and tooth-marks do not persist.

The meaning is that the inference of ultimate reality based on the fact that it is the activity of the wise—even if one were to claim "it is not even in our dreams the activity of the wise"—is contradicted by the subverting cognition of direct perception and thus fails to establish itself.
Thus, there is a third sovereignty intermediate between bondage and liberation. //4//
"But it is concealed by the meditation on another; for from that come its bondage and the opposite [liberation];
or else, because of its connection with the body, that [concealment] also occurs"—these two sūtras have been explained by us in the first sūtra.
And the commentary on these two has been explained by the word-for-word gloss (nigada). //5//
Or rather, that [cognition] also [arises] from connection with the body. (3.2.6)
The absence [of that state] occurs in the channels, in the heart, and in the Self, because of scriptural statements to that effect.
For here, the channels, the pericardium, and the Supreme Self are heard in scripture as the locations for the individual soul during the state of deep sleep.
In this regard, is there an optionality among these points or is there a combination?
What follows from this being so? This is what follows:

When the channels (*nāḍyaḥ*) or the pericardium (*purītat*) are the locus of deep sleep, then, even though erroneous apprehension has ceased, the individual soul (*jīva*) does not attain the state of the Supreme Self (*paramātman*).

Even upon the cessation of ignorance (*avidyā*), another cause must be required for the soul to attain the state of the Supreme Self; and that [cause] is indeed karma, and not the knowledge of reality (*tattvajñāna*), because the latter is useful only for the mere cessation of erroneous cognition, and since the cessation of erroneous cognition is possible even in deep sleep without the knowledge of reality.
Consequently, liberation is attained through action alone, not through knowledge.
As they say: "Janaka and others attained perfection through action alone.

However, since the Supreme Self itself is the locus of deep sleep by way of the channels (*nāḍīs*) and the pericardium (*purītat*), there is a partial utility for the state of the Supreme Self in the cessation of contrary knowledge.
For by that [ignorance], this living being remains in that very state;

however, because true knowledge is absent, and since ignorance has not been eradicated down to its very root, there occurs for the living being an emergence characterized by the states of waking and dreaming.
Therefore, this inquiry is purposeful.
What, then, has not been established?
It is the alternative regarding the locus of the soul in deep sleep among the three places—the channels (nāḍīs), the pericardium (purītat), and the Supreme Self (paramātman).
Just as a single king might sometimes hide in one palace and sometimes in another, so too the single soul sometimes resides in the channels, sometimes in the pericardium, and sometimes in Brahman.

Just as rice and barley, being heard in scripture as the material causes for the sacrificial cake (*puroḍāśa*) which serves as a means for the sacrifice, are optional alternatives because they serve a single purpose while being independent of one another;

so too, the channels (*nāḍyaḥ*) and other elements, which—by virtue of the locative case-ending or the term "abode" (*āyatana*)—serve the single purpose of being a resting place and are independent of each other, deserve to be treated as optional alternatives.

Even where there is a scriptural mention of their combination, such as in the passage, "Having descended by way of the channels, he rests in the pericardium (*purītat*)," or "Likewise, it happens in them when, being asleep, he does not see any dream," [the status of optionality remains].
Now, in the passage, "Then he becomes one with this very breath," there is the scriptural hearing of a combination of the two substrates, the channels and Brahman.
Furthermore, the word "breath" (prāṇa) refers to Brahman—as in, "Then in this breath, which is Brahman, that individual soul becomes one"—and thus they are not independent substrates.
However, this much is the distinction.
Sometimes the channels (nāḍīs) alone are the support; sometimes, for one moving through the channels, the heart (purītad) alone is the support;

and thus it is established that for one moving by means of those very channels, the Supreme Self (brahman) alone is sometimes the support. Consequently, regarding their status as supports, there is no mutual dependence among the channels, the heart, and the Supreme Self.
Thus, it follows that there is an option (vikalpa), like that between rice and barley, or like that between the Bṛhat and Rathantara chants. This is the position reached.

To this it is replied: the individual soul (jīva) approaches these [factors]—the channels (nāḍīs) and so forth—for the purpose of sleep by way of conjunction alone, not by way of option. This is the intended meaning: the contingency of things that are prescribed as if they were permanent is postulated only in the absence of any other alternative.
As they have said: "Thus, although there are eight defects in the case of the two scriptural injunctions regarding rice and barley..."
"Resorting to conceptual construction (*vikalpa*), no other course is found there.

For rice (*vrīhi*) and barley (*yava*) are prescribed as mutually independent alternatives, serving as the material source for the sacrificial cake (*puroḍāśa*) which is the means to the ritual at hand; and each of these is capable of producing the sacrificial cake on its own.
In that case, if the sacrificial cake were produced from a mixture of both, both scriptural injunctions—which prescribe rice and barley as being independent of one another—would be sublated.

Nor can this injunctive statement (prayogavacana) combine these two; for, proceeding as it does by taking into account the subsidiary elements (aṅga) exactly as they have been prescribed, it cannot alter them,
and their alteration would occur if there were a mixing [of the two].
Furthermore, it is not logical to repeat the principal act merely for the sake of the subsidiaries, as in the case of the Gosava sacrifice where one performs both [pressings].
For here, the repetition of the principal is not explicitly heard in the scripture; and to perform it for the sake of the subsidiaries would be improper.
Nor is it correct to argue that, just as the principal Soma sacrifice is repeated in accordance with the subsidiary cups dedicated to Indra-Vāyu and others, so too should it be here.

For in the injunction "one should sacrifice with soma" (*somena yajeta*), there is the prescription of a previously unknown sacrifice (*apūrva-yāga*). In that context, based on the consideration of other passages such as "he presses the soma" (*somam abhiṣuṇoti*) and "he pours out the soma" (*somam abhiplāvayati*), it follows that the substance of ten handfuls of soma— which serves as the means for the sacrifice by way of its juice— is to be separately prepared through individual portions taken in vessels one span high, dedicated to Indra-Vāyu and other deities.
The preparatory acts (saṃskāra) are enjoined,
but the deities such as Indra-Vāyu and others are not enjoined with reference to the Soma sacrifice;
for if they were, there would be an option (vikalpa) among them based on their having a single purpose, namely the accomplishment of the sacrifice.

Moreover, a single upright vessel measuring only one span is not sufficient for the purpose of holding ten handfuls of Soma juice; therefore, the vessels cannot be treated as optional alternatives on the grounds of having an identical purpose.
Nor is it reasonable to hold only as much as a single upright vessel can contain and discard the remainder.
For it would follow that the act of gathering ten handfuls of material would have no visible purpose;
this [act] would only have a visible purpose if all of that were employed in the sacrifice.
And when a visible purpose is possible, it is not logical to postulate an invisible one.

Therefore, since the entire Soma juice is fit for consecration as being subsidiary to the sacrifice, and since it is impossible to consecrate the whole by means of a single drawing (*grahaṇa*), when one part of it is consecrated by one [drawing], another part must be consecrated by a subsequent drawing; thus, due to the difference in the purpose (*kāryabheda*), the drawings should be combined (*samuccīyeran*).
For this very reason, there is the observation of their combination in the text: "The Adhvaryu draws ten cups at the morning pressing.
And when there is combination, a sequence is also possible, as in:
"The cup for the Aśvins is drawn tenth, but it is offered third."
Likewise, there is the injunction: "He draws the cups beginning with those for Indra and Vāyu.

Since these are to be combined, it follows by implication that as much as has been drawn for a particular purpose must be offered to that specific deity; thus, the sacrifice would have to be repeated.
However, if they were to offer them all together—having set them aside separately but then uniting them—intending them for a single deity, [the injunction would be violated].
Furthermore, the acts of separation and the designations of deities would become purposeless (adṛṣṭārtha).
And it has been stated that when a visible purpose is possible, it is not logical to assume an invisible one.
Therefore, since combination is inevitable in that case, the repetition of the primary act is undertaken even for the sake of following the subordinate elements (guṇa).

In this case, however, since there is no authoritative basis for assuming repetition (*abhyāsa*), and since any material substance whatsoever could have been prescribed as the substrate for the sacrificial cake (*puroḍāśa*) without restriction, the individual scriptural mentions of rice (*vrīhi*) and barley (*yava*)—each being independent of the other—serve as restrictive rules for a single purpose and thus admit of an option (*vikalpa*).

But this is not possible for the channels (*nāḍī*), the pericardium (*purītat*), and the Supreme Self (*paramātman*), which are mutually independent; for there is no possibility of them serving a single common purpose (as a place of rest) such that an option would arise.

The fact that multiple items are expressed with a single case-ending does not necessarily imply they have a single referent, for we observe the use of a single case-ending even for things that are conjoined,
as in "he sleeps on a couch" and "he sleeps in a palace.
Therefore, since the use of a single case-ending is inconclusive, some other determining factor must be stated.
And this has been stated by the author of the Bhāṣya: "Even where the scripture speaks of the channels as if they were independent, as the place of sleep," and so forth.
The meaning is that a scriptural passage which appears independent must be interpreted in accordance with a scriptural passage that shows dependence.
The rest is clear in its meaning.

Now, one might object: "If Brahman alone is the place of dissolution, let that much alone be stated; what is the use of introducing the channels (nāḍīs)? To this, he says: "Moreover, and here" (*apicātra*). The word "moreover" (*api ca*) is used in the sense of conjunction (*samuccaya*), not as an alternative (*vikalpa*).
The meaning is this: the previous account of the channels, accompanied by this present one, establishes the point;
thus, the mention of the channels here is for the purpose of praising those channels which are useful for the instruction of the path.

Since one whose organs are pervaded by bile does not perceive external objects, there is praise of the channels by way of the absence of pleasure and pain through that [bile], resulting in the absence of contact with the evil (*pāpman*) that causes them.
But when light is Brahman, then it is easily understood.
Furthermore, the channels (nāḍīs) and the pericardium (purītat) are merely the support for the limiting adjuncts (upādhi) of the individual soul (jīva).
This is the meaning: this was stated while provisionally accepting that the soul is something to be contained (ādheya).

From the perspective of ultimate reality (*paramārtha*), however, the individual soul (*jīva*) does not possess the quality of being something to be supported. For instance, neither the channels (*nāḍyaḥ*) nor the heart (*purītat*) are the locus of the soul’s limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*)—the organs; rather, because the soul is non-different from Brahman, it is established in its own majesty.
Furthermore, Brahman is not the support of the soul, because of their identity (*tādātmya*).
However, the alternative (vikalpa) mentioned refers to the fact that, from the perspective of the individual soul (jīva), Brahman is said to be its substratum (ādhāratva) by way of distinction.

Thus, in the state of deep sleep (suṣupti), because the limiting adjuncts (upādhi) do not manifest, the soul’s very identity with Brahman constitutes its being "supported by Brahman," rather than its being supported by the channels (nāḍī) or the heart (purītat).

On the other hand, the soul's support in the channels and the heart occurs only as the locus for its adjuncts in order to initiate the state of deep sleep. Since these two refer to different matters, they do not constitute an option (vikalpa).

Furthermore, the phrase "never [is it] of the individual soul" means that the essential nature of Brahman belonging to the individual soul— which is the general rule— cannot be altered during the state of deep sleep, provided there is no exception in the form of the waking or dreaming states.
Moreover, even those who maintain that there is an option regarding the location [of the soul] must admit that the state of deep sleep is characterized by the cessation of specific cognition.
And this [state] is not possible in places such as the channels (*nāḍī*), which are distinct from the Supreme Self, without identity with the Self;
for while situated there, this individual soul (*jīva*), maintaining the conceit of being separate from the Self, would necessarily possess specific (limited) knowledge.
Thus says the Śruti: "Or where there is, as it were, another, there one might see another."

But there is no fault if [the soul] has the Self as its locus, according to the Śruti: "But when for him everything has become the Self alone, then by what and whom should he see, and by what should he know?

Therefore, for this reason also, he states that the channels and so forth are not the door to the state of having the Self as one's locus: "Moreover, even if one accepts the alternative of different loci..."
Here he raises an objection: "But even for that which has difference as its object.
"Difference" (*bheda*) means that which is differentiated;
the meaning is "even for an object that is being differentiated."
He refutes this, saying: "Certainly, it would be so.
First of all, the individual soul (jīva) has no inherent limitation (*pariccheda*), because it is omnipresent (*vibhu*) by virtue of being identical with Brahman.
However, regarding limitation based on adjuncts (*aupādhika*), it would know only that which is in proximity to its adjunct, but not everything.
For it is not the case that because of the non-proximity of Mount Sumeru, Devadatta, being ignorant of it, fails to perceive it even when it is near him.

Therefore, in order to establish deep sleep as the state wherein all specific cognitions have ceased, one must declare that at that time there is a withdrawal of all limiting adjuncts (upādhi) for this [self].
And thus, its identity with Brahman as its Self is established; such is the meaning.

By stating that there is a combination [of the two paths] through the relation of subordinate and principal, and not as equals like the Āgneya and other sacrifices, he also rejects the possibility of an option (*vikalpa*), saying: "Nor do we here...

It is not proper for even a single syllable of the mass of the Veda—which has been established as serving the human goal by the injunction for the study of one's own recitation (*svādhyāyādhyayana-vidhi*)—to be something that does not serve the human goal.

Furthermore, there is no purpose in establishing that in the state of deep sleep the individual soul (*jīva*) resides in the channels (*nāḍī*) and so forth by its own nature; however, there is a purpose in establishing its becoming Brahman (*brahmabhūya*).
Therefore, the intention is that there is neither a combination (*samuccaya*) by way of equal primacy, nor an option (*vikalpa*).
The rest is of explicit meaning (*nītārtha*). //7//
Therefore, awakening arises from this. (3.2.8)
"But it is that very [Self] indeed, on account of the recollection of actions, of words, and of injunctions" (BS 3.2.9).

Although the individual soul (*jīva*) is non-different from the Lord (*īśvara*), this new section is commenced with the intention of describing their difference as delimited by limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*).
"That it is he" is difficult to establish.
The phrase "whether it is he or another" is introduced merely as a possibility, referring to God;
for in one whose nature is pure and liberated, there is no possibility of arising from ignorance.
For this very reason,
it is not introduced at the occasion of the *vimarśa* (reflective deliberation).

For when it must be stated that there is a memory of an action enjoined for one person— which is to be accomplished over two days or more— having been performed on the previous day, the prefix *anu-* serves to indicate recognition (*pratyabhijñāna*).
For this very reason it is said, "I am that," and further, "he runs back according to the rule and according to the womb. *Āya* means going; *nyāya* is a fixed course of movement.

The individual soul (*jīva*), according to its own rule, returns to its source (*pratiyoni*) from the state of deep sleep (*suṣuptāvasthā*)—the state of supreme tranquility (*saṃprasāda*)—to the waking state (*buddhānta*). For one who was a tiger in his previous birth and returns from deep sleep to the waking state becomes a tiger again, not another species.
This is what has been stated: "These [beings] here are either tigers or lions," and so forth.
Now, regarding the statement "he who has slept there shall arise":
the individual soul (*jīva*) that has slept arises in another body; however, one who has gone to another body arises in the body belonging to the sleeping soul.
Therefore, the meaning is that there is no cessation of worldly activity in another body.
Furthermore, there is no such thing as a "living soul" (jīva) that is distinct from the Supreme;
just as what is called the "space within a jar" is not different from the supreme space,
yet it appears as if distinct and persists only so long as the jar exists.
Nor is that [distinction] difficult to discern, because its limiting adjunct, the jar, is distinct [from the ether].

Likewise, the individual soul (jīva), which is fashioned by the distinction of the limiting adjunct consisting of the beginningless and indefinable ignorance (avidyā), does not in reality differ from the Supreme Self (paramātman); yet, through the emergence and submergence of its own limiting adjuncts, it appears as if emerged and as if submerged.
Consequently, even during states such as deep sleep, [the Self] appears as if suppressed, whereas in states such as waking it appears as if manifest.

Since its adjuncts—ignorance and its latent impressions—are beginningless and flow in the form of cause and effect, they are easily distinguished; thus, the individual soul (jīva) conditioned by them is also easily distinguished. //9//
In the state of fainting (mugdha), there is a partial attainment [of death], because of what remains.

(BS 3.2.10) Fainting is distinguished from the states of waking and dreaming due to the absence of specific cognition, and it is distinguished from the state of death because of the subsequent revival.

Therefore, deep sleep (*suṣupti*) itself is fainting (*mūrchā*), because there is no difference in the absence of specific cognition. However, long intervals between breaths, tremors, and so forth, are merely internal subdivisions of deep sleep.
For example, someone who has risen from sleep says: "I slept happily; my limbs are light and my mind is serene."
Furthermore, someone might say, "I slept uncomfortably; my limbs are heavy and my mind wanders without stability.
Yet, deep sleep (*suṣupti*) is not differentiated by this much.
Likewise, even in other states of transformation, fainting (*mūrchā*) is not differentiated from deep sleep.
Therefore, since this state is not established by worldly consensus, it follows that it is not the fifth stage. To this objection, it is replied:
although there is a similarity between delusion (*moha*) and deep sleep (*suṣupti*) due to the cessation of specific cognitions, nevertheless, they are not identical.
The non-distinction between dreaming and waking does not follow merely from the similarity in the existence of specific cognitions;

rather, they are distinct due to the presence or absence of the activity of the external senses. Furthermore, deep sleep (*suṣupti*) and delusion (*moha*) are also distinct, owing to differences in their purposes, their causes, and their defining characteristics. For deep sleep is a merging with Brahman for the purpose of dispelling fatigue.
However, the union with Brahman for the purpose of abandoning the body is delusion (*moha*).
Even though death does not occur when delusion is present, it likewise does not occur when delusion is absent; thus, delusion is for the sake of death.

This is because delusion has causes such as the striking of a club, whereas deep sleep (*suṣupti*) has causes such as fatigue, and because delusion is characterized by distortions of the face, eyes, and so forth.

Furthermore, although there is an internal difference between deep sleep (*suṣupta*) and non-sleep due to differences in characteristics such as the clarity of the face, they are one because of the identity of their cause, purpose, and characteristics.

Therefore, even though there is a merging with Brahman in both the states of deep sleep and delusion (*moha*), the merging in delusion is not the same as the merging in deep sleep; thus, "half-merging" is stated.
This "half-nature" arises from the combination of similarity and dissimilarity.
If this is not a distinct state, then because of their difference, another effort must be undertaken for their dissolution;
however, if there is non-difference, no further effort is required—this is the purpose of the inquiry. //10//
START BsVBh_3.2.5.11:
"Not even from the standpoint of place does the Supreme possess both characteristics, for everywhere [it is so].
(BBs_3.2.11) He states the intermediate connection: "by which Brahman [the soul exists] in deep sleep and so forth."

Although it was established in the sūtra "Non-difference from that [Brahman], on account of words such as 'originating' (Ārambhaṇa-śabdādibhyaḥ)" that Brahman is indeed devoid of phenomenal expansion (niṣprapañca), nevertheless, because many Vedic passages containing indications of phenomenal expansion (prapañca) are observed, doubt arises once again; therefore, this inquiry is commenced to remove that doubt.
Furthermore, since the knowledge of its true nature is useful for liberation (apavarga), this investigation possesses a purpose.
In that regard, because both characteristics are heard [in scripture], it follows that Brahman possesses a dual nature.

Even so, since there is a contradiction between having attributes (*saviśeṣatva*) and being without attributes (*nirviśeṣatva*), and since it is impossible for both to be innate, one must be intrinsic while the other is extrinsic.
Furthermore, that which is extrinsic is not ultimately real (*apāramārthika*).

For it is not the case that the lack of validity (aprāmāṇya) in the eyes and other senses—which are intrinsically valid—is non-ultimate, because that would entail the non-arising of the effect characterized by erroneous cognition. Therefore, since the scripture possesses both types of marks, it follows that the dual nature of Brahman is ultimate; to this, it is replied: "Not even by way of location or limiting adjuncts (upādhi) is there any possibility of the supreme Brahman possessing both characteristics."
For one [nature] is indeed ultimate, while the other is superimposed.
For if it were ultimate, there would be a transformation of Brahman into a form produced by limiting conditions (upādhi),
and that has already been refuted.

By the principle of elimination (*pāriśeṣya*), we see that—just as redness in a crystal, which is by nature transparent and white, is adventitious (*aupādhika*) due to the proximity of lac-dye—the qualities such as "having all fragrances" are superimposed upon Brahman; for the purpose of the Śruti texts is to establish its being devoid of distinctions (*nirviśeṣatā*).

Even regarding the existence of distinctions, passages such as "And that which is in this earth, consisting of light," etc., are intent on establishing the oneness of Brahman; and since unity and multiplicity cannot coexist in a single entity, [these descriptions of distinction] serve only as subordinate elements to that oneness.

Because the purpose culminates in establishing difference, and since difference is merely restated as being established by other means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), while unity—being previously unestablished—is fit to be the object of injunction; and because non-difference is directly established by numerous scriptural passages through the censure of the perception of difference; and because certain scriptural texts concerning Brahman as possessing form are understood to have meditation (*upāsana*) as their purport, even though this is perceived from statements intended for another purpose, provided there is no sublation.
Just as the deities possess embodied forms,
there exist here hundreds of scriptural passages (*śruti*) whose purpose is to establish non-duality (*advaita*) by directly negating duality;
and among those few passages that express duality, their intent is the dissolution of that duality.
Therefore, it is established that from the perspective of ultimate reality, Brahman is devoid of distinctions, uniform in nature, and has pure consciousness as its sole essence;

whereas distinctions such as "having all fragrances" and "being the leader of all" are superimposed by virtue of limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*). The remainder of the text has its meaning self-evident. //11//

If it is argued that [the whole] does not exist because of the difference [of its parts], we say no; for [the scripture] does not state that [the whole is non-existent] with respect to each [part]. (BBs 3.2.12) // 12 //
Moreover, some [teachers] maintain this very point. (BBs 3.2.13) // 13 //
For that [unmanifest] is indeed formless, because it is characterized by predominance. 3.2.14.14.
And it is like light, because [the scripture] is not purposeless. 3.2.15.15.
And it says: "It is merely that. (BBs 3.2.16) // 16 //
Furthermore, it is shown [in scripture], and it is also recorded in the Smṛti. (Sūtra 17)
And for this very reason, there is the analogy of the reflection of the sun and so forth. (Sūtra 18)
But it is not so, because [the Self] is not apprehended like water; [this is the view of the opponent]. (BSBh 3.2.5.19)
The participation in increase and decrease occurs because [the intermediate state] is included [within the womb], and thus there is consistency for both; so it is. (BBs 3.2.20) // 20 //
And because it is observed [in scripture].
Regarding this, some propose two distinct topical sections (*adhikaraṇa*).

Is Brahman characterized by both existence (*sat*) and luminosity (*prakāśa*), or is Brahman characterized by existence alone, or by luminosity alone? Regarding this, he presents the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*): "And like light, because it is not purposeless";
by the word "and" (*ca*), "existence" (*sat*) is also included.
This is because [otherwise] there would be purposelessness.
He establishes the conclusion based on the authoritative scripture regarding Brahman: "And it says that [Brahman] is merely that;
it is mere luminosity.
For that which is called *sattva* (pure being) is not other than the nature of luminosity."

The meaning is that, just as [qualities such as] "being all-fragrance" and so forth are also nothing but the nature of manifestation (*prakāśa*), Brahman does not possess both natures. This very point has been set forth and refuted by the following: if existence (*sattā*) and manifestation were one, there could not be the characteristic of both.
Since it has already been refuted [under the sūtra] "Not even on account of place" (*na sthānato 'pi*) that there is any difference, this does not necessitate a separate section.
In reality, however, there is indeed non-difference, just as in the case of light and its intensity.

Furthermore, if the purpose of all [the meditations] were equally the dissolution [of the individual self], then the statement providing a reason for determination—namely, "For that [meditation on the Self] is like the formless, because it is the principal"—would have no scope.
For such an occasion would exist only if some [passages] were to describe a form with the intent of worship, while others were devoted to establishing the formless Brahman; however,

since all [passages] have the purpose of dissolution and thus aim at establishing the formless Brahman, there would be no grounds for a definitive conclusion (*vinigamana-hetu*), which is the meaning [of the objection].

The statement "because a single injunction is understood, as in the case of the sentences concerning the *prayāja* offerings and the *darśapūrṇamāsa* sacrifices" intends to refer to the qualification (*adhikāra*);
however, due to the difference in their subordinate elements (*anubandha*), the injunction (*niyoga*) in these two cases is also distinct.
What, then, is this dissolution of the phenomenal world (*prapañcapravilaya*)?
The dissolution of either a real phenomenal world, like the [dissolution of] ghee through contact with fire,
or of a superimposed one, like the state of being a snake upon a rope through the thorough knowledge of the reality of the rope—
first of all, a real phenomenal world such as earth and so forth, which is common to all, cannot be eradicated by a single individual alone.
Furthermore, since the phenomenal world (*prapañca*) has been uprooted from its very foundation by Prahlāda, Śuka, and other preeminent men, the world would have to be empty;
yet it is impossible for a real entity to be destroyed by the knowledge of reality (*tattvajñāna*),
as it has been stated that such knowledge is in opposition only to superimposed forms.

However, since conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*), which consists of superimposed forms, can be eradicated by those very sentences that aim to make known the reality of Brahman and cause one to realize that reality, there is no need for an injunction here. For even by a hundred injunctions, one who is prompted with "Be engaged in the knowledge of the Self" or "Perform the dissolution of proliferation" is not able to effect the dissolution of proliferation without the realization of reality.
Nor is it the case that the realization of the reality of Brahman—the meaning of the Vedānta—does not occur without an injunction regarding the knowledge of the Self.

This is because the original injunction for the study of one's own Veda (*svādhyāyādhyayana-vidhi*) exists as such, intending its specific meaning and thereby establishing that the entire mass of the Vedas is directed toward the comprehension of fruitful results;
otherwise, even the sentences enjoining ritual acts (*karma-vidhi-vākyāni*) would require further injunctions.
Furthermore, we have demonstrated in the *Tattvasamīkṣā* that there is no injunction regarding reflection (*cintā*) or direct realization (*sākṣātkāra*).
This matter has been explained in detail in that very same place.

Therefore, these [injunctions] such as "The Self, indeed, is to be seen" (ātmā vā are draṣṭavya) have the form of injunctions like "One should offer an oblation of wild sesamum gruel" (jartilayavāgvā juhuyāt), but they are not actual injunctions.

Thus it has been said: "Even words such as 'is to be seen' (draṣṭavya) are primarily intended to direct one toward reality (tattva), and are not primarily intended as injunctions for the realization of reality."
Furthermore, the reality of Brahman is said to be free from conceptual proliferation (*niṣprapañca*); no one can possibly be enjoined therein.
For it might be the individual soul (*jīva*) that is subject to injunction;
yet if that soul belongs to the side of conceptual proliferation, who is there to be enjoined, since it has been utterly destroyed?
Now, if Brahman is the subject, even so it cannot be enjoined, because Brahman is not subject to injunction.
Or, if it is argued that although it is non-different from Brahman, it is as if different due to ignorance and is therefore subject to injunction; [we reply:]...
That is incorrect;
for since ignorance has been dispelled by the scripture that makes known the ultimate state of Brahman, there is no person to be enjoined.
Therefore, due to the absence of one who is to be enjoined, there can be no injunction.
This has been stated: "The so-called individual soul (jīva) belongs exclusively to the side of phenomenal expansion (prapañca).
Furthermore, if the [Upanishads] were intent on enjoining knowledge, since knowledge does not arise from that alone, one must admit that they are intent on propounding reality (tattva).
In that case, it is better that they be intent solely on propounding reality, because that must necessarily be admitted and is established for both disputants.
And thus he says that this has been accomplished by the rule for the knowledge of reality: "even for one who is directed toward the object of knowledge.
Furthermore, there is no utility whatsoever for an injunction for one who does not depend on a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) in the acquisition of knowledge.
For such utility would exist only if an injunction could cause a cognition to take on a form other than what it actually has.
And that [result] is neither possible nor logical; thus he says: "Nor by another means of knowledge.

Furthermore, since the Veda culminates precisely in the injunction (*niyoga*), that which you have accepted through an investigation of the scripture—that the individual soul (*jīva*) has Brahman as its self as the object of the injunction—is without authority because it contradicts the scripture.

Now, [the author] says "atha" (now), because this scripture establishes that the individual soul (*jīva*) has Brahman as its self—which is not subject to injunction—and yet it also enjoins the soul; therefore, it would follow that it has two purposes and thus contradictory purposes.

In sentences concerning the *darśapūrṇamāsa* sacrifices and so forth, it is appropriate for the soul to be enjoined, even though in reality it is not subject to injunction, because it possesses a superimposed state of being subject to injunction.

For that sentence does not teach its status as one subject to injunction, but rather, relying on a status as one subject to injunction established by worldly means of knowledge, it prescribes the *darśapūrṇamāsa* sacrifices.
The sense is that this is difficult to reconcile, as it would both remove the state of being one who is to be enjoined and simultaneously enjoin [one];
and regarding the "focus on injunction" (niyogaparatā),

the meaning is that through an examination of the preceding and following passages, the Upanishads (Vedāntas) are heard to be established in reality (tattvaniṣṭha), not heard to be established in injunction (niyoganiṣṭha).
Moreover,

if the sentence were to culminate in an injunction (*niyoga*), then— just as in the case of the *darśapūrṇamāsa* ritual— the attainment of liberation, which consists of the fruit of bliss, would result only from an intermediate operation consisting of an *apūrva*, just like the attainment of fruits such as heaven resulting from the knowledge of the Self as an action.
And thus, [if that were so], impermanence and the quality of being surpassable would follow, as in the case of heaven; therefore he says, "like the fruit of karma.
Furthermore, [he says] "in the passages concerning Brahman."

For in the case of instructions that involve conceptual proliferation (*saprapañca*) as well as those that are non-proliferated (*niṣprapañca*), the status of being a single injunction (*ekaniyoga*) is not established because of the difference in the objectives (*sādhya*) and their associated elements (*anubandha*).

However, in the case of the sentences concerning the *darśapūrṇamāsa* and the *prayāja* offerings, although there is a difference in the associated elements, there is nonetheless non-difference [of the injunction] because there is no difference in the objective of the qualification (*adhikārāṃśa*). //21//
"Indeed, it negates the finitude of that which has been previously described, and then it speaks further. (BS 3.2.22).
He states the subject matter of this section: "There are indeed two forms of Brahman. (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 2.3.1).

There are only two forms of Brahman. Although Brahman is in the ultimate sense formless, there are only two forms superimposed upon it, for by means of those two it is made to appear as having form. He shows them: "the formed and the formless.
This is a restrictive conjunction.

In this context, the three elements—earth, water, and fire—are the formal (mūrta) form of Brahman; that is to say, they consist of congealed parts, with their constituent parts mutually interpenetrated, and are solid.
There are further qualifiers for that very same [form]: it is mortal, meaning subject to death;
and it is stationary, meaning non-pervasive.
"Delimited" (avacchinna) means just that. "Existent" (sat) means being distinguished from others, that is, possessing unique properties (asādhāraṇadharma).
Odor, viscidity, and heat are the unique properties that serve as the causes for mutual exclusion.
Of this very Brahman, which consists of fire, water, and food and possesses these four attributes, this is the essence—the core—which is this Sun that shines.

Now, the formless consists of air and the intermediate space (*antarikṣa*), for that is not solid; thus it is "formless" (*amūrta*). It is "immortal" (*amṛta*), meaning its nature is not subject to death.
For that which is solid, being struck by another solid object, perishes through the disintegration of its parts; however, such a state of destruction is impossible for that which is formless.

"Etat" means that which goes, moves, and pervades; "tyam" means that which is eternally beyond the senses—this is the meaning. Of this formless one, of this immortal one, of this "tya," of this [pervading] one, this is the essence (rasa): namely, this person who is in that solar orb.

That which consists of instruments, called the vital breath (*prāṇa*) of Hiraṇyagarbha, is indeed its essence (*rasa*), its core; and its constant invisibility is its similarity—this is with respect to the deities (*adhidaivata*).

Now, with respect to the self (*adhyātma*): that which is material (*mūrta*), other than the vital breath and the internal space, namely the triad of elements that initiates the body, is mortal, it is stationary, it is existent (*sat*).
Of this material one, of this mortal one, of this stationary one, of this existent one, the eye is the essence, for the eye is the essence of the existent.

Now, that which is formless—namely, the vital breath (*prāṇa*) and this space within the self (*antarātman*)—is immortal; it is that which is *tyat*. Of this formless, immortal, and *tyat*-like reality, this person who is in the right eye is the essence (*rasa*).

For he is indeed the essence of that subtle body (*liṅga*), consisting of the instruments of action, which is Hiraṇyagarbha; this is understood from the Vedic scripture, that the right eye is the locus of that [subtle body].

Thus, the distinction between the conditioned forms of Brahman—the manifest and the unmanifest, pertaining respectively to the internal (ādhyātmika) and the divine (ādhidaivika), and denoted by the words *sat* and *tyat*—has been explained in terms of their relationship as cause and effect. Now, the form of that person (*puruṣa*), which consists of the subtle body (*liṅga*) and is composed of the consciousness of the impressions of the manifest and the unmanifest, must be described. This manifold form, which is like a great illusion (*māyā*) or a magician’s trick (*mahendrajāla*), is illustrated through various examples, beginning with the words: "Just as [a cloth] dyed with saffron... and so forth.

This has been stated: that the subtle body (*liṅga*), which consists of consciousness and is composed of the latent impressions (*vāsanā*) of the manifest and the unmanifest, possesses a manifold form.

Having thus explained, without exception, the nature of reality along with its latent impressions, this [section] is now commenced for the purpose of determining the essential nature of that Brahman which was called "the Reality of realities."

Since the nature of Truth has been explained in its entirety, what remains is the essential nature of that which is the Truth of Truth—the Supreme Self; therefore, following that, its definition must be stated. Thus he says: "Now, therefore, the instruction"—that is, the declaration regarding the Truth of Truth, the Supreme Self. He declares it as "not this, not this" (*neti neti*).
This section is intended for the purpose of explaining the meaning of this.
Now, one might ask: "Is this alone to be taught, or is there something else beyond this? To this he says: "Not indeed from this Brahman...
There is nothing other than what has been taught by "No" and so forth that could be further taught.
Therefore, the meaning is that this alone is to be taught; there is nothing else.

In this context, that which is proximate and referred to by the word "iti" is negated by the negative particle *nañ*; and what is proximate here is the two forms—the formed (*mūrta*) and the formless (*amūrta*)—along with their latent impressions (*savāsana*), as well as Brahman as the delimiting factor of those two.
Regarding this, the following is investigated: is it the case that both the two forms along with their latent impressions and Brahman itself are all equally negated?
Or rather, is it that both [the world and Brahman] are with their latent impressions (*savāsana*), while only Brahman remains?

For although the true nature of Brahman has been established in various sections of the Vedānta, and the knowledge of its non-existence has been censured, and its existence has been ascertained through the statement, "It is indeed as 'is' that It is to be perceived," nevertheless, that Brahman—consisting of existence and consciousness—is a universal (*sāmānya*) by virtue of being common to both the formal (*mūrta*) and formless (*amūrta*) aspects along with their latent impressions; and of that [universal], these...
The particulars are those such as the formed and the formless;
and when each of those particulars is negated, the universal cannot remain, because a universal devoid of particulars is impossible.
As they say: "A universal without particulars would not exist, like the horn of a hare.
Therefore, even when its particulars are negated, because that universal Brahman does not cease to exist, this is a negation of everything.
For this very reason, by the negation "Not this, not this," and by the statement "There is nothing else beyond this," the Śruti declares the truth to be precisely the negation of all.

The statement "He is to be perceived as indeed existing" is to be understood as an injunction for meditation (*upāsanā-vidhi*), and not as asserting that existence alone is His true nature (*tattva*).
Furthermore, the disparagement of the knowledge of non-existence is intended for the purpose of praising Him.
Furthermore, any other exposition of the nature of Brahman found elsewhere is also for the purpose of negation, just like the exposition of the forms with and without form (*mūrtāmūrta*).
And although the negation is not explicitly present there, it is connected [to those passages] by virtue of its suitability (*yogyatva*).
As they say: "Whatever has a connection with something, that connection exists even with what is situated at a distance."
Therefore, the first position is that there is a prohibition of everything without exception.
Alternatively, because the entire phenomenal world (prapañca) consisting of earth and so forth is established by means of perception and other valid cognitions (pramāṇa),
whereas Brahman, being beyond the reach of speech and mind, is devoid of all means of valid cognition;

Regarding the doubt as to which [of the two] is being negated, the middle position holds that since the negation of the phenomenal world (*prapañca*) would entail a contradiction with all means of valid cognition such as perception,

whereas the negation of Brahman would not involve such a contradiction, it is Brahman alone that is connected with the negation due to its suitability, and not the phenomenal world because of the opposite being the case; the repetition (*vīpsā*), however, serves to indicate the absolute non-existence of that [phenomenal world].
Therein, he refutes the first position: "First of all, the negation of both is not tenable, because it would entail the consequence of nihilism (śūnyavāda).

This is the intended meaning: these limiting adjuncts (upādhi), such as earth and so forth, are imagined through ignorance (avidyā), but they are not specific qualities (viśeṣa) of the substrate like the redness or whiteness of a horse.
Furthermore, upon the removal of the limiting adjunct, there is neither the non-existence nor the non-perception of that which is conditioned (upahita).
For when the adjuncts—the mirror, the jewel, the sword, and so forth—are removed, there is neither the non-existence nor the non-apprehension of the face.
Therefore, even when the adjunct is negated, it is not the case that the substrate (the upahita) becomes like the horn of a hare, nor is there any cognition of such a thing.
Nor is it logical to claim that everything must be negated because there is no difference in their proximity [to the negation].
For a negation is not possible without depending upon an entity; for something is negated only in relation to something else. Indeed, a negation that lacks a basis cannot be apprehended.

This has been stated: "If nothing else remains, then that which is the other [the object of negation] cannot be negated; since it would follow that it alone is the ultimate reality, the negation is untenable.
He rejects the middle position as well: "Nor is the negation of Brahman tenable.
It is logical that the phenomenal world (*prapañca*), which is acquired through innate ignorance (*avidyā*), should be negated, because negation must be preceded by prior acquisition.
But Brahman is neither established through ignorance nor through any other means of valid cognition;
therefore, that which is apprehended by verbal testimony must be negated.

And thus, since that word which conveys it is intent upon it, it is a means of valid knowledge (*pramāṇa*) regarding Brahman; how then could even its negation be supported by a means of valid knowledge?

Nor can there be an option (*vikalpa*) based on the logic of the prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*) in the section concerning exclusion (*paryudāsa*), because such an option is impossible in the case of a reality whose nature is already established.
Furthermore, that which is beyond the range of speech and mind cannot be grasped by the intellect.
And how can that which is impossible be negated?
It is logical, however, that conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*), established through beginningless ignorance, is first referred to and then negated with respect to Brahman.
With this inconsistency in mind, it was said: "Nor is the negation of Brahman tenable."
He states another reason: "He says, 'I shall tell you Brahman,' because it would contradict the introduction.
For, by examining the introduction, the intermediate reference, and the conclusion, it was established in the first chapter that all Vedānta texts have Brahman as their sole purport.
Furthermore, in the absence of such expectancy (ākāṅkṣā), a connection with these [negations] cannot be established by means of a prohibition situated at a great distance.

Regarding the claim that because Brahman transcends speech and mind, its negation does not contradict other means of valid cognition (pramāṇa), he says: "Even the transcendence of speech and mind... The Vedāntas establish Brahman with great effort.
Nor is its exposition for the purpose of negation, as it has already been stated above that such a thing is untenable;
now, however, it is said to be purposeless, according to the maxim: "For by washing away the mud... (i.e., one should avoid getting into the mud in the first place).

Therefore, because Brahman is brought into proximity with the mind through the words of the Vedānta, its transcendence of speech and mind is not direct; rather, this is merely the commencement of a method of exposition.
Just as objects such as cows are directly pointed out and perceived by "seizing them by the horn" (i.e., by direct definition), Brahman is not so apprehended.
As they have said: "The determination [of Brahman] occurs by way of the dissolution of the manifoldness of difference."

Now, one might ask: "If there is a negation of what is under discussion (*prakṛta*), why is Brahman not also negated? To this he says: "For that [is] under discussion and has been elaborated. The meaning is as follows: the *pradhāna* (the primary subject) is what is under discussion and what has been elaborated; and the *prapañca* (the manifold world) is the primary subject, not Brahman, because Brahman—being in the genitive case—is subordinate as the delimiter of the *prapañca*.

Therefore, the statement "it speaks of something other than that" means that by the negation "not this, not this," it speaks of something else that is more [substantial]. This is its etymological explanation.

When the explanation of the phrase "not indeed from this" (*naitasmāt*) is that there exists nothing else superior to Brahman—which is designated as "not this, not this" (*neti neti*)—then it must be explained that [the text] declares Brahman itself as distinct from the negation of the phenomenal world (*prapañca*). However, when the pronoun "this" (*etasmāt*) in the phrase "not indeed from this" refers back to the instruction regarding Brahman itself, even then one should not understand it as merely a negation of the phenomenal world; rather, by means of that negation, [Brahman is indicated].
Brahman is indicated as having the nature of existence.
Why? To this he says: "And it speaks further than that.
Because it speaks even beyond the negation.
Now, regarding the name of Brahman—namely, "the Truth of truth"—the Śruti explains it thus: "The vital breaths (prāṇas) are indeed truth.
It points to the subtle body (liṅga), which is compared to saffron and other such substances;
that [subtle body] is indeed truth in relation to others, but the supreme truth of even that is Brahman.
Thus, since he speaks after the negation [of the world], it follows that Brahman is not merely the negation of phenomenal proliferation (*prapañca*), but rather has a positive nature (*bhāvarūpa*).
In this way, in the previous explanation, it was interpreted as "he states the etymological derivation";
however, in this [present] case, it should be explained as "he says 'the Truth of truth'."
The remainder has its meaning not obscured. //23//
Moreover, regarding the attainment [of the Self], it is known through both perception and inference. (3.2.24)
And there is no difference [between the Lord and His powers], as in the case of light and so forth; and light [is manifested] in action through practice. (BSBh 3.2.25)
Therefore, [the soul] is not [identical with] the infinite, for there is an indicative mark [to the contrary]. (3.2.26)
START BsVBh_3,2.6.27:
But because of the designation of both [aspects], it is like a serpent and its coils (ahikuṇḍalavat).
By this, there is non-difference in the form of the serpent.

However, it has been stated that there is difference in the form of the earrings and so forth; therefore, because the objects are distinct, there is no contradiction between difference and non-difference. Or rather, there is no contradiction because they are always perceived as having a single object. For what is it that we consider "contradictory" if it is not contradicted by valid cognition (*pramāṇa*)? Furthermore, according to the authority of scripture (*āgama*), even difference and non-difference, when perceived as having a single locus, do not bring about contradiction, just like the sun and its light. Thus, both difference and non-difference are established through the means of direct perception (*pratyakṣa*). //27//

Alternatively, like light and its substratum, because it is luminous. (BBs 3.2.28) By another method, he states that there is no contradiction between difference and non-difference: "Alternatively, like light and its substratum, because it is luminous" (28).
Having thus presented the opinion of others, he states his own view:
"Or it is as before" (BBs 3.2.29). Start BsVBh 3.2.6.29.
This is the underlying intention: one who holds the view that there is non-difference in a thing by virtue of its being a substance (*vastutva*),
but difference by virtue of its being a bracelet (*kuṇḍalatva*),
must be questioned as follows:
Are the states of being a bracelet and being a ring distinct from the object, or are they non-distinct?
If they are distinct, one must say that the states of being a bracelet and being a ring are distinct, but not that the object possesses both distinction and non-distinction from them.

For it is not possible for something else to be either different or non-different from [two things] other than difference and non-difference, because that would lead to an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*).

Now, if the states of being a bracelet and being a ring do not differ from the object, then what distinction of domain could there be between difference and non-difference? For they would be non-distinct from the object, due to their non-otherness with respect to it.

Nor can it be argued that there is no contradiction between difference and non-difference simply because they are always experienced within a single object; for if even things whose essential natures are contradictory were not contradictory, where indeed would contradiction be established? Furthermore, that which is always experienced yet cannot withstand critical inquiry cannot be considered real, as this would lead to the absurd conclusion that the identification of the body with the self—which is also constantly experienced—is likewise real.
This has been elaborated by us in the first sūtra, and thus it is not elaborated here.
Therefore, the distinction of the single Self into the state of being a living soul (jīva) is merely the play of beginningless ignorance (avidyā), and is not ontologically real.
Consequently, upon the cessation of ignorance through the knowledge of reality, liberation (apavarga) is established.
If this [bondage] were real, its cessation through knowledge would be impossible;
nor is there any means for liberation other than the knowledge of reality.
As the Śruti says: "Only by knowing Him does one pass beyond death; there is no other path for the journey."
The remainder has its meaning not hidden. //29//
And because of the prohibition. (30)
Sūtra 3.2.31:
[The Brahman is] different from the highest [self], on account of the designations of a bridge, measurement, connection, and difference.

(BBs 3.2.31) Although it has been determined that there is no reality distinct from Brahman because of the abundance of scriptural texts [to that effect], nevertheless, this section is commenced for the purpose of resolving the apparent contradiction with those scriptural passages concerning the bridge and so forth, which are encountered at first sight.

The wild-land (jāṅgalasthala), the luminous (prakāśavat), the infinite (anantavat), and the radiant abode (jyotiṣmadāyatana)—these are the four feet of Brahman. Half of those four feet are eight, which are the hoofs (śapha).
Since these eight belong to this Brahman, Brahman is said to have eight hoofs (aṣṭaśapha).
That which has sixteen parts (*kalā*) is called "sixteen-parted" (*ṣoḍaśakala*).
These are as follows: east, west, south, and north—these four are like parts or limbs (*kalā*). This is the first foot (*pāda*), named "Luminous" (*prakāśavat*).
Because one becomes preeminently luminous through meditation upon this, it is the "Luminous Foot."

Now, another four parts—earth, intermediate space, heaven, and the ocean—constitute this second foot, named "The Endless" (*anantavān*). When meditated upon through the quality of endlessness, it brings about endlessness for the meditator; thus, it is called the "Endless" foot. Now, fire, sun, moon, and lightning—these four parts constitute the third foot, named "The Luminous" (*jyotiṣmān*). Through meditation on that, one becomes luminous; thus, it is called the "Luminous" foot.
Now, the four digits consisting of the nose, the eye, the ear, and speech constitute the fourth foot, named "Possessing a Basis" (*āyatanavān*).

For these [organs], beginning with the nose, having the objects of smell and so forth as their domain, become the means for experience by depending upon the mind as their basis; thus this foot is named "Possessing a Basis.
In this way, Brahman has been revealed by the Śruti as having four feet, eight hooves, and sixteen digits.
Therefore, there exists something else beyond that Brahman.
This might be argued: if it does exist, let it be stated definitively that "it is just this much."
Therefore he says: "It exists as immeasurable.
This means it is established by valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), but not that it is limited to this much.
And the designation of distinction is threefold: by way of locus, by way of extension, and by way of limit. //31//
But on account of similarity (sāmānyāt). (Sūtra 3.2.32) The commonality with a bridge (*setu*) consists in being that which upholds the world and its moral boundaries.

For just as threads support a cloth precisely because they are its material cause (*upādāna*), so too does Brahman support the world because it is its sustainer. Furthermore, Brahman is the upholder of the world's boundaries;
otherwise, the ocean—turbulent with garlands of exceedingly swift, massive, and powerful waves—would swallow the entire circle of the earth.
"The submarine fire, with its mass of flickering flames, might reduce the world to ashes;
or a fierce wind might suddenly shatter the cosmic egg.
And so says the Śruti: "Out of fear of Him the wind blows," and so forth. //32//
START BsVBh_3,2.7.33:
"The purpose is for the sake of cognition, like the feet" (BBs 3,2.33).
For the mind, which is a representative image (*pratīka*) of Brahman upon which the nature of Brahman has been superimposed, there are four feet: speech, smell, sight, and hearing.

For the mind (*manas*) moves through the spheres of the speakable, the smellable, the visible, and the audible by means of speech and the other senses; thus, because it is common to this movement, the mind is the "foot" (*pāda*), which pertains to the self (*adhyātman*).
Of space (*ākāśa*), which is the symbol (*pratīka*) of Brahman, there are four feet: fire, wind, the sun, and the quarters.
For these are perceived as being attached to the pervasive sky like the feet of a cow; thus they are the "feet," which pertains to the deities (*adhidaivata*).

Having thus explained the Vedic illustration with "like a foot," he states that this is also a worldly illustration: "Or else, 'like a foot'—just as that [is done], so it is here too, for the sake of the conventional practice of meditation for those of dull intellect. (33)
"Due to the distinction of location, as in the case of light and so forth.

(BBs 3.2.34) Because of its connection with the specific locations of the limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*) such as the intellect (*buddhi*), the specific cognition that arises during the waking and dreaming states ceases—that is, it is suppressed—when those adjuncts are dissolved, resulting in the state of deep sleep (*suṣupti*).

Likewise, the designation of difference regarding Brahman is also threefold, depending on the distinction of limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*). Just as the rays of the sun entering through the openings of a palace lattice appear divided due to the distinction of the lattice-openings as limiting adjuncts, yet upon the removal of those [adjuncts] they become one with the solar orb and are thus connected with it—so it is here as well. //34//
It might be argued:
why is unity (*ekībhāva*) here explained as a relationship in some figurative sense rather than in its primary sense? This [objection] is refuted by the following sūtra:
And because it is logically consistent: the phrase "he has entered into his own self" (*svam apītaḥ*) expresses a relationship with one's own essential nature (*svarūpa*).

If intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) is touched upon by this [phrase] as a form of relationship, then, being natural, it does not differ from identity (*tādātmya*); this is the meaning established in the *Tarkapāda*.
Likewise, difference is also of three kinds, or otherwise it is intrinsic; such is the meaning. //35//

Likewise, because of the negation of others.
This has been explained by the easily understood commentary. //36//
By this [sūtra],
"omnipresence" is established from the words "extent" (āyāma) and so forth.
Even though the non-duality of Brahman is established, omnipresence— the state of pervading everything— does not mean that everything is identical in its own nature with Brahman.

Since the possession of form (rūpavattva) is thus established, he says: by this refutation of the [analogy of] a bridge and so forth, by the refutation of other [external] causes, by the recourse to the negation of others, and by the presentation of its own proof, the all-pervasiveness of the Self is also established.

When non-duality is established, this entire manifestation of the world-appearance, which is indeterminable (anirvacanīya), has Brahman as its substratum; therefore, because everything is connected with Brahman, it is established that Brahman is all-pervasive. //37//
