"The fruit [proceeds] from Him (the Lord), because that is logical. (BBs_3.2.38) This section begins with the established conclusion (siddhānta).
This might be the case:

from where does Brahman, whose nature is eternally pure, awakened, and liberated, derive its status as the Lord (Īśvara), and from where its status as the cause of fruits? To this, he says: "Of that very Brahman, in its conventional [form]. This is not contemplated by relying upon its ultimate (pāramārthika) form, but rather its conventional (sāṃvyavahārika) one.
And this has been established by us while explaining the passage, "Brahman is built up by austerity.
The desired fruit is heaven.
As they say: "That which is not mixed with suffering, nor followed immediately by anything else that devours it..."
And the happiness brought about by desire has heaven as its locus;
the undesirable is that to be experienced in places such as the Avīci hell;
and the mixed is that to be experienced by humans.
In this regard, it is first established that the fruit must arise from this Lord (Īśvara) when He has been propitiated by ritual acts (karma).

Now, as to why the fruit does not arise from the action itself, he says: "But because the action perishes moment by moment; [that is,] it perishes perceptibly. An objection is raised: "Suppose this action were to perish..."
The meaning is that even though the fruit has been acquired, it is not experienced either because one is incapable of experiencing it or because of an obstruction by another karma.
He refutes this, saying: "That too is not cleared up."
For the qualified person does not desire heaven with the thought, "May it obtain itself," but rather, "May it become an object of enjoyment for us.
Therefore, since such is what is desired by them, that which is of such a nature constitutes the fruit; thus, the fruit is indeed that which is to be enjoyed.
And since such a thing does not exist immediately after the action, how can it be the fruit?
That too [is non-existent] by its very nature.
Furthermore, since heaven and hell consist of the most intense pleasure and pain, there must necessarily be an experience—another name for which is "enjoyment"—with respect to them.
Therefore, when something is capable of being experienced but is not being experienced, it is determined to be non-existent, like the horn of a hare.

The opponent objects: "Let it not be that the fruit arises immediately after the action; rather, the fruit will arise from the *apūrva* (unseen force), which is not the direct effect of the action. The author refutes this: "That too is not so.
For it has been established through both perception and scripture that whatever is insentient must all proceed under the direction of a sentient being.
Therefore, the meaning is that even the *apūrva* (unseen force), being insentient, must function only when presided over by a sentient being, and not otherwise;
nor is the *apūrva* established by any means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), as he says: "In its existence... (verse 38).
And because it is so stated in scripture (śrutatvāt). [Sūtra 39:
He is the eater of food and the giver of food. //39//

Having begun with the established conclusion (*siddhānta*), he takes up the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*): "Jaimini [holds that] Dharma [is known through the Veda], for this very reason. (BS 3.2.40)
He states the scriptural authority: "It is indeed heard [in scripture]...
Now, one might object: do not scriptural injunctions such as "One desiring heaven should sacrifice" enjoin the sacrifice as a means toward a result?

For instance, even if sacrifices and the like are themselves the action (*kriyā*) and there is no *bhāvanā* distinct from them, nevertheless, they [the sacrifices] are understood from their own words [as the means].

Since [the actions] are understood as having a nature to be accomplished (*sādhya*) that exists in a temporal sequence of prior and posterior, they do not require another thing to be accomplished; thus, they cannot be connected with heaven (*svarga*) as a further object to be accomplished.

Even if there were no entity distinct from those [actions], nevertheless, even when there is a requirement for something to be brought about (*bhāvya*), [the action] refers to what is conveyed by its own word and previously understood.

One must not abandon the meaning of the verbal root [to assume something else as the end to be accomplished]; nor can one accept heaven and the like—though mentioned in a separate word—as the object to be accomplished (*bhāvya*) while they function merely as qualifiers of the person.
Furthermore, it is impossible for two things to be connected as objects to be accomplished within a single sentence, as that would entail the fault of syntactical split (*vākya-bheda*).

Not only verbally but also in reality, it is the meaning of the verbal root (dhātvartha) alone that is the direct object to be accomplished (sādhya) by human effort—that is, by the mental cultivation (bhāvanā)—and not heaven (svarga) and the like, because the latter is not pervaded by that [effort].

Since heaven and so forth are denoted by nominal stems (nāman) and are thus of an already established nature (siddharūpa), they are connected as subordinate factors (guṇatvena) as means toward the meaning of the root, which is the object to be accomplished expressed by the verb (ākhyāta); this is according to the maxim: "That which is already established is taught for the sake of that which is to be brought into being" (*bhūtaṃ bhavyāyopadiśyate*).
Accordingly, there is a Sūtra of the Great Sage (Jaimini): "When substances are connected with an action, their connection is as subordinate factors."

And thus, since rituals such as sacrifice are not desired by a person because they are of the nature of suffering, and since [the desired end] such as heaven is not their result, sacrifices and the like do not benefit the person; and since a person does not have mastery over those things that do not benefit him, and one who lacks mastery cannot be an *adhikārī* (eligible participant), [the Sūtra] provides the following in order to avoid the charge of futility (*anarthakya*) established on the grounds of the absence of eligibility:

The entire Veda has as its ultimate purpose the knowledge of Brahman—which consists of eternal bliss and is entirely free from the association of suffering—by means of dissolving the phenomenal world of duality.
For instance, throughout the entire Veda, the dissolution of some particular form of duality is perceived in various places;
for example, in the injunction "one desiring heaven should sacrifice," there is the dissolution of the identification with the body as the self.
In this context, at first glance, the qualified seeker (adhikārī) is understood as one who is distinct from the body and capable of enjoying fruits in the hereafter.

Since that qualification has been refuted by the aforementioned sequence, and since even that which is perceived though non-existent cannot withstand critical inquiry and persists merely as a means, the dissolution of the identification with the body is effected by this sentence, which is intent upon that [dissolution].

Even in the case of the injunction, "One desiring cattle should fetch [water] with a milking vessel," there is a dissolution of the distinction between different qualified persons (adhikāribheda), because at first glance it appears to be an extension of the qualification for one already entitled [to the primary rite].

Furthermore, prohibitory statements directly negate activity; and other injunctive statements, such as "One desiring a village should sacrifice with the Sāṅgrahaṇī," do not aim at enjoining the performance of the Sāṅgrahaṇī and so forth, but rather intend to prohibit worldly means such as service by teaching an alternative means.

Just as one might say, "Eat poison" or "Do not eat in this person's house," so too the status of a treatise as a treatise is established by its prohibition of activity impelled by passion and the like. For if it were to permit activity based on passion by means of teaching methods, there would be the undesirable consequence of it being a non-treatise due to its increasing that passion.
However, by negating that [connection], the scripture would become a true scripture only if it instills focused attention upon Brahman.

Therefore, since the connection between action and its fruit lacks scriptural authority, the production of diverse fruits arises from the Lord alone— without dependence on karma— having beginningless and manifold ignorance as its auxiliary cause.

How then is there an injunction? What is it here? [The answer is: Because an injunction consists merely in an impulsion, and that is possible even without a qualified person (*adhikārin*). For not every agent who impels another requires a qualified person; for instance, the wind and other such impellers do not require one. Wishing to dispel this doubt, he says: "And in that case, because the sacrifice enters into the state of being the object of the Vedic injunction, it is understood to be the producer of heaven."
Otherwise, the sacrifice would result in being something that is not performed.
This is the intended meaning: for an injunction (*vidhi*) is indeed an instruction (*upadeśa*), as it has been said, "The means of knowing it (Dharma) is instruction."
Furthermore, instruction regarding an action that serves the purpose of one who is to be enjoined is well known in both worldly usage and the treatises;
for example: "One desiring health should eat when [the previous meal] has been digested," or "This is a good path; may you go by this."
However, unlike ignorance and the like, it does not have the purpose of an instigator (*niyoktṛ*) as its object, because intention (*abhiprāya*) is the motivator [of action],

and that [intention] is impossible in what is not of human origin (*apauruṣeya*). Furthermore, we have established in the *Nyāyakaṇikā* that this instruction has as its object an activity that serves the purpose of the person to be enjoined (*niyojya*), and that its scope is an activity conducive to what is required by the performer.
And thus, in injunctions such as "One desiring heaven should sacrifice," sacrifices and the like are understood to be the means for attaining what is desired by the one desiring heaven and so forth;
otherwise, they would not follow the person who is to accomplish [the result].
As it was said by the Seer: "But [the Veda] is not a means of accomplishment [for the agent], because its purpose is that [result]."

If [the words] such as "one should sacrifice" (*yajeta*) had as their sole purpose a mere instigation devoid of being a means required by the performer, then sacrifices and the like would be non-achieving actions;
the meaning is that they would not find an achiever.

Nor can these [results], even though they are the objects to be brought about (*bhāvya*) by the productive activity (*bhāvanā*), become the intended objects of that productive activity when its scope is delimited by an injunction that prescribes them as the means required by the agent.
By this [definition], those things which do not provide benefit to persons would not be eligible [as objects of action],
because suffering, being the nature of actions, is not a locus for the exertion of volition (*cetanā*),
whereas heaven and so forth are so because they are underlain by desire and preceded by cultivation (*bhāvanā*).
And because it consists of pleasure (*prīti*):

even for those things denoted by names and words—which serve as qualifiers of the person—there is the cognition of being an object to be brought about (*bhāvya*), characterized by being the objective of the productive activity (*bhāvanā*).

Furthermore, since the state of being an effect to be accomplished (*sādhya*) by sacrifice and the like—characterized by being the object to be brought about by the productive activity engaged for the sake of a result—is distinct from the state of being an effect to be accomplished by that same productive activity engaged for the sake of a result (which is the nature of the fruit itself), there is no possibility of their coexistence within a single sentence due to a lack of equal primacy.

Furthermore, there is no contradiction in the fact that even an instrument (karaṇa) can have as its object of accomplishment (sādhya) the mere state of being cultivated through meditative development (bhāvanābhāvyatva), such as the performance of a sacrifice;
otherwise, that status would be abolished everywhere,
since axes and other tools would likewise possess it in relation to acts such as cutting.

It is established that even though the fruit (*phala*) is not directly pervaded by the cultivation (*bhāvanā*), because it stands as the object of that cultivation and is thus omnipresent, the person desiring heaven (*svargakāma*) possesses the qualification (*adhikāra*) for sacrifices such as the *yāga* which are the means to attain heaven.
Furthermore, injunctions regarding sacrifices such as the *sāṃgrahaṇī*, which concern objects not already obtained, cannot function as exclusions (*parisaṃkhyā*) or as restrictive rules (*niyama*).
Moreover, in the absence of qualification...
Either the dissolution of the body into the Self or the dissolution of the distinction between different types of qualified aspirants can be established;
however, if this [dissolution] appears only superficially, then the sentence's purpose is that alone, not the attainment of the goal (liberation).

When it is possible for a sentence to have as its purpose a meaning perceived through its own inherent force (*svarasa*), it is not appropriate to claim that its purpose is merely incidental attainment.
Nor is the status of being a treatise (śāstra) contradicted by this much;
for its status as a treatise is established even when it teaches the means to heaven and so forth,
since being a treatise consists precisely in denoting the human good (puruṣaśreyaḥ).
Since it proclaims the welfare of both men with passion and those free from passion, and thus serves as a guide for all assemblies, there is no contradiction with reality.
Therefore, it is established that sacrifice, by virtue of being accepted as an object of injunction, is the producer of heaven;
or rather, it is a certain state of the ritual action itself.
It is the intermediate operation of the action.

What is meant is this: for that which is heard in scripture as the action's status as a means toward a result, it possesses an intermediate operation precisely in order to bring that status to fulfillment.
Nor is it logical to claim that an operation exists only when there is an agent possessing that operation and not when there is none;

for even though the Āgneya and other sacrifices are non-existent [at the time of the final result], their intermediate apūrvas serve as the intermediate operations for the production of the ultimate apūrva.

Furthermore, even though the act of drinking oil is non-existent [at the time of the result], the various transformations of the oil in the interim serve as the intermediate operations for the nourishment to be produced by it.
Therefore, it is logical that the *apūrva*— the effect of the ritual action— is the intermediate operation (*avāntaravyāpāra*) when the fruit is to be produced by the action.
Furthermore, when something is postulated because the arising of the fruit would otherwise be inexplicable, it must be either the prior state of the fruit itself,
or [the persistence] of a non-variegated cause.

The intended meaning is that if [the world] arises from Īśvara alone—this being the ellipsis—or from auspicious and inauspicious *karma*s, then there would be the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) that he possesses passion and other afflictions, due to the production of the duality of effects. //40//
But Bādarāyaṇa holds that [the soul] exists even before [birth], because of the mention of a cause;
for a conceptual construction following what is observed is logical, and not otherwise.

For it is never observed that lumps of clay, staffs, and so forth, when not presided over by a potter or similar agent, possess the capacity to initiate the production of jars and other objects. Nor is there a deviation [from the rule] on account of lightning, wind, and the like, which are not preceded by conscious effort; for since these too are themselves subjects of conceptual construction, it is impossible for them to serve as instances of deviation.

Therefore, an insentient entity—whether it be karma or the *apūrva*—is not capable of proceeding toward its own effect independently if it is not presided over by consciousness. Nor is mere consciousness alone sufficient, as it would be devoid of the specific knowledge required regarding the nature, general application, and particular deployment of the action; for if that were so, one could raise the objection of proving what is already established by means of a mere *kṣetrajña* (individual soul) lacking such [specific knowledge].
Consequently, it is well-ascertained through thousands of examples of the production of various palaces, watchtowers, gate-towers, and archways, that:

It has been clearly established in the *Devatādhikaraṇa* that because insentient things initiate action through the presiding presence of consciousness (*cetanādhiṣṭhāna*), so too the sentience of the deity— well-known from the *Śruti*, *Smṛti*, *Itihāsa*, and *Purāṇa*— cannot be denied in the absence of a subverting proof. Furthermore,
the worldly Lord is [worshipped] with devotion consisting of gifts, service, prostration, joining of palms, and hymns of praise, all imbued with supreme faith.

It is well-established that when a deity is propitiated and becomes pleased, it bestows upon the worshipper a fruit corresponding to that devotion; likewise, through hostility and harmful acts, it brings misfortune to the adversary.
Therefore, in this case, the claim that either mere karma or the *apūrva*—being insentient and not presided over by consciousness—produces a fruit, contradicts what is observed in the world.
It would be like [something] that has perished.
It is postulated that "karma does not produce its fruit" because this would contradict what is observed; the same applies here as well.
Likewise, the view that a sacrifice consisting of the worship of a deity produces its fruit without propitiating the deity is also contradicted by observation.
For a service consisting of the worship of a king cannot lead to a result without propitiating the king.
Therefore, for the sake of conforming to what is observed, the propitiation of the deity is produced even by means of sacrifices and other rites.
And thus, since the production of the enduring fruit is logically accounted for through the grace of the deity alone, there is no need for an *apūrva* (unseen potency).
Likewise, it is well known from the *Śruti* and *Smṛti* that even by means of inauspicious action, there occurs an antagonism toward the deity.
From that [state of being a deity], there would follow the production of undesirable results for those who abide [in their respective roles].

Furthermore, it is not logical that a deity who produces results corresponding to the good or evil deeds of beings should be characterized by partiality toward hatred. For a king, when favoring one who acts rightly or punishing one who acts wickedly, does not thereby become hateful or attached; likewise, so too is the case with the transcendent Lord (Īśvara).

And just as when the supreme *apūrva* is to be accomplished, there is the utility of the production-*apūrvas* and the subsidiary-*apūrvas*, so too in the propitiation of the Principal [Deity], there is the utility of the propitiations of the subsidiaries and the propitiations of the productions; it is like the propitiation of a king's ministers and their attendants being useful for the propitiation of the sovereign. Thus everything is the same, except for the difference in attachment (*abhiniveśa*).

Therefore, the fruit arises from the propitiation of the deity in accordance with what is seen [in experience], and not from an unseen potency (*apūrva*) or from action alone; thus, the scriptural and traditional designations of "cause" have been explained.

As for those who, believing that the operation of the Inner Controller (*antaryāmin*) for the production of results is eternal and common to all, have sought to refute the section of the Commentary (*bhāṣya*), [the author] says to them: "In the empirical state characterized by the distinction between the ruler and the ruled..."
One should explain the commentary. //41//
Thus ends the second quarter of the third chapter in the Bhāmatī, a commentary on the Bhāṣya, composed by the venerable Vācaspati Miśra.

Thus ends the second quarter of the third chapter, titled "The Purification of the Meanings of the Words *tat* and *tvam*. The Third Quarter of the Third Chapter. START BsVBh_3,3.1.1: The Nature of the Self as the Enjoyer of the Fruits of Actions. Now begins the consideration of the nature of the self as the enjoyer of the fruits of actions. It has been stated that the individual self (*jīva*), which is the agent of action, is distinct from the body, the senses, the mind, and the intellect; it is atomic in size, eternal, and possesses consciousness as its essential nature. Furthermore, it has been established that this self is the knower of the field (*kṣetrajña*) and the enjoyer of the fruits of actions. Now, the following must be determined: Is this self merely the enjoyer of the fruits of actions performed in this life, or is it also the enjoyer of the fruits of actions performed in previous lives? To address this, the scripture says: "Having experienced the results of those good and evil deeds in this world, he returns again from that world to this world for further action. (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 5.10.7) This indicates that the self returns from the world of the moon, where the fruits of its actions have been experienced, back to this world to perform further actions. This suggests that the self is the enjoyer of the fruits of actions performed in this life. However, another scriptural passage states: "He who performs good deeds becomes good, and he who performs evil deeds becomes evil. Becoming virtuous through virtuous conduct, he attains the worlds of the virtuous. Becoming sinful through sinful conduct, he attains the worlds of the sinful. (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 4.4.5) This indicates that one becomes good or evil according to the nature of the deeds performed in a previous life, and subsequently attains corresponding worlds. This suggests that the self is the enjoyer of the fruits of actions performed in a previous life. Therefore, a doubt arises: is the self the enjoyer of the fruits of actions performed in this life, or is it the enjoyer of the fruits of actions performed in a previous life? To resolve this, the Sūtra states: **Sūtra 1:** *saṃkalpād eva tu tacchruteḥ.* But [the soul's enjoyment of the fruits of action] is due to mere volition, because of the scriptural statement to that effect. The word "but" (*tu*) serves to set aside the doubt raised by the previous discussion. The soul's attainment of the fruits of action occurs through mere volition (*saṃkalpa*). Why? Because of the scriptural statement to that effect: "Whatever he desires in his mind, that very thing he obtains" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 8.2.1). This shows that the soul attains the fruits of its actions simply by willing them. Furthermore, the scripture says: "He goes to whatever object he desires" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 8.2.1). This indicates that the soul reaches the objects of its desire through mere volition. Moreover, the scripture states: "He moves at will among these worlds" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 7.25.2). This shows that the soul moves through various worlds according to its own will. Thus, since the soul attains the fruits of its actions through mere volition, it follows that it is the enjoyer of the fruits of actions performed in this life. However, an objection may be raised: if the soul were to attain the fruits of actions performed in this life through mere volition, then there would be no need for the performance of sacrifices and other rituals prescribed in the scriptures. To this, the Sūtra replies: **Sūtra 2:** *ata eva cānanyādhipatiḥ.* And for this very reason, it has no other lord. Because the soul attains the fruits of its actions through mere volition, it has no other master or controller over itself. Since the soul is independent in its attainment of results, it is not subject to the will of another. This independence is confirmed by the scripture: "He is the Lord of all, the King of all things, the Protector of all beings" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 4.4.22). This shows that the soul is the sovereign ruler of its own destiny. Furthermore, the scripture says: "He is the Lord of the past and the future" (Taittirīya Āraṇyaka 3.12.7). This indicates that the soul exercises mastery over both the past and the future. Therefore, because the soul is the enjoyer of the fruits of actions performed in this life through its own volition, it is established that it is independent and has no other lord. However, another objection may arise: if the soul is independent and has no other lord, then why does it not always act according to its own will? To this, the Sūtra replies: **Sūtra 3:** *vikalpagamanāc ca.* And because of the occurrence of alternative possibilities. The phrase "and because of the occurrence of alternative possibilities" means that the soul experiences various different states of existence. As the scripture says: "It becomes the form of fire, the form of water, the form of food" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 6.9.2–4). This shows that the soul assumes diverse forms according to its own volition. Furthermore, the scripture states: "It becomes a tiger, or a lion, or a wolf, or a boar, or a worm, or a moth, or a fish, or a bird" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 6.9.3–4). This demonstrates that the soul undergoes various transformations according to its own will. Thus, because the soul experiences a variety of states through its own volition, it is established that it is the enjoyer of the fruits of actions performed in this life and is independent of any other lord. Now, another question arises: if the soul is the enjoyer of the fruits of actions performed in this life, then what happens to the fruits of actions performed in a previous life? Does the soul experience them here, or do they remain unexhausted? To address this, the Sūtra states: **Sūtra 4:** *tadadhigama uttarapūrvāghayor aśleṣavināśau tadvyapadeśāt.* Upon the realization of That (Brahman), there is the non-clinging and destruction of subsequent and prior sins, because of the scriptural declaration thereof. When the soul attains the knowledge of Brahman, there occurs the non-clinging (*aśleṣa*) of future sins and the destruction (*vināśa*) of past sins. Why? Because of the scriptural declaration to that effect. Regarding the non-clinging of future sins, the scripture says: "As water does not cling to a lotus leaf, so no evil deed clings to him who knows this" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 4.14.3). Regarding the destruction of past sins, the scripture says: "Just as the fibers of a reed are burnt up when thrown into a blazing fire, even so all his sins are burnt up" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 5.24.3). Thus, upon the realization of Brahman, there is the non-clinging of future sins and the destruction of past sins. Furthermore, regarding the fruits of actions performed before the realization of Brahman, the Sūtra states: **Sūtra 5:** *anārabdhakārye eva tu pūrve tadavadheḥ.* But only those prior [sins] whose effects have not yet begun [are destroyed], for that is the limit. The term "prior" refers to sins committed before the realization of Brahman. The phrase "whose effects have not yet begun" means those actions whose fruits have not yet commenced. Only such actions are destroyed by the realization of Brahman. Why? Because that is the limit. The scripture sets this limit: "For him, the remaining works are exhausted only when the body falls" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 4.4.7). This shows that the realization of Brahman destroys only those actions whose fruits have not yet begun, while those actions whose fruits have already begun continue until the fall of the body. Therefore, it is established that the soul is the enjoyer of the fruits of actions performed in this life, and that upon the realization of Brahman, there is the non-clinging of future sins and the destruction of past sins whose effects have not yet begun. Thus ends the first section of the third quarter of the third chapter. START BsVBh_3,3.2.1: The Nature of the Self as the Enjoyer of the Fruits of Actions. Now begins the consideration of the nature of the self
"All the Vedāntas convey the same cognition because there is no difference in their injunctions and so forth.
[The author] states the connection with the preceding section: "It has been explained that [the nature] of Brahman, which is to be known..."
Considering that the cognition whose object is the reality of Brahman free from limiting adjuncts (*nirupādhi*) is [the ultimate], he raises an objection:
"But surely Brahman is that which is to be known (*vijñeya*).

For if Brahman possessed parts, then cognitions having as their object Brahman as qualified by those parts would differ according to the difference in their objects; thus, parts of Brahman were previously rejected by the statement beginning with "prior, posterior," and so forth.

And Brahman does not possess a manifold nature, for it has been stated that "it is of a single flavor" (*ekarasa*), meaning that cognitions are distinct only due to differences in their objective forms (*svabhāvabheda*).
*Dhanaṃ* means solid.
But surely, even a single entity is seen in the world to have multiple forms;
for example, Somaśarman, though one, is an ācārya, a maternal uncle, a father, a son, a brother, a husband, a son-in-law, and the best of the twice-born—thus he has many forms.
To this, it is said: "And because of its being of a single form."
It has been stated that many consciousnesses can arise with respect to a single object-field (*gocara*), but not with multiple aspects (*ākāra*);
[the text continues: "multiple forms. Form (*rūpa*) is the aspect (*ākāra*).
He explains:
"It is said—'with attributes' (saguṇā).

The meaning is that meditations (*upāsanā*) have as their objects Brahman as qualified by various attributes, as well as objects such as the vital breath (*prāṇa*); they differ according to the distinction of their objects, having as their fruits liberation through the seen (*dṛṣṭa*) or the unseen (*adṛṣṭa*) means.
Then, having arisen, he states the inquiry: "This reflection concerns them.
He takes up the prima facie position (*pūrvapakṣa*):
Regarding the word "therein":
first, concerning the name, there is [the passage]:
"Now this is the Jyotis; one should sacrifice with this [rite] accompanied by a thousand-fold sacrificial fee."

In this regard, there arises a doubt: does the statement "one should sacrifice" constitute an injunction of the accessory characterized by a thousand-fold sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) with reference to the proximate Jyotiṣṭoma, or does it enjoin a distinct ritual act (*karmāntara*) qualified by that accessory?
What, then, is the prima facie position (*pūrvapakṣa*)?

Since the Jyotiṣṭoma has already been introduced, the word "yajeta" (one should sacrifice) is a restatement of it; thus, having recited the nominal stem "jyotis" alone and then drawing in the word "etena" (by this), the status of it as the name of the ritual action is established through its grammatical coordination with the action.
Furthermore, since the action is the object of restatement, the name—which is dependent upon that action—is likewise established in the same manner.

Because the word *jyotis* is seen to denote the Jyotiṣṭoma sacrifice in the passage "In every spring, [one should sacrifice] with the Jyotis," and because it is a matter of common worldly experience that a name can be indicated by a part of that name— just as the word *Bhīma* indicates Bhīmasena—
and because the meaning of the word *atha* as "immediacy" would be untenable if there were no connection [to a preceding topic],
and because enjoining another action qualified by a quality is simpler than enjoining a mere quality.

Since the injunction of a twelve-hundred-fold sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) is not taught as an original prescription (*utpatti-śiṣṭa*), it is logically established that it may be treated as an option alongside the thousand-fold fee (*sahasra-dakṣiṇā*) which is so taught;
thus, this is a restatement (*anuvāda*) for the purpose of prescribing the quality of a thousand-fold fee for the very Jyotiṣṭoma under discussion, and not a separate ritual action (*karmāntara*).
This being the prima facie view, it is replied: there would be an injunction of a quality (*guṇavidhi*) regarding the previous rite only if it were within that same context (*prakaraṇa*).
But that [cognition] is interrupted;

for even when [the word] is in close proximity, a different designation perceived as having a meaning unconnected to the preceding [meaning]—in accordance with the maxim "it is improper for a single word to have multiple meanings"—generally excludes the previous cognition and produces a new cognition because it has a different meaning. This is established by common experience.

In common usage, people do not understand from the word "deva" that Devadatta is the recipient of a cow or that the god [Indra] is the recipient of a horse—as in the expression "give a cow to Devadatta" or "give a horse to the god.

Likewise, when the word "yajeta" (one should sacrifice) is heard later on, because it is separated by words whose meanings are unrelated, it does not evoke the cognition of that same ritual action; thus, being incapable of merely enjoining an accessory for that [action], it enjoins a distinct ritual action altogether.

Furthermore, one cannot resort to figurative indication (*lakṣaṇā*) based on the impossibility [of the primary sense] in a single instance—such as the word *jyotis* being applied to the *Jyotiṣṭoma*—when no such impossibility exists; therefore, a figurative interpretation is not appropriate here.
For the word *gaṅgā* is not metaphorical (lākṣaṇika) in the expression "the hamlet on the Gaṅgā" simply because it is metaphorical in the expression "the fish in the Gaṅgā.

Furthermore, even when a distinction has first been indicated by another name, its grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with the word *yajati* merely establishes that it is a name for the ritual action (*karmanāmadheya*); it is not capable of removing the cognition of distinction produced by that other name. Thus, the word *atha* has the sense of introducing a new topic (*adhikārārtha*), indicating a different context (*prakaraṇāntaratā*).
And since this word "this" (eṣa) refers back to that which is being introduced, there is a distinction [of the rite] due to the difference in designation.
One might object: "Granted that there is a difference of action due to a different designation, what does that have to do with the present case? To this he says:
"And there is [this distinction] here, as in the cases of those enjoined in other Vedāntas."
Just as designations such as "Kāṭhaka" and others are applied to a book, so too are they used by worldly people for knowledge;

nor is there any distinction on account of which [the term] would be primary with respect to the book and secondary with respect to knowledge. Furthermore, the act of composing is the common basis for the application [of the name] to both the book and the knowledge.
Therefore, even for knowledge (jñāna), there is a verbal designation (samākhyā).

And so, when another designation heard in proximity to the Jyotiṣṭoma serves as an indicator (pratīka) that differentiates the ritual action, then what need is there to mention the case of a knowledge belonging to a different recensional branch (śākhāntarīya), which is most remote and designated by a different, non-indicative name? Thus it is understood.
Likewise, a difference in form is well known to indicate a difference in ritual action, as in such cases as "The *āmikṣā* is for the Viśvedevas; the *vājina* is for the Vājins.
This is recorded in the scripture: "One pours curd into heated milk; that is the *āmikṣā* for the Viśvedevas.
For here, a sacrifice inferred from the relationship between the substance and the deity is enjoined.
Immediately following that, this is handed down in scripture: "The whey for the Vājins.

Here, a doubt arises: is the whey (vājina) enjoined as a subordinate element (guṇa) in the very same ritual action as the preceding one, or is a new, distinct ritual action—characterized by different materials and deities—enjoined?
What, then, is the prima facie position (pūrvapakṣa)?

Since enjoining a different action qualified by a different substance and deity would entail the fault of excessive complexity in the injunction (*vidhigaurava*), as well as the fault of postulating a different action and a different transcendental result (*apūrva*), there is no injunction of a different action; rather, it is an injunction of the *vājina* substance within the very same prior action. Nor is it correct to argue that, because the quality of curd (*āmikṣā*) is enjoined at the time of the action's origination (*utpattiśiṣṭa*), the *vājina* finds no room there and thus necessitates a different action.

Since both sentences operate at the same time, the *āmikṣā* and the *vājina* are taught equally in their production; thus, the *āmikṣā* is not "already taught" [in a prior sense]. How then could the ritual act, being already occupied by this [āmikṣā], not admit the *vājina*?

Nor is there a scriptural (*śrauta*) connection of the Viśvedevas with the *āmikṣā* in the word *vaiśvadevī*, by virtue of which it might be stronger than the connection with the *vājina* understood through syntactical context (*vākya*), for both are cognized as depending on other words.
Because there is no difference in their being understood through syntactical connection (*vākya*).

Indeed, when it is said "vaiśvadevī" (belonging to the Viśvedevas), we do not determine that it refers to the *āmikṣā* (curd-mixture) without depending on the word "*āmikṣā*" itself. Or, even if its status as being directly expressed by the Vedic text (*śrautatva*) were granted, nevertheless, the word "vājibhyaḥ" (to the Vājins) indicates the Viśvedevas who are connected to that [curd-mixture], based on the etymological derivation: "vāja" means food, and since the *āmikṣā* is that food, they possess it.
Although the word *vājī* is distinct from the word *viśvedeva*,

deityhood (*devatātva*) resides in that very word by which the injunction (*codanā*) is expressed, and not in another word; otherwise, because the referent would be one and the same, it would follow that the words *sūrya* and *āditya*— and thus the two forms *sūrya* and *āditya*— would constitute a single deity.

Nevertheless, because the word *vājinaḥ* is traditionally understood to have the sense of a pronoun (*sarvanāman*), and because a pronoun refers to what is proximate, and because the Viśvedevas have been brought into proximity by the word *viśvedeva*, these [deities] are presented by the word *vājinaḥ* as preceded by that very term; they are not independent, like the words *sūrya* or *āditya*.

Thus, for the purpose of indicating them, the word *vājinaḥ* indicates the deity precisely as it is qualified by the Viśvedevas; therefore, there is no difference in the deity due to the presence of different words.

Therefore, since the *vājina* (curd-whey) is enjoined for the Viśvedevas by depending upon its connection with the *āmikṣā* (coagulated milk), it is not sublated by the *āmikṣā*, but rather is combined with it; thus, it is concluded that this is not a separate ritual action (*karmāntara*), but rather a single ritual action endowed with two substances is enjoined by two sentences. To this, it is replied: This would indeed be so if the word "vaiśvadevī" did not denote the *āmikṣā* through the force of the secondary derivative suffix (*taddhita*).

However, because it is traditionally taught that the secondary suffix (*taddhita*) [denotes] the sense of a pronoun (*sarvanāman*) as in "of this" (*asya*), and because the proximate substantive is the referent of the pronoun, the function of the secondary suffix applies specifically to that [substantive], and not to all the gods (*viśve devāḥ*),
nor to their relationship, nor merely to anything related to them.
If this is so, why do we not understand *āmikṣā* from the word *vaiśvadevī* alone, and why do we require the word *āmikṣā*?
We do not understand it because the denotative power of a word ending in a *taddhita* suffix does not terminate there; we require [the other word] for that denotation to reach its completion.
For only a word whose denotative function has reached its conclusion is capable of producing a cognition of the meaning.

But this [word *tad*], denoting a specific object present nearby, requires that proximity and thus depends upon the word *āmikṣā* which brings about that proximity. Therefore, how could there be the consequence of a cognition of *āmikṣā* independent of the word *āmikṣā*, or how could there be independence with respect to it?

Consequently, even though there is dependence on another word, that word which expresses its meaning while depending on another word is both based on direct audition (*śrauta*) and more powerful, because it is understood from a word that arises first and constitutes a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*).

However, that which is to be understood through the comprehension of word-meanings denoted by words whose denotative function has already been exhausted, and which is reached by the final cognition as the meaning of a sentence, is weak; thus, because it is subordinated to the quality characterized as *āmikṣā* (curd-milk) understood through the direct statement (*śruti*) of the secondary derivative suffix (*taddhita*), the substance *vājina* (whey), which lacks connection with the previous action,
differentiates itself from the previous [action] by virtue of its own relationship.

And this being the case, *āmikṣā*— whose status as a means is understood as constant and independent— will not undergo either option (*vikalpa*) or conjunction (*samuccaya*) with the substance denoted by the word "horse" (*vājina*). Furthermore, because it functions independently due to its lack of dependence on the nature of a horse, the word *vājin* cannot in any way be etymologically derived (*yaugika*) to indicate the deity Viśvedevas— which is understood from the word *vaiśvadevī* as a subordinate element (*upasarjanībhūta*) in relation to the substance *āmikṣā*—
for a pronoun has as its scope only that which is under discussion (*prakṛta*).
Furthermore, that which is the primary subject is said to be the topic under discussion, not the subordinate element;

and in matters established by valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), the assumption of a ritual injunction (*vidhi*) and its attendant complexity (*gaurava*) must indeed be accepted, because the object of a *pramāṇa* is reality.

Therefore, just as in this case [of the *udbhid* sacrifice] there is a distinction of rites due to a quality that cannot belong to the previous rite, so too here the knowledge of the six fires (*ṣaḍagnividyā*) is distinct from the knowledge of the five fires (*pañcāgnividyā*).
Thus, in the dialogues concerning the vital breaths (*prāṇasaṃvāda*), there is a difference of knowledge (*vidyābheda*) due to the presence of fewer or more elements.
Likewise, a specific attribute (*dharmaviśeṣa*) also establishes a difference of ritual action (*karmabheda*).
For instance, the Taittirīyas, who study the *Kārīrī* texts, practice eating on the ground, whereas others do not.
Likewise, some who study the Agni-veda fetch water-jars for their teacher, while others do not;
similarly, some who study the Aśvamedha bring fodder for the horse, while others do not;
yet others practice an entirely different dharma.
Furthermore, it is not logical that those very same rituals should both require and not require the assistance produced by the enjoyment of the earth and so forth;
therefore, it is understood that the rituals in those various branches are distinct.
To the question, "Let that be so, but what does this have to do with the matter at hand? he says:
"And it exists here" means that for other reciters of the Veda, it does not exist; this is the ellipsis.
Likewise, [the faults of] tautology and so forth [apply].
In passages such as "He offers the samidhs," the word *yajati* (he sacrifices) is repeated five times.
In that regard, is there a single ritual production (*karmabhāvanā*), or are there indeed five?
What, then, is the prima facie position?

Since the *bhāvanā* is stated to be distinct in the section concerning "different words" (*śabdāntarādhikaraṇa*) due to the difference in the connection with the meaning of the verbal root (*dhātvartha*), and since a distinction in the meaning of the root is impossible without a distinction in the root itself, the ritual *bhāvanā* enjoined by the first-occurring sentence, "He offers the *samits*" (*samidho yajati*), is subsequently restated (*anūdyate*) by the following sentences.

Nor can it be argued that this is not a restatement (anuvāda) simply because there is no purpose, for one cannot demand a purpose for that which is established by a means of valid cognition (pramāṇa). Furthermore, if there were a difference in the ritual action (karman) and its productive activity (bhāvanā), it would entail the undesirable consequence of postulating multiple unseen potencies (apūrva); therefore, it follows that a single ritual action is that which possesses a single intermediate operation consisting of a single apūrva. To this prima facie view, the following is stated: "For the sentences concerning the *samit* and other [faggots] are indeed independent of one another."
Although all [the Vedas] are equally worthy of being studied first, they are studied sequentially because simultaneous study is impossible;
however, this sequence is not the primary motivator for their arrangement.
For it would be the motivator only if they were mutually dependent and formed a single syntactical unit (*ekavākyatva*).
Since there is no priority [of the action] in that case, the very notion of "attainment" does not exist; therefore, what is being restated, and of what?
For a mere mental recollection (*viparivṛtti*) lacks the capacity to set aside the definition of an injunction as that which impels toward what has not otherwise been undertaken by default.

Indeed, when a quality is heard, if one were to enjoin an action qualified by that quality, there would be the burden of a complex injunction; thus, out of fear of such complexity, there arises a need for a restatement of the action in order to achieve the simplicity of enjoining the quality alone, and it is in this regard that the recollection is of assistance.

Just as in the sentence "He offers with curds" (*dadhnā juhoti*), which is intent upon enjoining the curds, there is a restatement (*anuvāda*) of the oblation (*homa*) enjoined by "He performs the Agnihotra," which is present [in the mind] through recollection;
and in this case, there is no distinction [of the act] based on the accessory (*guṇa*).
Because words such as *samit* and others, being names of rituals (*karmanāmadheya*), lack the quality of denoting a subordinate attribute (*guṇavacana*),

and because no distinction is perceived, it cannot be determined which is the restatement (*anuvāda*) of a ritual enjoined by a particular word and which is the injunction of an attribute (*guṇavidhi*). Furthermore, that which is called "unprecedented" (*apūrva*)— like the *Jyotiṣṭoma* and other sacrifices— is not first understood as having a connection with an injunction.
For an action being enjoined by means of a previously interrupted cognition would exclude it from its prior designation;

however, since *samit* and the others are understood from the very beginning as being in grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with the action, they acquire the status of names for that action by virtue of that fact.
Thus, when the verb is a restatement (*anuvāda*), these are restatements, and when it is an injunction (*vidhi*), they are injunctions; they do not exercise independent authority over anything.

Therefore, since this repetition pertains to the injunction of an action not otherwise obtained— which is established by its own inherent force— it differentiates the meditative realization (*bhāvanā*) by differentiating the factors bound to that realization; just as it does so for the action, so too will this repetition differentiate the knowledges (*vidyās*) enjoined in one recension from those enjoined in other recensions.
And because of incapacity:

for a single person is not able to combine meditations consisting of the cognitions found in all Vedāntas, due to the inability to study all the Vedāntas; for if one were to combine the meaning of what has not been studied, it would result in the futility of the injunction to study.
However, if the meditations differ according to each branch (śākhā), this fault does not arise.
And because of the difference in their conclusions:
for some reciters of the Vedic branches, the conclusion occurs with the statement that the syllable Om is the self of all; for others, it occurs elsewhere.
Therefore, there is also a distinction between the meditations.
Furthermore, a distinction is established by the observation of other purposes;
for instance, in the passage, "One who has not observed the vow does not study this," the absence of study on the part of one who has not observed the vow indicates the absence of meditation.
In some cases, because study is observed even for one who has not performed the vows, it is understood that meditation (*upāsana*) exists [there too].
Therefore, there is a difference in meditation.
To this, he states the established conclusion (*siddhānta*):
"Based on all Vedānta texts, because there is no difference in the injunctions and so forth.
He explains this:
"The cognitions based on all Vedānta texts—the means of valid knowledge consisting of those various Vedānta passages—must be identical in each respective Vedānta text."
The meaning is that those [details] which are found in one Vedānta are the very same in other Vedāntas as well;
this is because there is no difference in the injunctions and so forth.
By the word "and so forth" (ādi), the connection, form, and name are included.
And here, "codanā" (impulsion) refers to that which impels; it is human effort, for that is indeed the activity of a person.
In that regard, this [effort] operates toward that which is delimited by the meaning of verbal roots such as *hu* (to sacrifice), and so forth.
Just as the human effort consisting of the act of pouring water and so forth— which is the limiting factor for that renunciation dedicated to a deity— is the same in other recensions (*śākhā*),
so too here the human effort directed toward the knowledge of the pre-eminence and excellence of the vital breath (*prāṇa*) is the very same as in other recensions.
Likewise, the connection with the fruit, characterized by becoming the eldest and most excellent, is also the same.
The form (rūpa) is also the same;

just as the form consisting of the substance and deity in a sacrifice is identical across different recensional branches (śākhā), so too the object of knowledge—namely, the nature of the breath's primacy and excellence—is the same in one branch as it is in other branches. //1//
Regarding the phrase "some particular feature":

it is logical that even when the Agniṣomīya [sacrifice], having already come into being, is subsequently connected with such features as the eleven potsherds (*ekādaśakapāla*), there is no difference [in its essential nature].

Since that [quality] which has arisen is recognized everywhere, whereas here the difference in quality pertains only to the state of being produced in the fires, how is it that it does not cause a division, as in the case of the *vaiśvadevī* offering?
With this distinction in mind, the author of the Sūtras raises the objection:
"If it be argued that there is no [division] because of the difference [of the fires]" (BBs 3.3.2a).
The refutation is a portion of the Sūtra: "not even in one.
For the Vājasaneyins as well, exactly five fires pertaining to the *saṃpanna* [meditation] are prescribed, just as for the Chāndogyas.
The sixth fire, however, is restated for the sake of completing the enumeration and is not prescribed;
whereas in the original production [of the Vaiśvadevī sacrifice], a quality is indeed prescribed—let there be a distinction on this basis.
Alternatively, even among the Chāndogyas, the sixth fire is certainly recited.
Alternatively,

let there be the injunction of six fires for the Vājasaneyins, and let it not exist for the Chāndogyas; nevertheless, because the number five is not enjoined [there], that number is not "enjoined as a primary element" (utpatti-śiṣṭa), but rather the number already present in the fires is restated as a result of their accumulation.
In order to exclude the fires that are merely superimposed (sāṃpādika),
there is recognition (*pratyabhijñā*) of those [fires] from which their origination occurs;

and since a number that is not so recognized cannot be the subject of a restatement (*anuvāda*), and because an additional element being enjoined would result in an option— as in the case of the *ṣoḍaśin* cup— the knowledge in different recensions (*śākhā*) is not distinct.

Since it is not established that [the rites] are taught as originating from the originative injunction (*utpattiśiṣṭa*), the dialogues with the vital breaths (*prāṇasaṃvāda*) and so forth are also recognized as non-different across those various recensional branches (*śākhā*). //2//

Because of the nature of the study of one's own Veda (*svādhyāya*), because of the qualification for the *Samācāra*, and because of its similarity to animal sacrifices (*sava*), there is a restriction regarding that [study].

(BBs 3,3.3) For those by whom knowledge is to be known through the means of the Ātharvaṇika texts, the fruit is bestowed only when it is understood from the text obtained through study preceded by the "Head-vow" (*śirovrata*); not otherwise.

However, it is understood from the connection with the study of the Atharvaṇa texts that this very same knowledge yields its fruit for others, such as those following the Chāndogya and other traditions, provided they have observed the Śirovrata.
And that connection [with the Atharvaṇa] is understood from the traditional recitation: "One who has not observed the vow does not study this";

furthermore, even though there is a connection with the knowledge in the statement, "To them alone one should declare this Brahma-knowledge," the use of the pronoun "this" (etām), which refers back to what has been previously mentioned, does not contradict the connection with the study; thus, it is the knowledge prescribed by the Atharvaṇa that is being spoken of.

Thus, all these seven oblations, beginning with those for Surya and ending with the Śataudana, are performed by the followers of the Atharvaveda in a single Atharvaṇika fire, not in the three sacred fires (tretā). //3//
Furthermore, it demonstrates the unity of knowledge. 3.3.4.1.4. BBs 3,3.4.

Since the unity of knowledge is seen repeatedly in the Vedas, even in cases where the Veda does not explicitly state the unity of various knowledges of Brahman with attributes (*saguṇa-brahma-vidyā*), those knowledges—being recited in that same context and having that same nature—are understood to be one by virtue of being seen in such a majority of instances.
For instance, seeing something written among a majority of "foremost" items, the thought arises: "This too must be foremost."
As for the claim that there is a distinction between meditations based on designations such as "Kāṭhaka" and so forth, that is incorrect.
For these designations are human in origin, applied to those recensional branches (*śākhā*) due to their connection with the teachings of Kaṭha and others, but not to the meditations themselves.
Indeed, these [meditations] were not proclaimed by Kaṭha and the rest, nor is the performance of these distinguished from the performance of others by Kaṭha and his followers.

Nor can it be assumed that these [passages] denote meditations (*upāsanā*), given that they could possibly be applied to the texts merely because they were spoken by Kaṭha, and that, through connection with that [name], they might somehow be applied to meditations by means of figurative indication (*lakṣaṇā*).
Furthermore, difference or non-difference in those [names] is not the cause for difference or non-difference in the knowledge [they convey].
Let it not be that, due to the non-difference of these [texts], there arises a unity among the cognitions belonging to a single branch, as would be the case for each [text] respectively.

Furthermore, since these designations—such as "Kaṭha" and so forth—are based on the oral teachings of persons like Kaṭha, it would follow as an impossibility that the distinction between cognitions based on them did not exist prior to Kaṭha and others, yet exists now.
Therefore, the distinction is not established by designation.
Even repetition does not cause differentiation here.
It is logical that the repetition of the *samidh* and other offerings occurring within a single recension (*śākhā*) acts as a differentiator;

for in that case, the inherent nature of an injunction (*vidhitva*)—namely, making known what was unknown and impelling one to act who has not yet acted—would otherwise be contradicted. However, in the case of different recensions, even though the text is one, there is no contradiction of the inherent nature of an injunction, because the students are different persons.
Thus, incapacity also is not a cause for difference. There is a rule regarding study: "One's own Vedic recension (svādhyāya) is to be studied.
Consequently, one will learn from other experts in that science those matters not contained in one's own recension and incorporate them [into one's practice].
Furthermore, the completion [of a whole] is designated even when only one of its constituent parts is completed.

For example, they designate the completion of the Jyotiṣṭoma sacrifice during the performance of the Adhvaryu's duties by saying, "The Jyotiṣṭoma is finished. Therefore, even a difference in completion is not a ground for a difference in meditation. Thus, since there is no sublation and because there is no distinction in the injunctions and so forth, it is established that the meditations taught in all the Vedāntas are one and the same. //4//

Having raised a certain objection regarding a specific point, the author of the Sūtras stated a matter already established in the previous treatise for the sake of proving the point to be explained hereafter.
The Sūtra is presented for the purpose of demonstrating the motive for this reflection:
"And [the conclusion] is the same, because there is no difference in meaning, as in the case of a supplementary injunction" (BBs 3.3.5).
Here, one raises this doubt: "Let it be so..."

Although the cognition [of the ritual] is one and the same across all recensions (*śākhā*), it does not follow that the subsidiary elements (*aṅga*) mentioned in other recensions must be combined (*upasaṃhāra*) within that [single rite] mentioned in another recension.

This is because the benefit of that single action is accomplished by exactly as many subsidiary elements as are prescribed in one recension, with no requirement for more. And if there were such a requirement, then even those additional elements would be prescribed therein.

And it has not been enjoined [as mandatory]. Therefore, just as an occasional rite (*naimittika-karma*), although enjoined with all its constituent parts (*aṅga*), is nonetheless assisted by the benefit produced by only so many parts as can be performed when one lacks the capacity, so too here it will be the same, precisely because other constituent parts have not been enjoined.

This being the position reached, it is said in reply: Since the oneness of the ritual action (*karman*) is established in all cases, a restriction of its auxiliary benefits (*upakāra*) is not tenable according to the principle of the *Gṛhamedhīya* sacrifice.
For it is not logical that the very same ritual action should at one time require a particular auxiliary and at another time not require it.

However, in the case of a conditional rite (*naimittika*), because it must necessarily be performed in accordance with the occasion (*nimitta*), and because it is impossible for the inclusion of all auxiliaries to be constant, a restriction of the auxiliary benefits is postulated.

In the case of the *gṛhamedhīya* sacrifice, since the *codaka* (transfer rule) brings forward the entire mass of archetypal auxiliaries (*prākṛta-upakāra-piṇḍa*), the prescription of the two *ājyabhāga* offerings would result in a restriction of those auxiliaries.

However, in this case [of the *śākhāntara*], the prescription of a few specific members merely enjoins those particular parts and does not exclude the others; nor is it a case where, upon the arrival of the entire mass of archetypal auxiliaries via the *codaka*, there is a prescription of only that portion as in the case of the *ājyabhāgas*.
Therefore, in reality, the inclusion of all constituent parts of ritual actions is the general rule; it is not proper to set this aside unless there is a powerful sublationary factor. //5//
If it is argued that there is a difference [in their nature] based on the scriptural statement, we say no, because there is no distinction.
There are two kinds, of two types, among the offspring of Prajāpati: the gods and the asuras.
Thereupon, the gods were indeed the younger and the asuras the elder.
The gods were endowed with a sattvic intellect born of the scriptures;
for they shine, therefore they are called "devas."

Those whose minds are not fashioned by scripture and reasoning, who are dominated by tamasic activity, and who— being *asura*s— delight in various objects through impure vital breaths (*prāṇa*) that are devoid of the senses, are for this very reason the "older" ones; whereas these gods are "younger," because true knowledge is preceded by ignorance.

The emergence of the sattvic function and the suppression of the tāmasa function of Prajāpati Prāṇa occur at one time; at another time, the emergence of the tāmasa function and the suppression of the sattvic functions occur.
This is their rivalry.
Those gods said,

"Come, let us overcome the Asuras by means of the Udgītha in this sacrificial rite; let us conquer the Asuras through this ritual action characterized by the Udgātṛ priest, who is defined by the Sāman-chanting portion known as the Udgītha, in this sacrificial rite of exorcism."

Having censured speech, breath, sight, hearing, and mind by means of the textual sequence beginning with "They said to Speech," on the grounds that they were pierced by the evil of the Asuras, they then said to this principal breath— the one residing in the mouth (āsanya), situated within the cavity of the mouth—
namely the deity presiding over breath: "Do thou sing for us."
Having agreed, saying "So be it," the vital breath (*prāṇa*) sang the *udgītha* for them. The Asuras understood: "By means of this *udgātṛ* priest, the gods will surpass us.

They rushed upon him and pierced him with evil (*pāpman*). Just as a clod of earth, having struck a stone or reached it, crumbles away, so did the Asuras, crumbling away, perish scattering in all directions.
This same point is stated concisely:
Regarding the phrase "in the Vājasaneyaka," he states that this is likewise said in the Chāndogya as well:
"tathā chāndogye 'pi."
Having shown the subject matter, he reflects:
"In that regard, there is doubt. [He states] the prima facie position (*pūrvapakṣa*).
He accepts [the view] that "the knowledge is one," and thus he refutes the prima facie position (pūrvapakṣa).

"Is it not improper?"—this means that in one place Prāṇa is spoken of as the Udgātṛ, while in another he is spoken of as the act of singing (udgāna); thus there is a clear distinction between the agent and the action.
He provides the resolution:
This is not a fault;
because of the recognition of many more forms, that which is not being recognized must be understood through secondary indication (lakṣaṇā),
and this applies not only to another recensional branch (śākhāntara).

He states that this [meditation] is seen even in a single branch, and yet there is no difference in the knowledge (*vidyā*) therein: "And also among the Vājasaneyins. Furthermore, the prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*) is that, for the sake of favoring the recognition of the same form in its many aspects, by the word "Om" one must indicate the *udgītha* itself through its constituent part, the *udgītha*. //6//
Or rather [it is not so], because of the difference in context, as in the case of the "higher than the high" (*parovarīyastva*) and so forth.

Even though there is a greater degree of recognition (*pratyabhijñāna*), because of the difference in the opening statement (*upakrama*) and because the concluding portion (*upasaṃhāra*) is described in accordance with that opening, within a single sentence there is a repeated mention of that very same *udgītha*; thus, in the case of figurative indication (*lakṣaṇā*), [the two are distinct].
In the Vājasaneyaka, the established conclusion (rāddhānta) is that there is a difference between the two knowledges due to the absence of authoritative evidence.
Having introduced the syllable *oṃ* as the object of meditation, there follows an explanatory exposition (*upavyākhyāna*) of its qualities, such as being the "most flavorful" (*rasatama*).
For instance, among the elements, earth, plants, persons, speech, Ṛg-verses, and Sāman-chants, each subsequent item is described as being more flavorful and more essential than the preceding one.
Among all of these, the *oṃkāra* is declared in the *Chāndogya* to be the most excellent essence;
nor is there any difference in the intended meaning,
for in one case the *udgītha* and the *udgātṛ* are intended as objects of meditation, while in the other case it is the *oṃkāra*, which is a constituent part of that [same *udgītha*].

For it is said in the passage concerning prosperity (*abhyudaya*): "Verily, he who, when the moon rises before his sacrificial oblation has been set out, is deprived of offspring and cattle and causes his rival to prosper—let him divide the rice grains into three parts; those which are medium-sized, let him offer them to Agni..."

"One should offer a cake on eight potsherds to Dātṛ; those [grains] which are the largest, he should offer as a caru-oblation to Indra Pradātṛ; those which are the smallest, he should offer as a caru-oblation cooked in milk to Viṣṇu Śipiviṣṭa.

Regarding this, there is a doubt: is this a separate sacrifice enjoined when there is a transgression of time, or is it a removal of the deities from those very same rites already under discussion when the transgression of time occurs as the occasion?

This, then, is the subject matter here: on the very day of the new moon (amāvāsyā), for the sake of the New Moon sacrifice (darśakarman), there is the preparation of the altar, the rite of bringing forward the fire (agnipraṇayana), and the purificatory rites (saṃskāra) for the sacrificer, such as the observance of vows; furthermore, the milking is for the purpose of obtaining curd. And on the first day of the lunar fortnight (pratipad), the commencement of the New Moon sacrifice takes place—this is the authentic sequence of performance.

However, in the case of a sacrificer who, due to some error, has commenced the ritual performance on the fourteenth day itself under the mistaken impression that it is the new moon day (amāvāsyā), and the moon rises while he is engaged in it—for him this is heard [in the scripture]: "By that sacrificer for whom the moon has risen, having completed the entitlement based on the occasion (*nimittādhikāra*) on that very new moon day, he should perform the acts such as the removal of the altar (*vedyuddharaṇa*) on that same day, and then commence the Darśa sacrifice on the first day of the lunar fortnight (*pratipad*)."

In this regard, concerning prosperity (*abhyudaya*), is this an occasional rite (*naimittika*) enjoined as a separate ritual act from the New Moon sacrifice (*darśa*), or is another deity prescribed for that very same New Moon ritual by means of the removal of the previous deities?
In this matter, because only the portions of the oblation are mentioned and because of the necessity of prescribing the *caru* (boiled rice), it is a separate ritual act.
For if it were heard [in the scripture] that "one should divide the oblations from the previous deities," then those very same oblations would [be offered] to another deity.

The injunctions [regarding the deities] do not necessitate a different ritual act; rather, it is the very same original ritual that should have its original oblation-material (havis) deprived of its former deity and joined with another deity.

Furthermore, because the scriptural statement "one should divide the rice-grains into three parts" prescribes the division of the oblation itself according to the sequence of middle-sized grains and so forth, the original connection is not removed.

Regarding the phrase "the previous deity in the oblation": when the oblation is already occupied by a previous deity, another deity being heard of [in the text] without having found scope would lead to the understanding of a distinct ritual action (*karmāntara*).
Furthermore, [this applies] when [the action] is already established.
In the previous ritual action, the connection of curd with rice, milk with rice, and [the connection] with deities such as Indra would have to be enjoined;
furthermore, since the status of being a *caru* (cooked sacrificial oblation) has not been enjoined here, that too would have to be enjoined.
Such being the case, because multiple subordinate elements (*guṇa*) would be enjoined within a single ritual action, there would be a syntactical split (*vākyabheda*).

However, it is possible to enjoin a new action (*karmāntara*)—characterized by multiple qualities—by means of a single effort; therefore, when there is a specific occasion (*nimitta*), a distinct rite is enjoined.
Since the *darśa* sacrifice is omitted due to the lapse of the proper time, this being the position reached, it is replied: it is not a different rite.
Because, following the previous deity, another deity is enjoined for the oblation (*havis*) after first effecting its division upon the occurrence of the occasion.
And because the purpose [of the action] is already established by its own meaning.

This would be so if this sentence were intended to enjoin the threefold division of the rice grains— namely, "one should divide the rice grains into three parts"— but rather, having merely restated the threefold nature of the rice grains as already obtained from another sentence, it enjoins only the act of dividing itself.

In this regard, by considering other sentences, it is understood that [the offering is made] "to the previous deities"; however, the mention of "rice-grains" (taṇḍulān) is not intended to be significant, just as the "duality" was not significant for the oblation (havis).

Thus, sentences such as "those which are middle-sized" and so forth, once the connection with the previous deities has been removed, are able to enjoin a connection with different deities for that very same oblation within that same ritual without any obstacle.

Consequently, because the original context is recognized through the medium of the substance, even though there is a connection with different deities, there can be no assumption of a separate ritual act.
Consequently, even though [the primary rite] has been completed, those very same rituals must be performed again for the sake of fulfilling the requirements of the occasional (naimittika) injunction.
Nor is there an injunction regarding the sacrificial oblation (*caru*) and the locative sense of "in curd" (*dadhani*), because both of these are already established by the context;
for in the ritual under discussion, the grinding of rice grains, the spreading out [of the dough], the baking of the *puroḍāśa* cake, and so forth, as well as the curd and milk, are already obtained.

In that context, regarding the occasion for prosperity (*abhyudaya*), by the sentence "one should divide the rice-grains mixed with curds and mixed with milk," the removal of the previous deities is effected; subsequently, by the sentences beginning with "those which are the middle ones" (*ye madhyamāḥ*), a connection with other deities is established.
Furthermore, the preparation of a sacrificial cake (*puroḍāśa*) is not possible with only a small quantity of rice-grains mixed with abundant curds and milk.

Thus, when the *puroḍāśa* cake is removed, its purpose—the spreading [of the dough]—is also removed; however, the baking is not removed because there is no exception to it, and thus that which is already implied by the purpose is enjoined.
Or, let there be the assumption of multiple sentences, for this too is logical due to the force of understanding the context of the subject matter under discussion.
Therefore, it is established that this is indeed that same ritual action and not a different action;

however, in the sentence concerning the desire for cattle (*paśukāma*), there is an injunction for a new ritual action (*apūrvakarman*), even though it shares a similar form with the sentences concerning prosperity (*abhyudaya*).

"He who desires cattle should, after performing the New Moon sacrifice, drive away the calves; those that are the largest, he should offer as an eight-potherd cake to Agni Sanimat; those that are of middle size, he should offer as a cooked mess of boiled milk in a pot to Viṣṇu Śipiviṣṭa; and those that are the smallest, he should offer as a cooked mess of curds to Indra Pradātṛ."

For here, in the statement "having performed the New Moon sacrifice," the injunction for the *paśukāmā-iṣṭi* occurs once the sacrifice is completed; it is not logical to regard this as an injunction for a different sacrifice due to the non-continuation of the previous rite, as in the case of the *parovarīyas-tva* and other examples. Just as, despite the similarity of the meditations on the *udgītha*, the meditation on the *udgītha* characterized by qualities such as being golden and having black pupils located in the sun is distinct from [the basic] *udgītha* meditation, so too is this case.
Because it is higher than the high and more excellent than the excellent, the Udgītha has become the "higher-than-high" (parovarīyas), having attained the nature of the Supreme Self;
for this very reason, it is infinite.

In order to cultivate the vision of the Supreme Self within the Udgītha, the text points to the Supreme Self by means of the word "ether" (ākāśa), stating: "For ether is indeed greater than these elements. //7//
If it is argued that [the identity] is established by name, that has already been addressed: "But even that exists" (BBs 3.3.8).
When a distinction is perceived more clearly, the identity of names is not proof of non-difference, because that would lead to an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*).
Furthermore, when examining the literal words of the Vedic revelation (śruti), the cognition of difference is both internal and independent;
whereas the identity of name is external, being outside the revealed text, and dependent, being of human origin.
Therefore, it is weak and not capable of establishing non-difference. //8//

And because of pervasion, [the theory of] superimposition is consistent. Regarding the phrase "what is called superimposition": it refers to the appearance of one thing in the form of another, as when the nature of silver is seen in mother-of-pearl, or the nature of a snake is seen in a rope. This is what is meant by superimposition. Furthermore, this superimposition is not a relation between two real entities; rather, it is the cognition of one thing appearing as another. For example, when a person whose vision is impaired sees a double moon, that second moon is not a real entity existing apart from the first; rather, it is simply the single moon appearing in a dual form due to a defect in the visual faculty. Similarly, the superimposition of the self upon the body and other non-self objects is merely the appearance of the self in the form of those things, and not the existence of a real entity distinct from the self. Therefore, superimposition is defined as the cognition of one thing appearing as another. Moreover, this superimposition is beginningless, for it has no known origin in time. It is sustained by the mutual latent impressions (*vāsanā*) of the self and the non-self, and it persists through the cycle of transmigration. Thus, it is established that superimposition is the cause of all worldly activity and the basis for the entire system of valid knowledge. And because of its pervasion over all objects of experience, the theory of superimposition is the most consistent and appropriate explanation. This concludes the section on superimposition. *Brahmasūtrabhāṣya* 3.3.4.9. *Brahmasiddhi* 3.3.9.
