Superimposition (*adhyāsa*) is figurative cognition (*gauṇī buddhi*).

Just as, for example, even while the cognition and designation of "boy" has not ceased in a boy, there occurs the application of the cognition and designation of "lion," such that one says, "The boy is a lion";
likewise, there is the cognition of Vāsudeva in an image, and the cognition of Brahman in a name; similarly, there are the cognition and designation of the *udgītha* in the syllable *oṃ*.
And the exclusions and the singular qualifiers have been stated;
furthermore, the employment of two words for a single meaning is observed.

Just as in the case of "the *āmikṣā* [curd-mixture] belongs to Viśvedevas" or "consciousness is bliss," and as in the commentary where synonyms are used together— such as *sindhura*, *karī*, *pika*, and *kokila*—
having reflected upon the position characterized by indecision (*anadhyavasāya*), he adopts it:
Regarding the phrase "one of them":
he states the established conclusion (siddhānta)—this is what is being said: "And because of pervasion."

Since the syllable *oṃ* occurs at the beginning and end of every *anuvāka* and every *ṛc*, pervading all the Vedas, there arises the question: "Of what nature is this *oṃ*—qualified by which attributes such as being the source of all (*āpya*), etc.—and for the attainment of which specific fruits, such as the fulfillment of desires, is it enjoined as an object of meditation? In response to this expectation, it is specified by the word *udgītha*.

By the word *udgītha*, which denotes a particular division of the *Sāman* composed of parts beginning with the syllable *oṃ*, the syllable *oṃ*—which is a constituent part related to that whole—is indicated, because it is logically impossible for a whole to be identical with its own parts.
Furthermore, there is no indication by means of the word *oṃ* of the whole, namely the *udgītha*;
for it is the *oṃ*-syllable itself that will subsequently be explained as qualified by various attributes and various fruits.

Moreover, a word denoting a whole is seen to be used figuratively (by indication) for a part, just as one says "the village is burnt" or "the cloth is burnt" when only a portion of them has been consumed by fire.
In the case of superimposition (*adhyāsa*), however, there would be both figurative indication (*lakṣaṇā*) and the postulation of a fruit.
For instance, this meditation on the *udgītha* as the *praṇava* possessing qualities such as "attainment" (*āpti*) is distinct from other meditations on the *praṇava*.
Furthermore, no fruit is heard of here, as is the case in those meditations on "attainment" and so forth.
Therefore, it must be so conceived.
There is no such fault in a passage dedicated to the meditation on the *praṇava* connected with the *udgītha*.
Moreover, the secondary function (*lakṣaṇā*) is stronger than the figurative function (*gauṇī-vṛtti*), because of its parsimony.
For in the case of secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*), a word has as its primary referent that which is indicated (*lakṣya*), because that alone is included within the sentence-meaning.
For example, in the expression "a hamlet on the Gaṅgā," the bank—which is being indicated—is included in the sentence-meaning by virtue of being its locus (*adhikaraṇatayā*).

However, in the case of "the Vāhīka is an ox" (*gaur vāhīkaḥ*), the word "ox" does not have that [Vāhīka] as its primary referent, because it indicates through secondary indication things such as the dewlap, urine, and dung associated with an ox.

Moreover, because it conveys the Vāhīkas as being determined by that [similarity] and as possessing those qualities, the secondary function (*gauṇī vṛtti*) is weak; this is what was stated in the phrase "even in the case of indication" (*lakṣaṇāyām api tu*).
The secondary function is also described as "indication" (*lakṣaṇā*) because it is a constituent part of indication.
Even though...
Although the term *vaiśvadevī* applies to the *āmikṣā*, there is nevertheless a very clear difference in meaning. For the term *āmikṣā* applies to the *āmikṣā* by virtue of its form (*rūpa*),
whereas the term *vaiśvadevī* applies to that very same thing as qualified by the Viśvedevas.
Thus, even though there is a single referent in Brahman, the difference in the grounds for the application (*pravṛttinimitta*) of the two words "Vijñāna" and "Ānanda" is very clear;
furthermore, the explanations of both are distinct because their meanings are well-known and because they have different referents. The rest has a meaning that is not obscure. //9//
START BsVBh_3,3.5.10:
"Because of the non-difference of all [these], they are other than these.
BBs_3,3.10: "Because of the non-difference of all, they are elsewhere."

The prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) is as follows: because the word *evam* (thus) has the sense of referring to a specific mode of presentation that is proximate, and because what is presented by the word itself is proximate, whereas what occurs in another recension (*śākhāntara*) lacks such proximity due to being separated by a sequence [of other texts], the passage concerning the dialogue on the vital breath (*prāṇa*) in the Kauṣītaki Upaniṣad does not intend for the breath to be meditated upon through qualities such as being "most excellent" (*vasiṣṭha*), but rather only through its being "eldest" (*jyeṣṭha*) and "best" (*śreṣṭha*). The established conclusion (*siddhānta*), however, is this: it is true that the particle *evaṃ* refers to what is proximate, but "proximate" does not mean merely what is presented by the word itself. [Rather, it refers to the entire context. Thus, the breath is indeed to be meditated upon through those qualities such as being most excellent. This is because the word *evaṃ* refers to the entire preceding section, which includes the statement of the breath's qualities; therefore, the breath is to be meditated upon with all its attributes, including being most excellent. Furthermore, since the term "most excellent" (*śreṣṭha*) is used in the singular, it is understood that the intention is to refer to the single quality of being most excellent among all things, and not to a plurality of qualities. Consequently, the breath is to be meditated upon with all its stated qualities. Thus, there is no contradiction between the two scriptural passages. Therefore, the meditation on the breath is uniform across both recensions. This concludes the second section.
However, that which is necessarily implied by the meaning expressed by the word "yat" is indeed present in the intellect, being as close at hand as anything else.
For example, in the passage, "He whose *juhū* ladle is made of *parṇa*-wood," the sacrifice (*kratu*) is brought to mind by the *juhū*, because it is invariably connected with the sacrifice.

Therefore, due to the recognition of the object of meditation and its fruit, even though the specific variety [of meditation] not invariably connected to them is not explicitly stated here, it is nonetheless present in the intellect; thus, by the word "evam" (thus), which refers back to what has been introduced, [the meditation is established].
It is established that the reference is appropriate; for it is possible to refer [to this] by means of the syllable *om* occurring in the Kauṣītaki Brāhmaṇa.
Nevertheless, with the intention of saying "even granting this, we shall speak," the author of the Bhāṣya stated:
"Even so, by means of that very same realization occurring in the Vājasaneyi Brāhmaṇa."

"Loss of what has been heard" (śrutahāni) means that there would be the loss of the revealed scripture (śruta) taken alone, and the postulation of the non-revealed (akṣuta) as being accompanied by something else; the rest is self-evident. //10//
"Bliss and other qualities belong to the Principal [Brahman]," because there is an injunction for meditation upon it as possessing those qualities.
This section is intended for the sake of discernment by way of explaining the actual qualities;
so that the qualities such as "being the center of blessings" and those such as "having true desires," which belong to the one Brahman, do not become confused.
Thus, qualities such as bliss and consciousness would not be conflated with qualities such as omnipresence and eternity mentioned in other passages;
or, if there were such a conflation, qualities like being the "center of blessings" (*saṃyadvāmatva*) would likewise be conflated with qualities such as having true desires (*satyakāma*).
For there is no distinction whatsoever within the existence of Brahman, the substratum of attributes—this is the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*).
The established conclusion (rāddhānta), however, is that non-determination and determination reside respectively in the nature of the thing and in the state of being to be performed;
for the property of a thing persists as long as the thing itself exists.
It cannot be said that a property which is stated in one place does not exist simply because it is not stated elsewhere.

But that which is to be accomplished depends on human effort; and human effort, being enjoined with respect to Brahman as qualified by whatever attributes [are specified], extends only so far and cannot bring about even an unenjoined attribute, because it is dependent on injunction and because injunctions are fixed in their scope.

Therefore, qualities such as bliss and consciousness, which are stated as being the very nature of the reality of Brahman, are obtained wherever Brahman is heard of, even if they are not explicitly mentioned there.

It is established that [attributes] such as "the gathering of all desirable things" (*saṃyadvāma*) and so forth—which are objects of injunctions for the effort of meditative worship—subsist according to the injunction and not according to the actual state of reality.
However, the logical principle was demonstrated by superimposing the status of being an object of worship upon [attributes] such as "having joy as the head" (*priyaśiras*).
But in that case, [attributes] such as "the gathering of all desirable things" were indeed mentioned.
Joy (*moda*) is mere delight; supreme joy (*pramoda*) is intense delight. These two are mutually dependent increases and decreases. //11//
START BsVBh_3,3.6.12:
There is no attainment of [attributes] such as having "the beloved as the head" because increase and decrease occur only where there is difference. BBs_3,3.12 // 12 //
"But the others [are included] because of the commonality of their meaning. (BBs 3.3.13) // 13 //
START BsVBh_3,3.7.14:
[The sūtra] "For the sake of meditation, because there is no other purpose" (BBs 3,3.14) states:
"The objects are indeed superior to the sense organs."

Is it intended here that the "supremacy" (paratva) of all things— beginning with wealth— is to be established, or is the establishment of the supremacy of the others merely for the sake of establishing the supremacy of the Person alone?

In this regard, since the scriptural revelation establishes the supremacy of each thing beginning with wealth individually, and since that specific supremacy is possible for each as it is heard, it is not logical to determine a single supremacy for all of them by disregarding those respective [individual] supremacies.
Nor can it be argued that [the teaching] is impossible due to a lack of purpose,
because for each [of these deities], the designation as "the highest" (para) serves the purpose of meditation (adhyāna),
and because there are traditional teachings (smṛti) stating that those various meditations possess their own specific purposes.
For thus says the Smṛti: "Those who contemplate the senses remain here for ten Manvantaras;
those who contemplate the elements remain for a full hundred, and those who contemplate the ego remain for a thousand."
Ten thousand Buddhists remain free from fever;
a full hundred thousand remain as those who contemplate the Unmanifest.
But having attained the Person devoid of qualities, no calculation of time exists.
Thus,

since a division of sentences must be accepted by one who follows authoritative means of knowledge, these sentences— "the objects are indeed higher than the senses," and so forth— are stated as *prāptis* (propositions) because each of those [categories], beginning with the objects, is intended to be shown as being higher [than its predecessor]. This section, therefore, is devoted to the exposition of the true nature of reality (*vastutattva*).
It is understood that [the Upanishads] are not intent upon injunctions for meditation,
because such [injunctions] are not heard there. Therefore,
in this context, since the fact that the cognition [of Brahman] possesses an immediate purpose is observed, all [Upanishadic passages] have that cognition as their primary aim.
Moreover, it is observed that for one who knows the supreme state of Viṣṇu, there is the cessation of ignorance, which is the cause of all misfortunes and saṃsāra;
for it is seen in various places that the arising of the knowledge of reality is characterized by the cessation of error.
However, no such observed purpose exists for the cognition that takes wealth and other worldly objects as its primary aim.
Moreover, when a visible purpose is possible, it is not logical to postulate an invisible one;
and when it is possible for a text to have as its purport the supreme human goal, it is not appropriate for it to have a merely intermediate human goal.
Therefore, because it possesses a visible purpose, [the Veda does not aim at ritual action].
It is understood that this section is intended to establish the supremacy of the Puruṣa.
Furthermore, he states— “Moreover, by means of the negation of another”— that this alone is its meaning because of the [author’s] reverence for it.
But surely, there is no injunction for meditation here; so how can it be said "for the sake of meditation"? To this he replies:
"For the sake of meditation" (ādhyānāya). //14//
And because of the word "self" (ātman):
since the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) have as their essential nature the communication of an object not previously apprehended— and this is especially true of scripture (*āgama*).

The meaning is as follows: since the Self, which is denoted by the word *puruṣa*, is determined by the Śruti itself to be difficult to comprehend, and because it is in fact difficult to comprehend while objects such as wealth are easy to understand, the designation of "being intent on wealth" and so forth is actually intended to mean "being intent on that [the Self].
The term "excess of intention" (*āśayātiśaya*) refers to what is like the supreme intention of the Śruti.
That is to say, it is because that is its intended meaning (*tātparya*).
Furthermore, this is so because it expresses what is required by other scriptural passages (*śruti*).
However, if the intrinsic nature (*svarūpa*) were intended as the primary object, then the scripture would not state what is required; thus he says:
Moreover, he reaches the further shore of the path. //15//
START BsVBh_3,3.8.16:
"The grasping of the Self [is meant] as in the other cases, because of what follows" (BBs_3,3.16).
For in both Śruti and Smṛti, the creation of the world is found to be presided over by the Supreme Lord and to have the Supreme Lord Hiraṇyagarbha as its agent.

Thus, here, by not mentioning the creation of the gross elements (mahābhūta-sarga), the initial creation of the world— which is perceived as the work of an intermediate Lord— along with the determination of the oneness of the Self prior to its arising, leads one to understand [this creation] as being connected to an intermediate Lord;
for the creation of the Supreme Lord consists of the gross elements such as ether and so forth, whereas this [creation] is the opposite of that.
For indeed, that very same single entity possesses the nature of fire in relation to its other modifications, and it also possesses the faculty of seeing;
moreover, in this preceding section of the Aitareya, the creation of the worlds is stated to have Prajāpati as its agent,
and it is understood from that very context that this is so here as well.
Moreover, worldly transactions such as "He brought a cow from them," which are mentioned in the Śruti, are well-known to apply to specific individual selves and the Supreme Self;
for this reason as well, the intermediate Lord alone is understood [to be the subject].

Furthermore, the use of the word "Self" (ātman) is observed here too; therefore, the prima facie view being reached is that this is a reference to the lower self. To this, it is replied: the Supreme Self is what is grasped here, just as in other accounts of creation, such as "From this Self... [Chāndogya Upaniṣad 7.26.1].
In passages such as "ether was produced," [the word *ātman* is used].

Therefore, because of the subsequent hearing of the creatorship preceded by reflection in the words "He thought" (*sa aikṣata*), and because of the restrictive determination that it is the Self (*ātman*), this is intended:
first of all, prior to creation, the primary states of being solitary, being the Self, and being the creator belong here to the Supreme Lord.
Therefore, since there is no inconsistency [in the text], it is not appropriate to explain it otherwise.
Nor is the failure to mention the creation of the great elements (mahābhūtas) a seed of inconsistency for the mention of the creation of the world;

for just as in the case of the actual creation from Brahman preceded by space, the mention of a creation preceded by fire in some places is not contradictory—given the scriptural vision that "from this Self, space was produced."
For just as it must be supplied there with the words "having created space and air," so too here it should be understood that [the text] means "having created the great elements.

Since knowledge is established by the Śruti based on the principle that all recensions (śākhās) are authoritative, one should exert effort to perceive what is not explicitly stated; however, one should not allow the creation of the great elements and so forth to be neglected when it is already established by the Śruti.

Furthermore, the mass of the Veda, which is acquired under the authority of the rule for Vedic study (svādhyāya-vidhi), expresses a purposeful meaning brought about by the injunction to study; thus, the more it attains an abundance of purpose, the more it is highly esteemed.
And just as this [knowledge] possesses utility for the supreme human goal when it has Brahman as its object, it does not do so when it has anything else as its object.
This very point has been stated: "As for this following of specific activities..."
Furthermore, it has already been stated that the creation of the world is not the activity of Hiraṇyagarbha, but rather that of the Supreme Self who has entered into him.

Therefore, because the passage begins with "The Self alone was this [in the beginning]," refers to that same agent through the intermediate mention of his activity of "seeing," and concludes by subsuming the entire range of differentiated entities along with the gross elements under Brahman as its foundation, it is certain that this text has Brahman as its sole subject matter.

However, where there is scriptural mention of the "person-like form" (puruṣavidha) and so forth, that must have another purpose because there is no other possible way [to interpret it]; thus everything is clear.
Another alternative view:
Is there a single intended meaning for this entire composition which begins with "Being" (sat) and continues with the "Self" (ātman), or is there a difference in meaning?

In this context, since the word "Being" (sat) applies without distinction to both the Self and the non-Self, it does not have the Self as its referent; rather, its referent is the universal Being (sattāsāmānya) that pervades all things. Thus, due to the difference in the initial statement (upakrama), there is a difference in meaning.

Furthermore, the conclusion—"That is the Self, That art thou"—must be explained as having the sense of "becoming one with" (saṃpatti) in accordance with the initial statement. For that universal Being is to be realized as being identical with the Supreme Self.
And because the Great Universal, namely *sattā* (Being), pervades the entire extension of all things, it might follow that through the knowledge of that [one thing], there is knowledge of everything.

To this, it is replied: there is indeed the grasping of the Self even for the Chāndogyas, just as for the Vājasaneyins, because of the instruction of identity in the subsequent passage, "That is the Self; thou art That.

Let it be granted, then, that the phenomenal world (*prapañca*), being indeterminable as either existent or non-existent, lacks true existence; however, since existence is determinable only as the reality of the Self-substance (*ātmadhātu*), therefore, the Self alone [is real].
Having accepted [the objection], he says:

Since the word "sat" (being) denotes the generality of existence (*sattāsāmānya*) and since it applies to each individual instance, and because the word "sat" applies both to the Self and to other things, when doubt arises, the term is restricted to the Self alone as "Being itself" (*sadeva*), in accordance with the concluding summary.

For the description of the conclusion must follow the introduction of the definitive meaning (*nītārtha*); the conclusion should not be described in accordance with an introduction whose meaning is doubtful.
Furthermore, the fruit must be conceived as occurring at the time of attainment;
moreover, when only the general [nature] is known, the knowledge of the specific [details] cannot arise.
Indeed, when a tree is known through its general form (*ākāra*), its specific particulars such as being a *śiṃśapā* tree are not thereby known.

Thus, in this manner, everything including the restrictive determination (*avadhāraṇa*) would be untenable if [the self] were not for the sake of the Self; therefore, it is established that the *Chāndogya* refers exclusively to the Self.
And here, in the previous prima facie position (*pūrvapakṣa*), there was meditation on Hiraṇyagarbha, whereas in the final conclusion (*siddhānta*), there is the contemplation of Brahman. //16//
If it is argued that [the self exists] because of positive concomitance (*anvaya*), [we reply: it would [be established] through definitive restriction (*avadhāraṇa*). (3.3.17)
START BsVBh_3,3.9.18:
Because it explains the result, [the Veda] is not something previously unknown.
BBs_3,3.18: He states the subject matter:
"The Chandogas and the Vājasaneyins"—*ana* means breathing (*prāṇana*); *anaḥ* is breath (*prāṇa*).
Making that breath "not naked" (*anagna*) means contemplating its state of being unclothed (*anagnatā*).
"Manana" (reflection) is that which is thought; it is said to be the contemplation [of knowledge] up to its full absorption (*vyāpti*).
He states a doubt: "What then? (*tat kim iti*).
Having initially taken up both positions merely by the sound of the words, the proponent (pūrvapakṣin) resorts to the middle position, namely:
"Or rather, it is simply the sipping of water.
To the question, "If this is so, what is the purpose of mentioning the state of being unclothed? he says:

"But it is for the sake of praising that very [practice]"—this is the intended meaning: although there is a Smṛti-based sipping of water (ācamana) for the purpose of purification, nevertheless, because it is not enjoined within the context of the meditation on the vital breath (prāṇa), it is not established as an ancillary part of that meditation; thus, its injunction becomes purposeful.

This is just like the prohibition against speaking untruth, which, though mentioned in the Smṛti, becomes purposeful as an ancillary to the Jyotiṣṭoma sacrifice when it is recited within the context of the Jyotiṣṭoma as "one should not speak untruth."
He states the established conclusion: "Thus, this being the case. He raises an objection:
"Is this not scripture? He replies:
"No."
The meaning is that the relationship of root and derivative exists between two things that have the same referent, not between those that have different referents.
He refutes the seed of the prima facie argument residing in the [opponent's] intention with the words: "And this is not the scriptural statement."

In the case of the two prohibitions against speaking untruth—one for the sake of the sacrifice (*kratvartha*) and one for the sake of the person (*puruṣārtha*)—it is appropriate that they are not redundant. However, in this instance, the *ācamana* (ritual sipping of water) prescribed by the Smṛtis is enjoined as a subsidiary part (*aṅga*) of all ritual acts, and it is also a subsidiary part of the meditation on the vital breaths (*prāṇopāsana*). Therefore, because it would be redundant due to the more extensive Smṛti rule for *ācamana*, [the present text] would be purposeless.
Nor is there redundancy of the Smṛti rule by means of this [text], because the Smṛti rule is pervasive (*vyāpaka*), whereas this [present text] has a restricted scope (*pratiniyataviṣaya*).
Having set aside the middle position, he refutes the first position:
for this very reason, there is no prescription of both.
He states another argument:
And regarding the prescription of both:
he concludes—
"Therefore, it is indeed already established."
Nor is this a doctrine concerning the state of being unclothed;

the meaning is that praise is not possible in the absence of something worthy of praise. Furthermore, that which is not already established by another means of knowledge (*māna*) should be praised as that which is to be enjoined.
Nor is the resolve regarding nakedness obtained from elsewhere such that it would be a matter of praise;
nor is the sipping of water (ācamana) obtained from elsewhere such that, being something to be enjoined, its existence could be praised. Thus he says:
"And [the praise] of the resolve regarding nakedness itself..."

Moreover, it is appropriate that a single action has only a single purpose; however, when there is no other possible recourse due to the force of a powerful means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), one may postulate multiple purposes for it.

But in the case of the *saṃkalpa*, since another action is being enjoined, this fault does not arise; thus he says: "And this being so, [the fault does not apply] to a single act of sipping water (*ācamana*)."

Furthermore, because it occurs in conjunction with an injunction regarding a mental visualization (*dṛṣṭi*), it is logical that this is indeed an injunction for a visualization and not an injunction for sipping water; thus he says:
"Moreover, whatever this may be.

For just as a visualization of food is enjoined because it is impossible to eat food ranging from that of a dog down to [other impure things], so too here, since it is impossible to actually wear water as a garment, only a visualization is enjoined. This is understood from its association with the injunction for the visualization of food.

Although the quality of being "non-verbal" (aśabdatva) is common to both seeing and eating, nevertheless, seeing is perceived as being performed directly by the word itself, because it is invariably concomitant with the verbal object of vision. Eating, however, must be supplied [by implication] through mere suitability; this is the distinction. Furthermore, in the case of the *ācamana* (sipping water) for the Chāndogyas and the Vājasaneyins, there is generally the statement in the present tense, "they sip water" (*ācāmantīti*). Thus, even where an injunctive suffix occurs, the injunctive force is not intended, just as in the case of "one should offer oblations of wild sesame gruel" (*jartilayavāgvā vā juhuyāt*).

He says that because it has the sense of "they consider" (*manyante*) and thus aims at the attainment of something [not yet known], it is indeed an injunction (*vidhi*), like the passage "he offers the *samidh* oblations" (*samidho yajati*), etc.; this is what is meant by the words "and also, 'they sip water'. The remainder of the text has a meaning that is not obscure. //18//
It is the same because there is no difference. Here,
the prima facie position (*pūrva-pakṣa*) is established according to the principle of the locus of repetition (*abhyāsādhikaraṇanyāya*).

Since there is no certainty as to which [injunction] is a restatement (*anuvāda*) of the other when two injunctions regarding knowledge belong to the same Vedic branch (*śākhā*) and their specific distinctions are not grasped— and since the nature of an injunction, consisting in making known what was unknown or impelling toward what has not yet begun, is established by its own inherent force— there is a difference in the meditation (*upāsanā*) in both cases. Furthermore, it cannot be that a restatement occurs in one place for the sake of enjoining a different quality (*guṇa*), because another different quality is observed to be enjoined in both places as well, due to the absence of a reason for decisive selection (*vinigamanā-hetu*), and because it would follow that qualities common to both would not be mentioned.

Therefore, since it might be argued that—as in the case of "he offers the fuel-sticks" (*samidho yajati*) and so forth—a distinction between meditations (*upāsanā*) arises from repetition, the following is stated: there is a single action because of recognition [of the object] as being one and the same.
Nor is there a lack of perceived distinction;

for where many qualities are enjoined for a particular action, there is an injunction of that primary action itself, whereas elsewhere, by way of restating that [action], only a few qualities are enjoined.

Just as where there is a multitude of umbrellas, chowries, banners, elephants, archers, spearmen, staff-bearers, bowmen, swordsmen, javelin-throwers, and infantry, it is understood that "the King is there," but not when only a few elephants, horses, and foot soldiers belong to his minister— so it is here as well.
Nor is the mention of qualities prescribed in one place for another purposeless, because it serves to strengthen recognition (*pratyabhijñāna*).
Or rather, let this be a restatement (*anuvāda*) regarding this [meditation], for it is not necessary that all restatements must have a specific purpose;
for we find even mere restatements here and there.
Therefore, it is established that the meditation is indeed the same in the *Bṛhadāraṇyaka* as well, because of the inclusion of those qualities. //19//
START BsVBh_3,3.11.20:
Because of this connection, it is the same elsewhere as well. BBs_3,3.20:

If, even within a single branch (śākhā), there is a blending of the meditations (upāsana) and the duties prescribed therein because they are recognized as being identical in essence; [then the same would apply elsewhere].

That being the case, since there is no difference in the single Truth (*satya*), there would follow the undesirable consequence of a confusion between the two secret names (*upaniṣad*) residing in the two circles.
Furthermore, because the word "of that" (*tasya*) refers back to the subject under discussion, there is a distinction;

and since the principal subject, Truth, is what is under discussion, while the term "with regard to the divine" (*adhidaiva*) is merely an adjunct and thus not the primary topic, there would be a confusion of attributes as before, due to the non-difference of the principal subject, Truth.
When this [objection] has been raised, it is said in reply:
"Or rather, it is not so, because there is a distinction. (BBs 3.3.21)

It is true that where the connection of attributes with the mere essential nature (*svarūpa*) alone is heard, it is precisely there [that this rule applies], because the essential nature is recognized everywhere and because the attributes are connected with that alone.

However, where the principal entity is understood as possessing qualifiers (*saviśeṣaṇa*), the connection of the attributes belongs to that very entity as qualified, not to the unqualified entity, nor to one accompanied by other qualifiers.
For when it is said, "Bring the man with the staff," it is not the man without the staff who is brought.
A water-pot (kamaṇḍalu) is brought [along];
therefore, the secret doctrine (upaniṣad) of the Truth has been stated with reference to the divine (adhidaiva), and it cannot possibly apply to that same Truth with reference to the self (adhyātma).
Just as following behind is prescribed for a teacher who is walking, but not for one who is standing still;
Therefore, there is no confusion between the two Upaniṣads, but rather a fixed distinction;
this is what was stated [in the verse]: "because their essential nature does not depart. //21//
And the scripture shows this as well:
"Because there is an extension [of the rule], it must be exactly so; for if it were the ultimate reality (tattva), there would be no extension. //22//

And for this reason, there is also the accumulation and the pervasion of heaven: "The heroic powers were accumulated with Brahman as the eldest; in the beginning, Brahman stretched out the eldest heaven. (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 3.3.23)
"Of those that have become Brahman, he was born as the first; therefore, who is able to rival him with Brahman?
Those for whom Brahman is the eldest are the *brahmajyeṣṭhāḥ*; he was born among them.

Although, in various meditations such as the Śāṇḍilya-vidyā and others, a distinction of substrata (*āyatana*) appears—whereby qualities such as the "accumulation" (*saṃbhṛti*) and so forth are associated with the internal substratum while others are associated with the celestial substratum—nevertheless, [the point remains].

Nevertheless, because the passage beginning with "Greater than heaven" identifies the divine manifestations (*adhidaivika-vibhūti*), and because the bases (*āyatana*) are not heard of in the "Sixteen Parts" (*ṣoḍaśakalā*) and other such meditations (*vidyā*), it is possible to identify them as being equal insofar as they ultimately have Brahman as their locus; thus, the prima facie view (*pūrva-pakṣa*) is that the qualities such as "being concealed" (*saṃvṛti*) and so forth are to be combined in both the Śāṇḍilya and other meditations, as well as in the "Sixteen Parts" meditation and others.

The established conclusion (*siddhānta*), however, is as follows: Reciprocal hearing of identical qualities leads to recognition (*pratyabhijñā*), whereby one incorporates even those qualities not heard in a particular context;
yet, in this case, within the Brahma-vidyā characterized by qualities such as *saṃbhṛti* (supporting), there is no hearing of qualities belonging to the Śāṇḍilya-vidyā and others.

As for whatever supermundane manifestation (*vibhūti*) is heard in the Śāṇḍilya-vidyā and others, because it is dependent upon its own specific context, only that much shall be accepted; one cannot, on this basis alone, extend [the inclusion of] qualities such as *saṃbhṛti*.
In this regard, it has been stated that there is an absence of recognition (*pratyabhijñāna*).
However, to establish recognition on the basis of Brahman as its substratum would lead to an over-extension (*atiprasakta*),
because it would entail the undesirable consequence of the identity of many [entities].
This has been stated:
"But the 'Accumulation' (saṃbhṛti) and so forth are within the scope of the Śāṇḍilya and other passages.

Therefore, it is established that because there is no recognition [of these qualities] in the Śāṇḍilya and other meditations, the "Accumulation" and the "Pervasion of Heaven" (dyuvyāpti)—that is, this pair of "Accumulation and Pervasion of Heaven"—are not to be combined [with those meditations]. //23//
If it is argued that [the details] are not mentioned in the others as they are in the Puruṣavidyā, [we reply:
the status of being a "Person-sacrifice" (puruṣayajña) is common to both, without distinction.

Nor is it impossible for there to be grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) between "of the sacrifice" and "of the knower," because the word "self" (*ātman*) in the expression "the self of the sacrifice" denotes its own essential nature (*svarūpa*).
Since the sacrificer is the essential nature of the sacrifice, and because he is a conscious being, coreferentiality with "the knower" is possible.

Therefore, since there is no distinction in the fact that the person is the sacrifice, and because of common features such as death being the final bath (avabhṛtha), it follows that when a single meditation is determined, the attributes of both [texts] must be combined in both places.

This being the position reached, the following is stated: the manner in which the person is constituted as a sacrifice by the Tāṇḍins and the Paiṅgins, and the manner in which life-span, divided into three parts, is constituted as the three pressings (savana), is as follows.

Furthermore, the accomplishment of the state of initiation (*dīkṣā*) and so forth for those beginning with [the verses on] "desiring to eat" (*aśiśiṣat*) does not apply to the Taittirīyas in this way.
For them, there is no realization of the sacrifice within the person;
indeed, in the passage "The self is the sacrificer," this word "self" (*ātman*) does not denote one's own essential nature (*svarūpa*).
For the sacrificer does not become the very nature of the sacrifice, because there is no identity between the agent and the action,
and because it is impossible for the conscious and the unconscious to be one, given that the sacrificial act is insentient.

Because the sacrificer is sentient, it is appropriate for the sentient self to be both the sacrificer and the possessor of knowledge. Thus, the meaning is as follows: that sacrifice which belongs to a person who possesses such knowledge, [the self is connected] by way of being related to that sacrifice.

The sacrificer is the Self; thus, both the sacrificer's status as the sacrificer and the connection of the sacrifice to the knower would be primary. Otherwise, if the word "Self" (ātman) were to denote mere individual form, then the expressions "the sacrificer of the knower" and "the sacrificer is the nature of the sacrifice" would be merely figurative.
And when a primary sense is possible, such [a figurative interpretation] is not appropriate.

Therefore, since the status of the person as a sacrifice (*puruṣayajñatā*) does not exist in the Taittirīya [text], there is no similarity based on that. Furthermore, the preparation of the wife, the sacrificer, the Vedas, and the sacred knowledge (*vidyā*), as found among the Taittirīyas, is not present among the Tāṇḍins or the Paiṅginas; their realization of the *savana* periods is likewise entirely different. Thus, when there is such great disparity, it is not appropriate to claim the identity of the knowledge (*vidyaikatva*) on the basis of a mere partial similarity, for that would lead to over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*).

Furthermore, the meaning is that when there is a restatement in the scriptural text "of one who knows thus" (*evaṃvidaḥ*), the fault of syntactical split (*vākyabheda*) would result from enjoining multiple matters.
Moreover, this knowledge of the human sacrifice (*puruṣayajña-vidyā*) among the Paiṅgis and Tāṇḍins is perceived as independent, being associated with a different fruit;

however, for the Taittirīyas, because of the hearing of the words "of one who knows thus," because of the reference back to what was previously mentioned, and because of the hearing of its specific fruit, it is dependent.
And since it is not appropriate for the independent and the dependent to be identical, he says: "Moreover, [it is] the knowledge of the Self together with renunciation.
He concludes: "Therefore... //24//
START BsVBh_3,3.14.25:
Because of the difference in meaning such as piercing and so forth (vedhādi), [the author] shows the object of investigation at BBs_3,3.25.
Regarding the phrase "of the Ātharvaṇikas":
at the beginning of the various Upaniṣads of the Ātharvaṇikas and others, those respective mantras and those respective rituals such as the Pravargya are recited.
He states the doubt:
"What is this?
[The author] takes up the prima facie position (pūrvapakṣa):
"These [rites] are indeed to be included within the meditations (vidyās)."

For all the mantras and ritual acts (karmāṇi) recited in the presence of those [Vidyās] are indeed taught as being fruitful; by the maxim "that which is fruitless in the proximity of that which possesses fruit is a subsidiary part (aṅga) of it," they are understood to be subsidiaries of the Vidyās. [The opponent] objects:
Regarding the phrase "nanveṣām" (surely, for these):

indeed, in this case, there are no means of proof—such as direct assertion (*śruti*), indicative mark (*liṅga*), syntactical connection (*vākya*), context (*prakaraṇa*), position (*sthāna*), or name (*samākhyā*)—that serve to apply [the mantras].

For it is not the case that, just as the *samid* and other [offerings] are recited having commenced with the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices, so too are mantras or ritual acts recited having commenced with any particular knowledge (*vidyā*).
Furthermore, in the absence of a general connection, it is not possible for something to be for the sake of another merely by the proximity of related entities.

Nor does the knowledge (vidyā), which has its own constituent parts (aṅga) fully stated in the text, stand in need of these [rituals], such that the mere proximity of those whose general connection is established by context (prakaraṇa) could serve to establish a specific connection. This is the meaning.
He provides the resolution:
"Certainly, even though they are not perceived"—
let there be no expectation regarding those sciences that possess fruits and have all their constituent parts complete.

However, for mantras whose status as means to human ends is established by the injunction for their own study (*svādhyāya-vidhi*), and for rituals such as the *pravargya* whose status as means to human ends is established by their own injunctions— both of which desire what is sought by the person— their connection is based on mutual expectancy due to proximity, according to the maxim of the "red-clad" (*raktapaṭa*). Furthermore, since the meditations (*vidyās*) possess fruits, the mantras and rituals that lack fruits are subservient to them.

Furthermore, heaven cannot be postulated as the fruit for the Pravargya and other such rites in the manner of the Piṇḍapitṛyajña, because [the former] descend to that status by virtue of being in proximity to a rite that possesses its own fruit;
for inference has no power when it contradicts the force of proximity.

Indeed, when this [sentence] is heard in proximity to a Vedic text (*vidyā*) whose expectancy has ceased, it arouses expectancy even in that [Vedic text], because—even if it itself possesses expectancy—it lacks the capacity to connect [directly] with one whose expectancy has ceased.
And having aroused [that expectancy], it attains syntactic unity (*ekavākyatā*).
Furthermore, since that which lacks capacity cannot function as a benefactor, it conceives of its own capacity to assist the subject matter of the context (*prakaraṇin*).

And even though capacity exists, that which is not enjoined there by direct Vedic statement (śruti) cannot attain the status of being an auxiliary to it; thus, through this sequence, proximity (saṃnidhi) implies a direct statement (śruti) by means of presumptive testimony (arthāpatti). He raises an objection: "But surely, of these mantras... and so forth.

For it was stated in the section beginning with "But the meaning of the sentence is not distinct" (*aviśiṣṭas tu vākyārthaḥ*) that the utility of mantras consists in illuminating matters connected with ritual performance (*prayoga*);
yet we do not perceive any such matter connected with knowledge (*vidyā*) within these mantras.

And although the Pravargya is not heard of as being enjoined with reference to anything specific, nevertheless, through syntactical connection (*vākya-saṃyoga*) and connection with the sacrifice (*kratu-saṃyoga*), it attains a relationship with the sacrifice, as in the statement:
"They proceed with the Pravargya prior to the Upasads.
This is because the Upasads, like the *juhū* ladle, have an invariable connection with the sacrifice.

Although there are *upasads* even in the modifications (*vikṛti*) of the Jyotiṣṭoma, nevertheless, those in the modifications are inferential (*ānumānika*), whereas in the Jyotiṣṭoma itself they are directly enjoined (*pratyakṣavihita*). Therefore, by virtue of its rapid application, it is understood through the sentence that [the Pravargya] is indeed an auxiliary (*aṅga*) of the Jyotiṣṭoma. Furthermore, since the Pravargya is enjoined in the archetype (*prakṛti*), it is extended to its modifications as well by the *codaka* (transference rule), just like the *upasads*. Moreover, according to the principle "or rather, in the archetype, because of non-duplication," it belongs to the Jyotiṣṭoma.
This very procedure is joined with the *upasad* rites;
regarding this, he says:
"And how [are] the *pravargya* and so forth?"
The sense is that a sentence is stronger than immediate proximity because it involves a greater distance from the actual meaning. He provides the resolution:
"This is not a fault."
"First, as for its capacity":
just as in the mantra "I offer thee, acceptable to Agni," the words "to Agni" and "I offer" reveal a meaning inherent in the ritual action,
while the remaining words are explained in some way or another as being syntactically connected with them— so too here, in the case of the meditation on the word "heart."

Since the meaning [of the mantra] is already inherent [in the rite], the other words forming a single syntactical unit with it must be interpreted somehow through figurative (gauṇī) or indirect (lakṣaṇā) functions; thus, there is no lack of inherent meaning in the mantras.
Furthermore, he says that the application of mantras is not unobserved in meditations (upāsanās), such that one would have to postulate an entirely unseen result.
"And it is seen in the case of the attendant rites.
Although proximity (*saṃnidhi*) is weaker than a syntactical connection (*vākya*) and is therefore sublated by the latter, nevertheless, such sublation occurs only when there is a contradiction;
however, in this case, there is no contradiction.

For even though the Pravargya rite has been enjoined by a direct statement (*vākya*) for the Jyotiṣṭoma sacrifice, its application (*viniyoga*) to the knowledge [of Brahman] is also possible through proximity (*saṃnidhi*).

Just as the Bṛhaspatisava sacrifice—though having the splendor of sacred knowledge (*brahmavarcasa*) as its fruit—is enjoined as a subsidiary (*aṅga*) to the Vājapeya, according to the injunction: "Having sacrificed with the Vājapeya, one should sacrifice with the Bṛhaspatisava."

For here, by virtue of the rule prescribing the suffix [ktvā] when there is a connection between verbal roots (*dhātu-sambandhe*), the fact that they share the same agent (*samāna-kartṛkatvam*) is understood;
yet how could there be a connection with another root-meaning while the agent remains the same,
unless there were a single performance (*ekaḥ prayogaḥ*)?
For agency is indeed that which is entered into through application (*prayoga*).
And how could that [agency] be one when there is a difference in application?

Therefore, because they share a single agent, the *vājapeya* and the *bṛhaspatisava* constitute a single application; this is also because of their connection with distinct meanings of verbal roots. Nor is it the case that...

The unity of performance and the connection [between acts] exist even without a relationship of subordinate and principal; in that case as well, because it is recited within the context (*prakaraṇa*) of the Vājapeya, the Vājapeya is the principal and the Bṛhaspatisava is the subsidiary.
However, this does not entail the status of subsidiary and principal in the case of the statement: "Having sacrificed with the Darśapūrṇamāsa, one should sacrifice with Soma."
This statement is not recited within the context (*prakaraṇa*) of either the Darśapūrṇamāsa or the Soma sacrifice.

Thus, since both [the Darśapūrṇamāsa and the Soma] possess the status of being principal acts (*sādhikāra*) and no distinction is perceived between them, there is no basis for determining a relationship of subordinate and principal (*guṇapradhānabhāva*). Therefore, the identity of agent (*samānakartṛkatva*) is taken figuratively (*lākṣaṇika*) with the intention of referring merely to the substratum (the person), and thus there is no fault.
However, if in some Śākhā this were taught as an *ārabhyādhīta* (an injunction introduced in connection with another), namely, "having performed the Darśapūrṇamāsa," [then the context would apply].
Nevertheless, it is logical that there is a recognition (*pratyabhijñāna*) of that which was taught as unconnected (*anārabhyādhīta*) within that which was taught as connected (*ārabhyādhīta*).

This being the case, since both are perceived as having separate qualifications (*adhikāra*), their status as equally primary (*samapradhānatva*) remains unrenounced; otherwise, by means of a subordinate-superordinate relationship (*guṇapradhānabhāva*), that status would be abandoned.
Therefore, it is established that this conjunction has time (*kāla*) as its purpose.

He introduces the established conclusion (*siddhānta*) with the words: "Thus, it being so attained. The mantra "pierce the heart" (*hṛdayaṃ pravidhya*), by its own inherent force, is indeed connected to all [the parts] of a rite for malevolent magic (*ābhicārika-karman*).

When words are perceived as denoting a meaning, that capacity for denotation constitutes a *liṅga* (indicative mark). This *liṅga* is stronger than both *vākya* (syntactic connection) and *prakaraṇa* (context), which are respectively more powerful; how much more so, then, than *krama* (order)?
Therefore, by means of this *liṅga*, *saṃnidhi* (proximity) is set aside, and it is established that [the mantra] is indeed a subsidiary (*śeṣa*) to the *abhicārika* (malevolent) rite.
And although, in the case of meditations (*upāsanā*), the word "heart" alone has a directly relevant meaning,
nevertheless all the other words lack such relevance; however, this is not the case in the ritual of malevolent magic (*ābhicārika-karman*).

If it is argued that "the meaning is connected with all [the words]," what will the fact of being connected with the meaning of a single word accomplish? Nor is it logical that one should establish a mantra in those *upāsanās* (meditations) which are grasped by mere proximity.

For even in the case of the word *hṛdaya* used in a malevolent rite (*abhicāra*), since its meaning is connected [to the ritual] and it forms a syntactical unity with the other words, it is accompanied by the authority of the sentence (*vākya-pramāṇa*) [which restricts it] to the malevolent rite.

Since it is impossible to move [the mantra] from its proximity [to the ritual action], even though the mantra beginning with "O God Savitṛ, impel the sacrifice" possesses the indicative mark (*liṅga*) of impelling the sacrifice,
once its status as a subsidiary (*aṅga*) to the sacrifice is established, what can the secondary proximity (*jaghanya-saṃnidhi*) to knowledge (*vidyā*) accomplish?

The same applies to others, such as the *Śvetāśvatara* and so forth— some by virtue of their indicative mark (*liṅga*), some by direct statement (*śruti*), some by another means of proof (*pramāṇāntara*), and some by context (*prakaraṇa*).
Why, then, is proximity (saṃnidhi) sublated by indicative power (liṅga) and the other means of proof? To this he says:
"For proximity is weak.
The meaning established in the first section of the Tantra is now being recalled.

In this regard, however, when there is a conflict between *śruti* (direct statement) and *liṅga* (indicative power)—characterized by their having the same object—the inquiry is: which is more powerful?

An example here is as follows: there is an *aindrī* (verse dedicated to Indra), such as the direct statement (*śruti*) "Never art thou a reviler, O Indra," which serves as the means of application; [and there is the injunction] "One worships the *gārhapatya* fire with an *aindrī* verse.
For in this case, from the *liṅga* characterized by capability, the application [of the verse] appears to be toward Indra.

Furthermore, from the scriptural mention of "the Gārhapatya fire" with the accusative case-ending, the subordinate status (*śeṣitva*) of the Gārhapatya fire is understood; and from the scriptural mention of "the Aindrī verse" with the instrumental case-ending, the subordinate status of the Aindrī Ṛc is understood.

Although the subordinate status of the Gārhapatya fire toward the Āgneyī Ṛc is possible due to the accusative case-ending in "the Gārhapatya fire," and although the subordinate status of the Aindrī verse toward Indra is possible due to the instrumental case-ending in "the Aindrī," there is no contradiction [in our position].
But when there is a connection with another word, it is the sentence itself that is contradicted by the indicative mark (*liṅga*), and not the direct Vedic statement (*śruti*);
and in that case, the relative strength and weakness are reversed.
Nevertheless, there is no fault, because *śruti* and *vākya* differ in their formal nature and their respective functions.

For the second and third case-endings, being *kāraka*-case endings, convey the status of the base-meaning as either an object (*karman*) or an instrument (*karaṇa*) with respect to the action; thus, they are *viniyojika* (determinative of application).

Indeed, application (*viniyoga*) consists in the fact that, with respect to the action, the object possesses the status of the principal (*śeṣin*) and the instrument possesses the status of the subordinate (*śeṣa*).

And since the relationship of subordinate and principal with respect to the action is understood from the mere hearing of the word (*śruti*) without depending on other words, these are called *śrauta* (based on direct audition).
Thus, this application (viniyoga), which is understood in a general sense through direct audition (śruti), is established in a particular instance by the force of another word.
This relationship, characterized by the qualifier-qualified (viśeṣaṇa-viśeṣya) relation, falls within the scope of the sentence (vākya);
however, the relationship of subsidiary and principal (śeṣa-śeṣibhāva) is based on direct audition (śrauta).

Therefore, since the syntactical relation between the subordinate and the principal (śeṣa-śeṣibhāva) derived from direct audition (śruti) is contradicted by the indicative power (liṅga) when it depends upon a distinction obtainable only through the sentence, in this conflict between direct audition and indicative power, should the accusative case-ending in the word "gārhapatyam" be interpreted— in accordance with the indicative power— as having the sense of the locative, such that Indra is to be worshipped near the Gārhapatya fire by means of the Aindrī verse?
Or rather, let the indicative mark (*liṅga*) be explained in accordance with the direct statement (*śruti*).
For the Gārhapatya fire is capable of performing its own appropriate function; and Indra [is the deity] because the root *ind* signifies sovereignty.
What, then, is the prima facie position? That the indicative mark is more powerful than the direct statement.
Indeed, that which is incapable in a certain respect cannot be applied there even by a thousand scriptural injunctions,
just as one cannot say, "one should sprinkle with fire" or "one should burn with water.
Therefore, having first taken into account the capacity [of the means], one should apply it according to the scriptural injunction.
And this [meaning] of the verse is understood to refer to Indra through other means of knowledge and through the words themselves;
for instance, one who knows the words and their meanings clearly understands Indra from the verse beginning with "kadācana."

And because of the word "Aindrī," it follows that the application of the *aindrī* verse is to the Gārhapatya fire, just as the application of fire— which normally burns wood— is [restricted] to burning water.
Nor is it appropriate to assume a capacity based on secondary figurative usage (*vṛtti*) in deference to the direct Vedic statement (*śruti*).
Since the capacity [of a word] exists prior [to its application], the scriptural text (*śruti*) is established solely in accordance with it.

Therefore, when it is argued that Indra alone—by virtue of the *aindrī* verse—is to be worshipped in the vicinity of the Gārhapatya fire, the following is stated: "The scriptural text does not exercise its directive function by placing the knowledge of the indicative mark (*liṅga*) at the forefront;
rather, the indicative mark is the director by placing the knowledge of the scriptural text at the forefront."

For if the knower were to determine the application of the *śruti* only after having understood its capacity (*sāmarthya*), then the *śruti* would be weak with respect to that application because it would depend upon the knowledge of the indicative power (*liṅga*).
But this is not the case;
the *śruti* requires the capacity for application, but it does not require the cognition of that capacity.

Once the application (*viniyoga*) has been understood from that [scriptural statement], however, it is not the case that something incapable [of performing an action] is so applied; therefore, in order to effect that application, capability (*sāmarthya*) is postulated. That capability exists prior to the application by the scriptural statement, but it is not apprehended beforehand.

Since the application (*viniyoga*) is already established, its subsequent cognition—arising through the impossibility of its otherwise being accounted for—is posterior to the application by direct audition (*śruti*); therefore, that cognition of capacity (*sāmarthya*) must be established in conformity with it.
However, indicative power (*liṅga*) is not itself the applicator; rather, having postulated an applicatory [text], it implies a direct audition (*śruti*).
For instance, from indicative power alone, one does not naturally understand that "Indra is to be worshipped by this [mantra]."
However, because of the force of its mention within that specific context— that "Indra is such"— and because the general purpose established by the context would otherwise be inexplicable,

one must indeed postulate an application (viniyoga). Nevertheless, since the application thus to be postulated is more remote from the meaning than the direct Vedic application (śrauta-viniyoga), it is proper to postulate the *śruti* itself rather than the application for its sake.
For it is not possible for the Śākyas to establish through reasoning that which is heard [in scripture] as being untenable;

nor do they, when faced with the statement "There are three Brahmins here: Kaṭha and Kauṇḍinya," seek to justify it by means of Māṭhara who is presented by other sources of knowledge, or, even if they were to so justify it, they would not be ridiculed.
They accept that [the words] "Śābdas" and "Māṭhara" are being made to hear [the name].
Therefore, the impossibility of the arising of the meaning as it was heard must be established by means of another meaning that is itself heard.
It is established in common worldly experience that [an application] does not occur merely through a different object brought forward by another means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*).
Nor is it appropriate to subject what is established in the world to injunctions or challenges, because that would contradict the world, which serves as the means for knowing the meaning of words.
Therefore, an enjoining *śruti* must be inferred.
And thus, while the operation of the indicative power (liṅga) has only just begun to postulate an applicatory scriptural statement (śruti),

the application to the Gārhapatya fire is already established by direct scripture; therefore, since the context (prakaraṇa) has ceased its expectancy, for what deficiency would the indicative power postulate an applicatory scriptural statement?
Because the application of the collection of mantras has already been established by the direct Vedic injunction (*viniyoga-śruti*), as they have said:
"As long as that which is to be known remains unknown or doubtful, it is sought to be known; but once it has been known, the desire for further knowledge of the knowers is stilled."

Therefore, it is established that when the capacity of a mantra is interpreted in accordance with a well-known Vedic application (*viniyoga*), it should be guided even by a secondary function (*jaghanyā vṛttiḥ*) without abandoning its primary function (*prathamā vṛttiḥ*). Here, the conflict between indicative power (*liṅga*) and syntactical connection (*vākya*) is as follows: "I prepare for you a pleasant seat; I fashion it well-fitting with a stream of clarified butter. Sit upon it, O immortal one, and take your stand, O essence of rice, being well-disposed. In this [mantra], the word *tasmin* (in it) indicates through its indicative power (*liṅga*) that the entire mantra is intended for the preparation of the seat (*sadanakaraṇa*), while the syntactical connection (*vākya*) of the words *tasmin sīda* (sit on it) connects the latter part of the mantra to the act of sitting (*āsādana*). Thus, there is a conflict between indicative power and syntactical connection. Since indicative power is stronger than syntactical connection, the mantra is applied to the preparation of the seat. However, because the word *tasmin* (in it) lacks a referent if separated from the preceding portion, the two parts must be construed together as a single sentence. Consequently, the mantra is applied to both acts: the preparation of the seat and the placing of the oblation upon it. This is the view of Bādari. Alternatively, since the word *tasmin* has no purpose in the first part, it is connected to the second part alone; thus, the mantra is applied solely to the act of sitting. This is the view of Jaimini. Because the word *tasmin* cannot be separated from the preceding portion, the mantra is applied to both acts. This is the view of Ātreya. Among these, the view of Bādari is not tenable, because the word *tasmin* would then have to be construed twice. The view of Jaimini is also not tenable, because the word *tasmin* would then lack a referent. Therefore, the view of Ātreya is correct, because the word *tasmin* cannot be separated from the preceding portion. Thus, the mantra is applied to both acts. This is the conclusion. Furthermore, the application of the mantra to the preparation of the seat is established by the indicative power of the words *syonaṃ... kṛṇomi* (I prepare a pleasant seat), while the application to the act of sitting is established by the indicative power of the words *tasmin sīda* (sit on it). Since the indicative power of the former is more proximate to the preparatory act, it prevails over the indicative power of the latter, which is more remote.
