Is this entire mantra to be employed both for the preparation of the seat and for the placing of the sacrificial cake (puroḍāśa), or is it that the portion ending with "I prepare" (kalpayāmi) is for the under-spreading [of ghee], while the portion beginning with "on that, sit" (tasmin sīda) is for the placing of the cake? If the syntactical unity (vākya) is more authoritative, then the entire mantra applies to both;

for the portion beginning with "on that, sit" attains syntactical unity with the preceding part by depending on the words "I prepare a pleasant [seat]" (suśevaṃ kalpayāmi), such that one understands: "On that which I prepare, may he sit."
Now, if the indicative mark (liṅga) is more powerful, then [the mantra] should be applied to the making of the seat and its illumination, for it is capable of that;
and to the placing of the sacrificial cake (puroḍāśa), with the words "may he sit upon it," for it is capable of that as well.
What, then, is the prima facie conclusion?
Since syntactical connection (*vākya*) is stronger than indicative mark (*liṅga*), the entire mantra is applied to both actions.

For here, when syntactical unity is established through the co-occurrence of those words—due to their being mutually expectant when divided—then, in accordance with that unity, the capacity to denote [the respective meanings] must subsequently be inferred.

Just as in the mantra "devasya tvā," because the two words "agnaye nirvapāmi" have a meaning directly connected to the ritual act, they form a single syntactical unit; consequently, the other words are understood as being subordinate to them, and their capacity to signify that [subordinate sense] is inferred therein.

Thus, since the capacity (sāmarthya) has been postulated in accordance with that [context] in order to maintain the established unity of the sentence, it cannot be subverted; rather, while postulating an applicatory direct statement (viniyojikā śruti), it must postulate one that is consistent with that very [capacity].

And so, because the sentence is stronger than the indicative power (liṅga), it follows that the entire mantra should be employed both for making the seat and for preparing the sacrificial cake (puroḍāśa).
This being the case, it is said in reply: This would indeed be so if the determination of semantic capacity (*sāmarthya*) were preceded by the comprehension of syntactic unity;

however, rather, for words whose capacity has already been determined and which are recited in close proximity (*praśliṣṭa*), the determination of their syntactic unity occurs through the force of that capacity, by virtue of their having a single purpose.
As many words as are capable of conveying a single principal meaning and are expectant (*sākāṅkṣa*) when separated, they constitute a single sentence.
Furthermore, among the matters to be performed that are revealed in the mantras,
the primary ones are the preparation of the seat and the placing of the sacrificial cake (*puroḍāśa*), since these are the two things to be performed as the principal acts.

Of these two, the mantra ending with *kalpayāmi* is capable of revealing the preparation of the seat, while the mantra beginning with *tasmin sīda* is capable of revealing the placing of the sacrificial cake.

Furthermore, while the capacity [of the sentence] is being inferred on the basis of syntactic unity (*ekavākyatā*), the capacity already perceived in each individual part projects a direct Vedic statement (*śruti*) that assigns each part to its respective meaning. Thus, when each part is assigned to a single purpose by the direct statement itself, the mere recitation within the context (*prakaraṇa-pāṭha*) becomes justified; consequently, the indicative power (*liṅga*) constructed from the sentence cannot project another assigning direct statement. Therefore, even though the cognition of syntactic unity has arisen, it becomes a mere semblance (*ābhāsa*) because it is sublated by the indicative power.

However, where there is no conflicting indicative mark (*liṅga*), the syntactic unity (*ekavākyatā*) of one, two, or three words whose meanings are combined (*samaveta*) postulates the capacity (*sāmarthya*) of even other words; thus, the sentence possesses the power of application (*viniyojakatva*), as in the case of "syonaṃ te" and so forth in this very context.
Therefore, it is established that the indicative mark is stronger than the sentence.
An example of the conflict between syntactical connection (*vākya*) and context (*prakaraṇa*):
here, *vākya* refers to words that, by virtue of their mutual dependence, culminate in a single specific meaning;
whereas *prakaraṇa* is the connection of those words, having already attained the status of a sentence, with another sentence due to the requirement for a further purpose.

The elders declare that *prakaraṇa* (context) is the statement of that which is to be performed— the cultivation of the fruit— which, having obtained the meaning of the verbal root as its instrument, requires a specification of the procedure (*itikartavyatā*),
such as: "One desiring heaven should sacrifice with the New and Full Moon sacrifices."

For this statement constitutes the context (*prakaraṇa*). When this [context], through its own collection of words, has reached a certain point in its meaning, there arises an expectation for another effect characterized by the assistance of the instrument; it is then that there occurs a connection with other sentences such as "He offers the *samits*" (*samidho yajati*). For the productive operations (*bhāvanā*) of the *samits* and so forth, being presented by their own injunctions, require a beneficial result to be produced for the person. Since no other fruit is obtained—whether by the logic of the *Viśvajit* sacrifice, by textual ellipsis (*anuṣaṅga*), or from an explanatory passage (*arthavāda*)—they connect with the productive operation of the New and Full Moon sacrifices (*darśapūrṇamāsa-bhāvanā*).

Therefore, when there is a desire for that [principal], these sentences which have fallen into its vicinity—being themselves dependent on their own functions—attain a function characterized by the assistance of the instrument required by it; thus they both complete and fulfill the principal.
This is a conjunction between the two, like the case of the lost horse and the burnt chariot.
Thus, the example of the conflict between *vākya* (syntactical connection) and *prakaraṇa* (contextual setting) regarding their respective characteristics is the *sūktavāka* recitation.
For in that case, the deities of the full moon sacrifice and the deities of the new moon sacrifice are recited together;

yet, since they cannot properly form a single syntactical unit with one another, the word "Indrāgnī" must be displaced from the full moon sacrifice by means of its indicative power (*liṅga*), and employed at the new moon sacrifice because it has a relevant meaning there.

Now, a doubt arises: regarding that which is perceived as forming a single syntactical unit (*ekavākyatā*) with the words "Indra-Agni"—namely, "you two have increased; you two have made [it] greater"—should this not be displaced, or should it be displaced along with the words "Indra" and "Agni"?

In this regard, if the context (*prakaraṇa*) is stronger, then the subsidiary (*śeṣa*) should be employed even when its deity has been removed; but if the sentence (*vākya*) is stronger, then it should be employed only where the word for the deity occurs. What, then, is the prima facie view? That the subsidiary should be employed even when its deity has been removed, because it is the context alone that establishes the connection with the constituent parts (*aṅga*).
For a fruitful *bhāvanā* (efficient force) brings about the status of being both the primary action (*pradhāna*) and the procedure (*itikartavyatā*).
This is because, by depending upon that *bhāvanā*, the *śruti* (direct assertion) and other means of proof bring about specific relationships [between elements].

Therefore, it follows that when there is a conflict with the *prakaraṇa* (context), which is characterized by the statement of the primary *bhāvanā*, the sentence that depends upon it must be sublated.

This being the position, it is replied: this would indeed be so if the context (*prakaraṇa*) were to apply [a mantra] without regard for the inherent capacity (*svarūpasāmarthya*) of the thing to be applied;
rather, it depends upon that for the sake of application. Otherwise, there would be no displacement (*utkarṣa*) of the *pūṣānumantraṇa* mantra or of the twelve-fold *upasat*.
And when examining their form, whatever is understood more quickly [is to be applied first].
However, that which is more remote is weak.

In that case, if it is enjoined elsewhere by means of direct statement (*śruti*), indicative mark (*liṅga*), or syntactic connection (*vākya*), then it is displaced from the context (*prakaraṇa*) by overriding it.
By the remaining [means of proof], the requirement for the procedure (*itikartavyatā*) of the context (*prakaraṇa*) is fulfilled.
Now, if there is no direct statement (*śruti*) or other such means that functions more rapidly than itself, then the context becomes the applicator (*viniyojaka*),
as in the case of the *samidh* and other [subsidiary rites].
Therefore, in this context, it is stated that syntactical connection (*vākya*) operates more swiftly than context (*prakaraṇa*).
For in the case of context, one observes merely a mutual requirement between sentences that are complete in their own respective meanings;
whereas in the case of syntactical connection, there is a direct relationship between the words themselves.

Furthermore, while a syntactical unity (*ekavākyatā*) is being postulated between the sentence and the context as they proceed together, the capacity for expression (*abhidhāna-sāmarthya*) resides in the sentence;

while there is capacity in the other case through the sentence, there is [capacity] in the other case through that capacity in the form of direct assertion (*śruti*); while there is direct assertion in the other case through that capacity, here the application (*viniyoga*) occurs by means of direct assertion, and by that much, the expectancy (*ākāṅkṣā*) being severed, the inference of direct assertion is obstructed.

Since it is established by the strength of the scriptural statement that "they dissolve" as conceived within the context, it is proven that there is indeed an extraction (*apakarṣa*) of those things which are subordinate to those deities.
An example of a contradiction between order and context:
In the context (*prakaraṇa*) of the Rājasūya sacrifice, the narrative of Śunaḥśepa and other such elements are recorded in proximity only to the principal rite of the Abhiṣecanīya.
Is that [narrative] an auxiliary (*aṅga*) of the entire Rājasūya, or of the Abhiṣecanīya alone?
If context is more powerful, then it applies to the entire Rājasūya; if, however, it is order that is more powerful, then it applies to the Abhiṣecanīya alone—
what, then, is the prima facie conclusion?

For mere expectancy is not the cause of syntactic connection (*saṃbandha*). If it were, then in the case of the sentence "Bring the cow; look at the palace," since the word "cow" requires only an action, it would be possible for it to be connected with "look" as well, which would lead to the undesirable consequence of there being no criterion for selection (*vinigamanābhāva*).
Therefore, proximity (*saṃnidhāna*) is the cause of connection.
And thus, by this very [word] "bring," the connection with "the cow" is determined.
Nor is mere proximity (*saṃnidhāna*) the cause of connection;

otherwise, in the case of "The king's son comes, let the man be removed," there would be no definitive determination (*avinigamana*), since the word "king's" is equally proximate to both the words "son" and "man."
Therefore, expectancy must be stated as the cause of determination.

In this case, since the word "son" (*putra*) has an expectancy arisen by virtue of its denoting a relative, the word that happens to occur nearby—which itself possesses an expectancy for another relative—satisfies that very expectancy.

Thus, there is no connection with an independent term that denotes merely the form of a person; rather, it is connected with the subsequent word "let him be removed," which requires something to be removed.
Even when proximity exists, there is no connection due to the absence of expectancy (*ākāṅkṣā*).
Thus runs the proverb: "The heated [iron] connects with the heated [iron].
Likewise, even if something is expected, it cannot be connected as long as it is not brought into proximity.
Thus, since even that which is proximate is not connected so long as it is not required,

and because sequence and context possess equal force with respect to the connection between the two, and because their combination is impossible, it follows that the application of the *Śunaḥśepa* narrative and other such elements is by way of option (*vikalpa*) between the *Rājasūya* and the *Abhiṣecanīya*.
This is the prima facie position (*pūrvapakṣa*).

This being the case, it is said in reply: In the Rājasūya sacrifice, the requirement for the "manner of performance" (kathaṃbhāva) extends from the Pavitra rite up to the Kṣatrasya Dhṛti. And according to the principle—"When the manner of performance is not yet complete, whatever action is recited that has no ascertained fruit belongs to the context of the primary rite"—the Śunaḥśepa narrative and other such elements are subsidiary parts of the Rājasūya.

However, in the case of the *abhiṣecanīya* sacrifice, which has no expectancy for the constituent elements already provided by its own statement, the syntactic unity with the *rājasūya*—which possesses an established expectancy—is postulated as soon as that expectancy is aroused by the recitation in proximity (*saṃnidhi*). And while the syntactic unity with the *abhiṣecanīya* is being postulated through its expectancy, the indicative power (*liṅga*) characterized by capacity (*sāmarthya*) is established by the already existing syntactic unity with the *rājasūya*, because it serves to assist that [entire sacrifice]. Furthermore, while the indicative power is being postulated through syntactic unity with the *abhiṣecanīya*, [the application is already determined].

An indicative mark (liṅga) postulates an expressive power (śruti) capable of enjoining [a mantra] only so long as that expressive power has not yet been postulated elsewhere by an indicative mark derived from a syntactical connection (vākya).

Once the application is established by the already existing expressive power, the context (prakaraṇa) being thus accounted for, the intermediate [application] postulated by mere proximity (saṃnidhāna) dissolves,
because it lacks any basis of proof (pramāṇa) and thus remains unestablished.
Furthermore, because the *rājasūya*, as the subject of the context (*prakaraṇin*), is always present in the mind, its proximity need not be postulated.
Therefore, when there is a conflict with the context, the order of sequence is necessarily sublated; it is established that there can be no option, because the latter is weaker.

An example of the conflict between *samākhyā* (name/designation) and *krama* (order): In the section (*kāṇḍa*) designated as *pauroḍāśika*, and within the sequence (*krama*) of the *sānnāyya* offering, the mantra "Be purified for the divine rite" (*śundhadhvaṃ daivyāya karmaṇe*), which serves the purpose of purification, is recited.

In this regard, a doubt arises: is it to be employed for the purification of the vessels of the *puroḍāśa* cake because the designation is stronger, or is it for the purification of the vessels of the *sānnāyya* offering because order is stronger?

What, then, is the prima facie position? That the designation (samākhyā) is more powerful; for by the term *puroḍāśika*, those things related to the *puroḍāśa* are expressed, and the section (*kāṇḍa*) that proceeds with reference to them is called the *puroḍāśika*.
And therefore—

Since the relationship must be established through a sequence of inference starting from context (prakaraṇa) and so forth, whereas it is established directly by the name (samākhyā) itself through the Vedic text, the name is stronger than the others due to its proximity to the meaning; thus, it follows that the mantra should be employed for the cleansing of the *puroḍāśa* vessels, not for the cleansing of the *sānnāyya* vessels.
This being the case, it is replied: "The order [of sequence] is stronger than the name (samākhyā) because of the remoteness of its connection to the meaning.
For instance, a name does not directly express a relationship; rather, it denotes a section (kāṇḍa) qualified by the term *puroḍāśa*.
However, since such qualification would otherwise be inexplicable, a relationship of the section is inferred, but not directly of the Vedic mantra-text itself.
And by means of that [connection], there is also the inference of the specific mantra falling within its scope.
Furthermore, this relationship—the status of the subsidiary (śeṣa) and the principal (śeṣin)—is not understood through direct audition (śruti) alone;
rather, it is merely the general connection [that is understood].

Therefore, its similarity to the Vedic revelation (śruti) is far-fetched, and thus it is not appropriate for it to compete with [the direct injunction] in sequence. Furthermore, since its purpose is established generally through the context (*prakaraṇa*) of the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices, it cannot be connected to the primary rite alone—just as in the case of the legend of Śunaḥśepa and other such elements—because it serves as a remote auxiliary (*ārādupakāraka*).
This is because a mantra functions as an integral constituent (*sāmavāyika-aṅga*) by means of reminding one of the matters associated with the performance.

And thus, since it is not contradictory for this [text], which illuminates whatever meaning pertains to the current ritual application, to be an auxiliary part of that context (prakaraṇa), when there is a requirement for a specific detail,

the sequence of the Sānnāyya offering is capable of establishing its application toward the Sānnāyya by means of inferring the context and other factors; however, the name (samākhyāna) is not so capable.
Because that [name] is weak.

For instance: when a name (*samākhyā*) exists as the basis for a relationship, it brings about proximity (*saṃnidhi*) for the sake of establishing that [relationship]; meanwhile, while the expectancy (*ākāṅkṣā*) is being inferred through the proximity directly perceived in the Veda, and while the expectancy is being inferred through the established proximity, in the other case, syntactic unity (*ekavākyatā*) is achieved through the established expectancy; and while syntactic unity is being achieved through the established expectancy, in the other case, [syntactic unity is achieved] through the [established] syntactic unity.
The capacity for assistance is established [by syntactic unity].

To the extent that there is a capacity for assistance here through syntactic unity (*ekavākyatā*), to that same extent there is an explicit scriptural injunction (*śruti*) as the means of application (*viniyojikā*) elsewhere by means of indicative power (*liṅga*).

To the extent that there is an explicit scriptural injunction as the means of application elsewhere by means of indicative power, to that same extent there is an application elsewhere by means of a pre-established scriptural injunction; it is by this much alone [that the distinction is made].

Because it is logical that the recitation follows the context (*prakaraṇa*), everything based on the designation (*samākhyā*) becomes rootless—like a crop being reaped without seeds—due to its severed foundation.
One should understand that the designation *pauroḍāśika* (pertaining to the sacrificial cake) applies to this section because of the abundance of mantras denoting the *puroḍāśa*.
[This distinction] is caused by the intervention of one, two, three, four, five, or more entities.
A disparity among the indicative marks (liṅga) and the others is perceived with respect to the meaning of the direct Vedic statement (śruti).
Thus, the remoteness of meaning has been stated.
And in that regard: "The direct Vedic statement (śruti) always sublates [the others], while the name (samākhyā) is always sublated;
as for the intermediate ones, their status as either sublated or sublating depends on their relative position."
"Thus has the distinction been stated by the elders.
Although we fear prolixity, out of compassion for those unacquainted with the first tantra, we have fallen into a detailed exposition and now desist.

Therefore, just as in the case of the request for permission (*anujñāpanā*) and the granting of permission (*anujñā*), whose sequence is well-known, the two mantras *upahūta* and *upahūyasva* are handed down in that very order; by virtue of the similarity of the context, they are obtained as constituent parts (*aṅga*) in that same manner."

The mantra *upahūtaḥ* (you are invited) has, by its indicative power (*liṅga*), the character of a mantra for permission (*anujñā*), not for requesting permission (*anujñāpana*); and the mantra *upahūyasva* (be invited), by its indicative power, has the character of a mantra for requesting permission, not for permission itself.
Thus, here, by means of the indicative power, the sequence (*krama*) is set aside and a contrary status as a subordinate element (*śeṣatva*) is established.

For while it would take time for the context (*prakaraṇa*) to be produced through position (*sthāna*) and a syntactic unity (*ekavākyatva*) to be inferred, the application (*viniyoga*) is already accomplished by the indicative power through the inference of a direct scriptural statement (*śruti*). Therefore, there is a sublation of the sequence, which has not yet inferred a scriptural statement based on indicative power.

Similarly here, too, in the matter of application (*viniyoga*), there is a sublation of the sequence of the knowledge (*vidyā*)—which is separated by four [steps]—by the indicative mark (*liṅga*) which is separated by only one.
Although this point has already been established in the first *tantra*, that establishment was for the sake of resolving a contradiction; here, however, there is no contradiction.
For the connection with the rite of sorcery (*abhicārika-karman*) indicated by the *liṅga* is not contradicted by the sequence produced by the connection with the knowledge.
Nor can there be a contradiction here characterized by the application of what has already been applied, for that would entail such a consequence even in the case of the Bṛhaspatisava sacrifice.
If it is argued that this is a contradiction of cognition and not a contradiction of reality, that is equally the case when the mantra is applied to meditation (vidyā).
Therefore, since there is no contradiction, the mantras concerning piercing and so forth serve as auxiliary elements to meditation; thus, there is a further objection to be considered.
To this it is replied: "It is not said that there is a sublation of the order by contradiction with the indicative power (*liṅga*);
rather, once [the application] is determined by the indicative power, the order is incapable of being postulated.

For while the recitation within the context (*prakaraṇa*) is established, that which has not yet been applied by means of direct statement (*śruti*), indicative power (*liṅga*), syntactical connection (*vākya*), or context is subsequently applied through the sequence, by way of the vital channel consisting of the postulation of context, syntactical connection, indicative power, and direct statement."
For at that time, since [the mantra] has already been applied, there would be the consequence of the reading within the context (*prakaraṇa*) being purposeless.

However, once the reading within the context has been established by direct statement (*śruti*) and other means, presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*) is exhausted; therefore, the order (*krama*) cannot produce its own appropriate means of valid cognition, because there is no desire to know [anything further].

However, in the case of the Bṛhaspatisava, the direct scriptural mention of the suffix -ktvā—prescribed under the rule governing the connection between verbal roots (Pāṇini 3.4.21)—establishes a common agent;

and since this establishes a specific application through the principle of "separateness of connection" (*saṃyogapṛthaktva*), that scriptural authority cannot be sublated by another scriptural statement regarding its own means of knowledge. This constitutes the difference.
Thus it has been said:
In the Vājapeya sacrifice, however, there is a clearly distinct application for the Bṛhaspatisava.
Furthermore, this Pravargya rite is one and the same;

thus, through the removal of the doubt that it might be equal to the Bṛhaspatisava due to their equal strength, they are to be combined, rather than being mentioned separately as if they were mutually independent.
He establishes the reading based on proximity with the words "as in the case of the mention of 'forest' and so forth. //25//
But in the case of "losing," because the word for "taking up" is supplementary, it is like the *kuśa* grass, the meters, the hymns, and the chanting; this has been stated [in the Sūtra].

Where both "losing" (*hāna*) and "taking up" (*upāyana*) are heard, there is no dispute regarding their conjunction. Even where only "taking up" is heard, "losing" is implied as an inseparable necessity; thus, there is a conjunction.

However, where only the abandonment (*hāna*) of good and evil deeds is heard and their acquisition (*upāyana*) is not heard, there arises the doubt: does the acquisition—that is, the taking over—occur there or not?
Regarding this, he states the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*):
Regarding the term "non-occurrence" (*asaṃnipāta*):

it might be argued that, just as a detail heard in one recensional branch (*śākhā*) as an auxiliary to a meditation is integrated into that very same meditation even when it is not heard in another branch; [so too should it be here].
Thus, because he intends to bring together the act of bringing [the fires] as heard in another recensional text (śākhā), he says:
"And because they fall within the scope of different meditations.
For if there were identity [of the meditation], then even those acts of worship heard in one place could appropriately be combined with those in another.
But here, there is no unity among the meditations (*upāsanā*), because they are distinct by virtue of being either with attributes (*saguṇa*) or without attributes (*nirguṇa*); this is the meaning.
Now, one might object: "Just as the scriptural mention of 'attaining' (*upāyana*) necessitates 'losing' (*hāna*), so too should 'losing' necessitate 'attaining'"; to this, he says:
Furthermore, regarding the phrase "having oneself as the agent":
for indeed, possession does not occur without the departure [of the previous owner]; thus, from possession, the establishment of departure is necessarily implied.
Moreover, departure is observed even in the absence of another's possession, just as the removal of sin occurs through penance (*prāyaścitta*).

This statement regarding the difference in agents is for the purpose of strengthening [the argument], but it is not a necessary determinant, because it is inconclusive (*anaikāntika*) due to the possibility of [the soul] taking hold [of the subtle body].
He introduces the established conclusion (*siddhānta*) with the words:
"In this case, having reached... (*asyāṃ prāptau*).
This is its meaning: for that which is enjoined in one ritual action is not transferred to another ritual action, due to the absence of any authoritative means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*).

However, that which is not enjoined, but is mentioned as an established fact for the purpose of praise (*stuti*), cannot be abandoned when there is no sublation (*bādhaka*), because it is perceived through the word itself according to the logic of the section on deities (*devatādhikaraṇa-nyāya*). And thus, in the case of the *nirguṇā* [meditation], where good and evil deeds have been shaken off once and for all—

When the question arises as to what occurs regarding knowledge—similar to the case of a horse's hair and so forth—it cannot be that its dissolution occurs through [knowledge] in the same way that [impurity] is dissolved by expiation; for if that were so, the analogies of the horse's hair and Rāhu would be untenable.
There is never a dissolution of the horse's hair or the face of Rāhu;
rather, there is simply their separation from the horse and the moon.
Furthermore, when [the soul] has perished, the meanings of "shaking off" (vidhūnana) and "releasing" (pramocana) are not possible.

Therefore, since there is a requirement for an explanatory passage (arthavāda), even a distinction established by the proximity of words can bring "appropriation" (upāyana) to mind and thus fulfill that requirement.
Even though knowledge is devoid of qualities (*nirguṇa*), it is to be praised by means of [the description of] its relinquishment and acquisition.
However, the excellence of praise is the purpose, not the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*);
for even in the absence of excellence, praise is logically possible.
Nor is it observed that explanatory passages (*arthavāda*) require other explanatory passages; nor is it the case that they do not fulfill [the purpose]. Thus he says:
"And it is well-known."
And because this statement regarding the "taking up" (upāyana) is for the purpose of praising knowledge (*vidyā*):
even if the good and evil deeds belonging to one person were to yield fruit for another—
just as the *śrāddha* rite performed by a son brings satisfaction to the father, or as the *vaiśvānara* sacrifice of a father [benefits] the son.
And as for the drinking of liquor by a woman leading her husband to hell—
even so, there arises a doubt based on the intention that good and evil deeds belonging to one person cannot directly accrue to another.
The resolution is that this is a praise by way of attaining the result [of the act].
Even the phrase "when there is the intention to combine the qualities" does not intend a literal transfer of good and evil deeds in their own nature.

Anticipating the objection—"But in the section concerning the combination of the qualities of knowledge (vidyā), why is this discussion regarding the purpose of praise introduced out of context?"—the author dispels it while concluding:
"Therefore, by way of the incidental discussion on the combination of qualities..."

In connection with the integration of the qualities of knowledge (*vidyā*), the integration of the qualities of praise has been examined. Furthermore, the purpose is that one should practice kindness toward the meditator and not unkindness; thus, *ācchanda* means "desire" because it covers [the mind], and it becomes *ācchanda* through such covering. And just as there is singing without distinction [of the individual singers].
The statement "the officiating priests sing along" (*ṛtvija upagāyanti*) indicates that the singing along (*upagāna*) applies to all the officiating priests without distinction;
however, the Bhāllavins specify it by stating, "the Adhvaryu does not sing along."
Therefore, this statement of the Bhāllavins, "the officiating priests sing along," is understood as a supplementary explanation (śeṣa).
What is meant is this: "the officiating priests, with the exception of the Adhvaryu, sing along.
Why, then, is it explained in this way?
Now, one might object: "Let the sentences be independent [of one another]. To this he replies:
"That which is established by another Vedic text.
Out of fear of the contingency of an eightfold fault-ridden dilemma (*aṣṭadoṣaduṣṭavikalpa*), even the venerable Jaimini accepts that one sentence is a supplement to another sentence; thus he says:

This has been stated in the *Dvādaśalakṣaṇī*: "But rather it should be a supplementary statement (*vākyaśeṣa*), because an option (*vikalpa*) is improper; it should be a partial specification (*ekadeśa*) of the injunctions. He recites this very sūtra by way of its meaning:

"But rather, because it is a supplementary statement, there should be an exclusion (*paryudāsa*) of the other; for if it were a prohibition (*pratiṣedha*), there would be an option, and that is improper—this is the remainder [of the sūtra]."
Thus it is indeed heard: "This seventeenfold Prajāpati is indeed attached to every sacrifice. Therefore, one does not perform the *yeyajāmaha* formula in the *anuyāja* offerings.
Thus, here, without reference to any specific sacrifice, the performance of the *yeyajāmaha* in sacrifices is taught.
Having taught that [the *yeyajāmahe* formula], it is traditionally handed down [in the scripture] that "it is not [to be used] in the *anuyāja* offerings.

Regarding this, there is a doubt: is there an option (*vikalpa*) between the injunction and the prohibition, or is it an exclusion (*paryudāsa*), meaning the *yeyajāmahe* is to be performed in all offerings except the *anuyāja*s?
Let it not be that there is an option when something already established by implication is prohibited by a scriptural injunction.
For perception reveals its beauty at that moment, but it does not negate its defectiveness in the future,
because it remains indifferent to that [future state].
However, the prohibitive scripture, without contradicting its immediate beauty, restrains the person who is intent on engaging in it and makes known that its fruit will be suffering in the long run.

As it has been said: "That which results in suffering is not to be done. Therefore, even when one is impelled by passion, the scriptural prohibition is more powerful than that impulse from passion because it can restrain a person who fears future suffering; thus, it does not admit of being set aside by such [impulse].
However, scriptural injunctions and prohibitions, being of equal force, are treated as optional alternatives, like the taking up of the *ṣoḍaśin* cup.
For in that case, because an injunction is observed, a greater degree of benefit for the principal rite is inferred;
and because a prohibition is observed, [the result follows] even when there is a deficiency.
The accomplishment of the result is understood.
Thus it is said: "If it is argued that [the injunction] is like the attainment of the object, no; for both are characterized by the word.

Nor should it be said that the performance of the *yeyajāmaha* formula in all sacrifices approaches the specific sacrifice of the *anuyāja* through the medium of the general category of "sacrifice" (*yajati*).

In that case, because the prohibition pertaining to the *anuyāja* offerings operates swiftly by negating that [general rule], the specific prohibition is stronger than the general scripture (*sāmānya-śāstra*). This is because, in injunctions such as "Let curd be given to the Brāhmaṇas; but buttermilk to Kauṇḍinya," the injunction regarding buttermilk does not depend upon the injunction regarding curd to function. However, here, since a prohibition presupposes a prior attainment (*prāpti*), and since the *ye-yajāmahe* formula is not attained from any other source, it is for the sake of attaining the prohibition through its negation that—
Therefore, that injunction must be taken into account.
Nor is it correct to argue that, because of this dependence, the injunction alone is stronger and thus not an option due to unequal status, but rather that the prohibition is simply set aside;
for if that were so, the scriptural text containing the prohibition would be the utterance of one who is negligent.
And that is not tenable, for the traditional authority is equal [in both cases];
nor can it be an explanatory eulogy (arthavāda), as in the case of the statement "he does not do those two on the sacrificial animal," because its meaning is not inherent [to the ritual].
For it is logical that the two *ājyabhāga* offerings do not exist in the animal sacrifice;
however, there is no such absence of the *yeyajāmahe* formula here, because the *yeyajāmahe* is prescribed for all *yajati* sacrifices.
And because those [offerings] exist among the *anuyāja*s;
nor is it a *paryudāsa* (exclusion) regarding "those which are not *anuyāja*s," since, according to the opinion of Kātyāyana, this would result in a restrictive rule (*niyama*).
Therefore, it follows that there is an option (*vikalpa*) because one [action] is enjoined and the other is prohibited.

This being the position reached, it is said in reply: It has been stated that there is an option regarding the two instances of taking up the *ṣoḍaśin* cup; for in that case, no other course is possible.

Therefore, even though it is vitiated by eight defects, the alternative interpretation (*vikalpa*) is resorted to on the grounds that [the injunction] possesses authority even as a partial rule (*pakṣe*), lest it be rendered meaningless by the words of the learned. But here, since an interpretation through exclusion (*paryudāsa*) is possible, it is improper and unjustified to resort to an alternative interpretation.

For in this way, the connection of the negative particle (*nañ*) would be with the sacrifices other than the *anuyāja*s—that is, the *ye-yajāmahe* formula is to be performed in those sacrifices which occur apart from the *anuyāja*s.
What follows from this being so?

This is what follows: the sentence "not in the *anuyāja*s" (*nānuyājeṣu*) is incomplete and expectant; it will be connected with a portion of the preceding sentence, "he pronounces the *ye-yajāmahe*," such that as much as was intended by "he pronounces the *ye-yajāmahe*"—namely, "except in the *anuyāja*s"—is thereby expressed.
"It occurs [only] not in the *anuyāja* offerings.

Thus, because it serves to qualify the root *yaj* ("to sacrifice"), this is indeed a prescription regarding what is not an *anuyāja*; since there is no prohibition, there can be no option (*vikalpa*).
Furthermore, it is impossible for Kātyāyana—who maintains that compounds are obligatory—to be an unreliable speaker when he contradicts Pāṇini, who is more highly proficient in grammar.
For he teaches the compound formation within the section on *vibhāṣā* (optional rules).
Therefore, it is established that the injunction for the *yeyajāmaha* formula applies to those [offerings] excluding the *anuyāja*s.
He states another interpretation:
Or rather, [the meaning of] "in these" is as follows:
for just as the attribution of good and evil deeds— which are formless— to [the body] is not direct, since trembling conforms to a physical form,
so too the transfer of what belongs to one thing to another is untenable, precisely because they are formless.

Therefore, where only "shaking" (*vidhūnana*) is heard, it is better that by "trembling" one should indicate merely the cessation from the commencement of its own function, and not movement elsewhere after departing from there, as that would entail the fault of conceptual over-elaboration (*kalpanā-gaurava*). Thus, when it is argued that "shaking" means being moved away from the commencement of its own function, it is replied: Wherever there is a scriptural mention of "taking up" (*upāyana*), "shaking" must necessarily be understood as "abandoning.
If "shaking" signifies abandonment even in some instances, then it ought to signify that very same thing in other instances as well.
For it would not be so if "shaking off" (vidhūnana) were understood here in its primary sense;
but this is not the case,
because even there, what is observed is the displacement from one's own activity.
Furthermore, a conceptual complexity that is supported by authoritative evidence does not incur the stigma of being like iron.
Moreover, because verbal roots possess multiple meanings, even when [the root] *dhū* signifies "abandoning," it will still primarily mean "shaking off" (*vidhūyate*),
since we observe its usage in common parlance with the sense of "abandoning" in an abundant number of instances.
Because there is no decisive reason [to the contrary],
and because the author of the *Gaṇapāṭha* is seen there to provide explanations of meaning even by way of illustration (*upalakṣaṇa*),
it is therefore logical that here [the term] has the meaning of "loss" (*dhāna*). //26//
START BsVBh_3,3.16.27:
[The soul crosses the river] at the time of departure (sāṃparāye), because there is nothing further to be crossed; for so it is with others. BBs_3,3.27:
But surely, according to the order of the text, the crossing over of good and evil deeds is understood to occur halfway.
Moreover, these two are understood even prior [to the ritual] by the power of knowledge (vidyā);
likewise, according to the Śruti of the Śāṭhyāyanins and the Tāṇḍins,
both the word and its meaning are more authoritative than the order of recitation (pāṭhakrama).
It is just as in the case of [the statements]: "He performs the agnihotra" and "He cooks the gruel.
Therefore, since there is no prima facie position (pūrvapakṣa), this [topic] need not be commenced.
To this, it is replied:

This is not merely the order of the recitation; rather, it is the *śruti* [text] itself that says, "He shakes off his good and evil deeds. For the pronoun *tat* (that), when used in the sense of "therefore" (*tasmāt*), refers to what is proximate and indicates its status as the cause. And what is proximate is that which immediately precedes it.

It is heard [in scripture] that the approach to the river Virajā occurs at the halfway point; thus, the abandonment of good and evil deeds takes place precisely at the halfway point. Nor is there any contradiction with other scriptural passages.
Even on the half-way point, because the shaking off of evil occurs prior to the time of birth in the world of Brahmā,
there is no contradiction with the Śāṭhyāyanins either;
for in that [text], neither "living" nor "of one who lives" is heard.
Thus, the relinquishing of good and evil deeds occurs precisely on the middle path;

and so, it is the prima facie view (*pūrva-pakṣa*) that their destruction does not result from the *paryaṅka-vidyā*. However, the established conclusion (*siddhānta*) is as follows: for one who possesses knowledge and whose impurities have been shaken off by the power of that very knowledge, there is attainment of Brahman while traveling by the northern path; and it is not possible for one whose impurities are undestroyed to proceed upon the northern path.
Just as the Agnihotra is not performed before the cooking of the gruel (yavāgū), so too,

because it is heard in scripture that knowledge— when conjoined with the performance of restraints (yama) and observances (niyama)— is the means for attaining Brahman seated upon the couch via the northern path,
and because such attainment is impossible for one whose sins have not been destroyed.
Knowledge itself of such a kind destroys impurity, and once impurity is destroyed, it leads one to the higher path; how then could there be impurity halfway along?
Therefore, by overriding the order of the text, the order of the meaning must be followed.
But is it not the case that here there is more than just the order of the text?
It has been stated that this is because the word "that" (tad), being a pronoun, refers to what is proximate;
however, that is incorrect,
for in this context, mere proximity in the intellect is what is required, and nothing else.
And since that [mention] belongs to knowledge as well—just like the immediately preceding [context] because it occurs within the section on knowledge—the scriptural statement is common to both cases;
thus, only the meaning and the textual order remain, and among those, the meaning is more powerful.
Furthermore, there is no contradiction with the *Tāṇḍya* and other scriptural passages in the prima facie view.
For the phrase "shaking off [evil] like a horse its hairs" speaks of the activity of a self-dependent person;
yet one who has passed away possesses no self-dependence.
Therefore, there is a contradiction with that [scriptural statement]. //27//
START BsVBh_3,3.16.28:
"According to one's wish, because there is no contradiction with either [alternative].
(BBs_3,3.28) This sūtra follows from certain words.

Now, one might raise the objection: "Just as it is the fruit of knowledge that the deceased attains Brahman by way of the northern path, so too might the casting off of good and evil deeds occur for him at the halfway point. This sūtra is the answer to those points of doubt.
It explains as follows:
And as for the phrase "of one who has departed from the body," even the fruit of knowledge, which is the attainment of Brahman, cannot belong to anyone else, because of the grounds for doubt;
as they say: "One does not go there without having been born [there]."

Since the destruction of good and evil deeds is possible even while one possesses a human body, it is established that the destruction of good and evil deeds occurs for the living person itself; for it is illogical that knowledge—when it is a potent cause accompanied by restraints (yama), observances (niyama), and so forth—should fail to effect the destruction of karma. "At will" (chandataḥ) means according to one's own desire (svacchandataḥ), that is to say, by one's own choice.
The performance according to one's own will belongs to that knowledge accompanied by restraints (yama), observances (niyama), and so forth;
it would pertain to a living person, not to one who is dead.
And the abandonment of good and evil deeds preceded by that [knowledge] would occur only for one who is alive.
Because that which is capable cannot be delayed.

Thus, when the effect arises immediately after the cause, the relationship of cause and effect (nimitta-naimittaka) is established; furthermore, the consistency between the two scriptural passages of Tāṇḍin and Śāṭhyāyani is maintained. Otherwise, due to the lack of independence [of the cause], it would have been stated that there is no such consistency.
By this, the non-contradiction between both [scriptural statements] has been explained.
As for those who have interpreted the Sūtra as an answer to the doubt— namely, "How do the good and evil deeds of one who knows pass over to another?"—
it is simply because there is no contradiction between the Śruti and Smṛti, which state that [the transfer occurs] "by will" (*chandataḥ*) and "by resolve" (*saṃkalpataḥ*).
However, in this matter, which is to be understood through scripture (*āgama*), independent reasoning (*yukti*) should not be introduced;
for when it is possible for those [reasonings] to enter into the body of the formal discussion (*adhikaraṇa-śarīra*), to describe a different meaning would be entirely inappropriate. //28//
The purposefulness of the ascent is established in both ways; otherwise, there would be a contradiction.
For instance, as it is heard elsewhere that the "approaching" (upāyana) occurs in proximity to the "abandoning" (hāni). (BSBh 3.3.29–30)
Even where only the abandonment [of good and evil deeds] is heard, it necessarily implies the acquisition [of a body], since the path of the gods is heard of in close proximity to that very context;
therefore, even where only the abandonment of good and evil deeds is heard, it is appropriate that the path of the gods be implied there as well.
Nor is there any contradiction with the statement, "The stainless one attains supreme equality."

Since the attainment of the world of Brahman by means of the path of the gods results in the state of being stainless (*nirañjana*) and the realization of supreme equality, it follows that the path of the gods is connected merely to the removal [of merit and demerit]. This being the position reached, the following is stated: "The wise man, having shaken off both merit and demerit, becomes stainless and attains supreme equality. For this text declares that for the wise man who has shaken off merit and demerit, there is the attainment of security through knowledge.
That which is rooted in delusion and is insecure must be turned away by knowledge characterized by the realization of the true nature [of reality].
This does not depend upon a particular place;
for the knowledge of the true nature of the rope, once arisen to remove the delusion of a snake in a rope, never depends upon a particular place.
For the very arising of knowledge (*vidyā*) consists in the cessation of ignorance (*avidyā*), which is its own opposite.
Furthermore, the attainment of the world of Brahman (*brahmaloka*) need not be awaited for the arising of knowledge;

for one whose inner being (*sattva*) has been purified through restraints (*yama*), observances (*niyama*), and so forth, knowledge arises right here in this life through hearing (*śravaṇa*) and other means.

If it is argued that since the exhaustion of karma whose effects have already begun depends upon the fall of the body, there is no purpose here for the path of the gods (*devayāna*), and thus it need not be considered because it contradicts what is seen in the scriptures—[the author replies] that its purpose does indeed exist in the context of the *paryaṅka-vidyā*, as stated in the second Sūtra.
However, some introduce the Sūtra by raising the doubt: "If even merit (*puṇya*) is discarded, then for what purpose is the path [of the gods] undertaken?"
The purposefulness of the "going" (to the world of Brahman) is established in both ways: by the cessation of evil deeds and by the cessation of meritorious deeds.
If, however, merit were to persist, then even for one who has gone to the world of Brahman, there would be a return here for the enjoyment of the fruits of that merit.
In that case, there would be a contradiction with the scriptural texts concerning non-return, which teach that such a person does not return.
Therefore, they have raised a doubt that should not have been raised at all, namely, that just as there is an exhaustion of evil deeds, there is likewise an exhaustion of good deeds.
For when a rebirth is projected by knowledge (*vidyā*), what room is there for this doubt: "If his merit is exhausted, why does he go [to that state]?
This rebirth is not based on merit, but rather it is based on knowledge.
Therefore, the description stated by the elders alone is correct. //29//
There is no restriction; there is no contradiction with all [the factors], according to scripture and inference. For the context is the regulator of the dharmas.
If, however, that [distinction] were not respected, then the ritual details (dharma) of the Darśapūrṇamāsa, Jyotiṣṭoma, and so forth would become intermingled;

nor would there be an extension (prāpti) of those [details] into their modifications (vikṛti), such as the Saurya sacrifice or the twelve-day rite (dvādaśāha), by means of the general rule of transfer (codaka), because in all such cases the details are directly enjoined (aupadeśika).
Furthermore, it is not the case that the *darvihoma*, being neither an archetype (*prakṛti*) nor a modification (*vikṛti*), is devoid of ritual properties (*adharman*);
nor is it possible to perform any ritual action endowed with every single property.

And this being so, the direct statement (*śruti*) and other means of application are not themselves the applicators, for even they function as applicators only when a general connection has already been established by the context (*prakaraṇa*).

Even in cases where application is understood through direct statement (*śruti*) and so forth without recourse to context (*prakaraṇa*), context must necessarily be postulated there as well in order to sustain that application.
Therefore, context must certainly be accepted for the sake of application and its restriction; otherwise, the authority of direct statement and the other means would be undermined.

Therefore, the path of the gods (devayāna) or the path of the fathers (pitṛyāṇa) is prescribed only in those meditations (*upāsanā*) where it is specifically mentioned, and not in other meditations, because it is not so mentioned there. Nor can it be argued that the attainment of those paths applies to all meditations on the basis of the general statement, "And those who in the forest worship with faith and austerity" (*śraddhā-tapas*), for it is heard in scripture that the attainment of those paths belongs only to those for whom faith and austerity are the supreme goal.
But this is not the case for those devoted to knowledge (*vidyā*).

Moreover, if this were so, since the instruction on the path occurs within one *vidyā*, it would follow that the instruction on the path should be performed in only one place and not in other *vidyās*;
yet it is heard [to occur] in other *vidyās* as well.
Therefore, the conclusion is reached that not all forms of meditation result in reaching the Path.

This being the position, it is replied: In the passage, "And those who in the forest meditate with faith and austerity," it is not said that mere faith and austerity lead to reaching the Path; rather, in the context of "by means of knowledge they ascend there," it is understood that ascetics who are not ignorant [of the truth] are intended, and not those possessing only [faith and austerity].

By prohibiting the attainment of that [world] through austerity (*tapas*) and faith (*śraddhā*) alone, and by stating that austerity and faith combined with knowledge (*vidyā*) are the means for its attainment, the text shows that even those who possess other forms of knowledge share the same path as those who know the five-fire-vidyā (*pañcāgni-vidyā*).
Likewise, in another passage concerning the five-fire-vidyā, it is stated: "Those who know this thus, and those who, in the forest, worship faith as the Truth (*satya*)."
Because the word "truth" (satya) applies to Brahman alone with absolute independence;

for that alone is the truth, since everything else is in some way only relatively true due to its falsity. Furthermore, those who know the five fires are included [in this context] precisely by virtue of possessing such knowledge.
Moreover, because of their association with knowledge (*vidyā*), it is logical that this [instruction] refers specifically to those who are devoted to other forms of knowledge;
for it is heard in scripture that those who have fallen away from the two paths meet with a downward course.
And even among those, by virtue of their fitness, the path here is connected specifically with the path of the gods (*devayāna*).

This is what is meant: the context (prakaraṇa) might be the determining factor if there were no scriptural (śrauta) or traditional (smārta) statement establishing non-restriction; however, such a statement does exist, and it possesses greater authority than the context.

Therefore, the path of the gods (devayānaḥ panthāḥ) applies to other meditations with attributes (saguṇa-vidyās) as well. Furthermore, the purpose of the repeated instruction regarding the path has been explained by the author of the Commentary (Bhāṣyakṛt). //31//
START BsVBh_3,3.19.32:

"The abiding of those who hold office lasts as long as their office. (BBs_3,3.32) Having completed the reflection upon knowledge with attributes, he now reflects upon the knowledge without attributes.
Liberation cannot be the fruit of knowledge that is devoid of attributes (nirguṇa),
for in the Śruti, Smṛti, Itihāsa, and Purāṇas, it is heard that even among the learned— such as Apāntaratamas and others— there occurred both the assumption and the abandonment of various bodies;
this would not be possible if liberation were the fruit [of such knowledge].
Because that [liberation] is impossible for one who has turned away [from the world]; or, even if it were possible, it would lack the defining characteristic [of liberation].
For non-return is indeed the defining characteristic of that [liberation].
Therefore, even though knowledge exists, liberation does not result because that [liberation] is logically untenable.
As for the fruit, the various supernatural powers (vibhūti) are indeed the fruits of that knowledge;
however, he considers the scriptural statement regarding non-return (*apunarāvṛtti*) to be merely for the purpose of praising that [knowledge].

Nor is it correct to argue that, just as the scripture "For him there is delay only so long as he is not released; then he shall be merged" implies that the knower awaits the fall of the body, so too for Vasiṣṭha and others there must be an awaiting of the enjoyment of the fruits of their *prārabdha* karma;
for they would have to await only that specific karma by which their current bodies were initiated.
And thus, they would not take on another body;
nor does it coherently follow from a straightforward interpretation that "they remain for only that long," because delay is impossible when the efficient cause is present.
Therefore, even this [statement] must be understood as being for the purpose of praising knowledge (*vidyā*).
Consequently, liberation (*apavarga*) is not the fruit of knowledge;
thus, the prima facie position (*pūrvapakṣa*) is established by way of challenging the attainment of liberation.
And here, while it may appear that liberation is a partial cause, the reality of the prima facie position (*pūrvapakṣa*) is rather that it is not a cause at all.
The established conclusion (*rāddhānta*), however, is as follows: [Liberation occurs] when impelled by the Lord, who is gratified by the performance of both knowledge and ritual action.
Having completed their office, these [beings] attain the supreme state.

In the case of knowledge devoid of qualities (*nirguṇa-vidyā*), it is not appropriate to explain the liberation (*apavarga*) that is heard [as its fruit] as being merely a figurative praise (*stuti-mātra*).
This is because, upon a thorough examination of the preceding and following passages, the intention (*tātparya*) of the majority of the Śrutis is determined to lie in this very point;
and it is not proper to alter that which constitutes the primary intention.
For it has been said: "In an injunction, the primary meaning of a word is not [its etymological] secondary sense.

Nor is it correct to argue that the knowledge of Brahman is not the cause of liberation because Apāntaratamas and others, despite possessing that knowledge, were not liberated due to their succession of various bodies;
for even when a cause exists, the non-arising of the effect occurs if there is an obstacle, which does not detract from the status of that thing as a cause.

For it is not the case that gravity, being obstructed by its connection with the stalk and the fruit, did not produce falling; rather, when the obstruction is removed, it produces it, yet it is not the cause of that [falling] in itself. Nor is it the case that water, obstructed by a dam, does not flow toward lower ground; rather, upon the breaking of the dam, it flows toward the lowlands.

In the same way here as well, although the knowledge of Brahman—being obstructed by the station of authority ordained by the Lord, which was secured through the performance of knowledge and ritual action—has not granted liberation, nevertheless, upon its completion and the removal of that obstruction, [it grants liberation].
He will give [the answer].

For just as one who has realized Brahman in his final body remains even while awaiting the exhaustion of the karma whose fruition has already begun, and then attains liberation upon that exhaustion; so too a wise person such as Vasiṣṭha, though possessing knowledge and action characterized by the fruit of an already commenced office, [remains] until the exhaustion of that [office].

Awaiting [the time], whether simultaneously or sequentially, performing the successive taking up and relinquishing of various bodies, even though liberated, he continues to dwell as if in saṃsāra through a manifestation characterized by non-exertion (*anābhoga*).
This is what has been stated:
For their store of karma (*karmāśaya*) functions only once to yield its fruit of office;

however, with the exception of those karmas whose fruition has already begun (*prārabdhavipāka*), all others have been exhausted by knowledge alone and have passed away. Furthermore, these [liberated ones] are not "rememberers of past births" (*jātismara*).

For one who, being dependent on another, is cast off from this body and led to another body, remembers what was experienced in a previous birth; he is called "one who has taken birth" (*janmavān*) and "one who remembers his former births" (*jātismara*).
One who, by his own will, moves from one body to another as if from one house to another, is not designated as "one who remembers his former births.
Having resolved and settled the dispute.
He states the negative concomitance (*vyatireka*):
"For if, when one karma whose fruition has begun has been set in motion by being experienced once, there were another karma whose fruition had not yet begun... [this would be the case].
This is what he means.

When ignorance and the other afflictions (*kleśa*) have ceased through knowledge, it does not necessarily follow that the entire accumulation of karma (*karmāśaya*)—which has been deposited over a succession of births beginningless in time and whose timing of fruition is indefinite—is also eliminated, because that accumulation of karma is incalculable.
Nor is it the case that once ignorance and the other afflictions have been burnt away, [the karma remains].
For when the cause of destruction is the same for all, it cannot be said that one thing is destroyed while another is not.
In that case, would even karma whose fruit has already begun to manifest perish?
And if so, there would be no maintenance of the body for the wise, such as Vasiṣṭha and others; therefore, he says:
"But of karma whose fruit has already begun to manifest..."

On the basis of the authority of the Śruti text, "For him, the delay is only so long," it is understood that only karma whose fruit has not yet begun is exhausted, and not that which has already begun to bear fruit. Furthermore, this prima facie view (pūrvapakṣa) is not universally applicable even to all sages who possess the qualification [for knowledge], because they do not all possess knowledge of the reality of the Self; thus he says:
"And in other cases of knowledge..."
In that case, is there no liberation for them at all? No, he says:
"Later, when their sovereignty perishes, they become weary and dispassionate."
*Pratisaṃcara* means dissolution (*pralaya*).

Furthermore, regarding matters such as heaven that do not enter the path of direct experience and are to be understood solely through scripture, even those of dull intellect might harbor doubt concerning their having results in the afterlife;
as the explanatory passage (*arthavāda*) states: "For who indeed knows whether there is [anything] in that other world, or whether there is not?"

He states that "because its fruit is directly perceived" (*pratyakṣaphalatvāt*)— meaning that since liberation is established by experience as the fruit of the knowledge of non-duality (*advaita*), there is not even a scent of doubt regarding it—

that direct realization of the reality of non-duality (*advaitatattva-sākṣātkāra*) indeed strikes down, root and branch, the phenomenal world (*prapañca*) superimposed by ignorance (*avidyā*). This [realization] is formidable...
That it pacifies the burning heat of the coals of saṃsāra for a person is clear both from experience and from the strength of logical reasoning; thus the Śruti has been shown.
And that is established through the experience of Vāmadeva and others.
Now, one might ask: how does the sentence "That thou art" (tat tvam asi) illuminate experience itself? To this he says:

The meaning is that for the statement "That thou art" (*tattvamasi*), which is a description of the present, it is impossible to interpret it as having a future sense or to supply the word "dead" (*mṛta*) by ellipsis. //32//

But there is an inclusion of the cognitions of the syllable [Om] because of the commonality and the presence of that [state], as in the case of the *aupasada* offerings; this has been stated [in the Sūtra]: "But there is an inclusion of the prohibitive cognitions regarding the syllable belonging to all the Vedas, because of the commonality of the prohibition and because of the recognition of its being that very same state. This means that the prohibitive cognitions concerning the syllable (*akṣara*) which reside in all the Vedas are included—that is, they are to be combined—because the prohibition is common to them all and because there is a recognition of the identity of that state in the syllable.

Regarding the statement "Bliss and so forth belong to the Principal," although this meaning is established for positive attributes by virtue of their being primary, and is likewise established for negative attributes,
nevertheless, this [present discussion] should be understood as an elaboration of that very point. An illustration:
Regarding the phrase "in the case of Jāmadagnya, it is not deficient":
although another example has already been provided here in the Śābara-bhāṣya, this one is nevertheless shown as an alternative example because it can be cited by the same underlying principle.

In this regard, there is an example from the Śabara-bhāṣya concerning the establishment of the sacred fires (*ādhāna*), which is prescribed in the Yajurveda: "He who, knowing thus, establishes the fire. As a subordinate part (*aṅga*) of that [rite], it is likewise prescribed in the Yajurveda itself: "He who, knowing thus, sings the Vāravantīya; he who, knowing thus, sings the Yajñāyajñīya; he who, knowing thus, sings the Vāmadevya. And these...
The *sāmans* originate within the *Sāmaveda*.

Regarding this, a doubt arises: should these be employed at the time of the fire-installation (*ādhāna*) with the loud pitch characteristic of the place where they originate, or with the low pitch characteristic of the place where they are applied? For there is a scriptural injunction: "The *sāman* is recited loudly; the *yajus*, softly."

What, then, is the prima facie position? Since the subsidiaries (*aṅga*) are enjoined by the very injunction of origin (*utpattividhi*) as being means required [for the primary act], and since that [origin-injunction] comes first, it follows that the loud recitation (*uccaiḥsvara*) applies to them. To this, it is replied:
"In the case of a conflict between a subordinate and a principal [element], the Vedic connection prevails because of its being for the sake of that [principal]. (Jaimini Sūtra 3.3.9)

The meaning is this: the originative injunction (*utpattividhi*) is subordinate (*guṇa*), whereas the applicatory injunction (*viniyogavidhi*) is primary (*pradhāna*). When there is a conflict or transgression between these two—namely, loudness (*uccaiṣṭva*) based on the consideration of the originative injunction and whispering (*upāṃśutva*) based on the consideration of the applicatory injunction—this conflict or transgression is resolved by the primary factor, which consists in being enjoined according to its principal nature.
In the case of the *vāravantīya* and other such [rites], the connection with the Veda is to be understood as primary, not by way of the subordinate quality of "being produced.

Why? Because "being enjoined" (*viniyujyamānatva*) is primary while "being produced" (*utpadyamānatva*) is subordinate; that is, because the state of being produced exists for the sake of that which is being enjoined.

What is meant is this: although even in the originative injunction (*utpattividhi*) there is a fourfold form, since the nature of being an injunction is no different [from that of an applicatory injunction].
Furthermore, since the fourfold nature [of injunctions] is invariably concomitant with that alone,
nevertheless, the purport (*aidaṃparya*) of the sentences differs.

Among the four forms— namely, origin (*utpatti*), application (*viniyoga*), entitlement (*adhikāra*), and performance (*prayoga*)— only one particular form is delineated by a specific sentence, provided it has not been established by another.

In this regard, although the Sāman chants are prescribed in the Sāmaveda, nevertheless, those sentences have as their sole purpose merely the origination (*utpatti*) of the chants, because their application (*viniyoga*) is already established by sentences belonging to the Yajurveda. Thus, since the desired object is not obtained from the sentences of origination, and since that [application] is understood from the sentences of application, the sentences of origination serve that very purpose; therefore, it is the specific accent associated with the means of accomplishment that belongs to the sentence by which they are applied.
The apprehension [of the mantra] occurs, however, not by touching upon mere form.
The example provided by the author of the Bhāṣya should also be applied in this very same way:
when it would follow that mantras produced in the Udgātṛ-veda are to be employed by the Udgātṛ.

Since they are already assigned to the sacrificial cake (puroḍāśa) offered by the Adhvaryu, they must be employed by the Adhvaryu alone in accordance with the primary rite, and not by the Udgātṛ; he applies this principle to the present case with the words:
"so it is here as well. //33//
START BsVBh_3,3.20.34:
"Because of this much being taught" (iyadāmananāt) / BBs_3,3.34:
Even though the matter is established in the passage, "The two selves have entered the cave," it is here further elaborated.
In one case, there is knowability for both the enjoyer and the non-enjoyer;
in the other, it belongs to the enjoyers alone. Thus, due to this difference in the objects of knowledge (*vedya*), there is a difference between the two Vidyās.

Furthermore, it is not appropriate to interpret the term "the two drinking" (*pibantau*) as referring to a secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*) of one who drinks and one who does not drink, as is done in the case of the expression "he places the creation."
Because when the primary meaning is possible, it is improper to resort to a secondary one; nor can one resort to it merely out of deference to a supplementary passage (vākyaśeṣa),
for a supplementary passage provides a definitive conclusion only in cases of doubt, and here there is no possibility of a conflict between accepting the primary sense and the figurative sense.
Because there is an absence of equal strength [between the two passages], and because the context is sublated by a sentence that is stronger than it;

therefore, when it is argued that a difference in knowledge follows from a difference in what is to be known, the following is stated: in the passage "Two birds" (*dvā suparṇā*) and in the passage "The two drinking the *ṛta*" (*ṛtaṃ pibantau*), the number two is perceived at its origin; thus, by virtue of that commonality, the general rule applies.
Regarding the phrase "the two who drink," that which refers to "the two drinkers" is what must be refuted;
however, in accordance with the opening and the conclusion, this should not be understood as applying to both literally, but rather explained figuratively according to the "umbrella-bearer maxim.
For the middle portion is to be understood in conformity with that by which it is introduced and that with which it is concluded.

Just as in a textual passage where the discourse begins with the proclamation of the defect of *ajāmitva* (lack of barrenness) and concludes with its resolution, the intermediate statements such as "Viṣṇu is to be sacrificed to inaudibly for the sake of *ajāmitva*" do not attain the status of independent injunctions; rather, their injunctive force is disregarded and they are interpreted as *arthavādas* (explanatory passages).
Why is this? Because syntactic unity (*ekavākyatā*) is indeed superior to the fragmentation of sentences (*vākyabheda*).

Likewise here as well, in accordance with that [usage], the word "the two who drink" (*pibantau*) must be understood by secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*) as referring to a group consisting of both those who drink and those who do not drink.
And thus, because there is no difference in the object of knowledge (*vedya*), there is no difference in the knowledge (*vidyā*).

Moreover, in all three of these Vedāntic passages, even across the three contexts, it is understood through a consideration of what precedes and follows that it is indeed the knowledge of the Supreme Self (*paramātma-vidyā*) alone.
If this is so, then how can there be the mention of the individual soul (jīva)? To this he says:
"By the intention of expressing identity.

In this [passage], the individual soul is not being propounded; rather, it is mentioned as a restatement (anuvāda) in order to demonstrate the non-difference of the individual soul from the Supreme Self.
Furthermore, since the knowledge of the Supreme Self has non-duality as its object, there is no occasion for an inquiry into difference and non-difference.
Therefore, it is established here that there is only one single knowledge. //34//

Regarding the doubt as to whether there is a difference or not between the two knowledges taught consecutively in the *Kauṣītaki* and *Kahola-Cākrāyaṇa-Uṣasta-questions*, we maintain that there is indeed a difference, on the grounds that [the objects] are like the various classes of beings within one's own self.

Why? Although no difference is perceived between the question and the answer in both instances, nevertheless, because that same single [instruction] is heard again without distinction, it follows—lest it be rendered purposeless—that there must be a difference, just as in the case of the repetition of the *yajati* (sacrificial) act.

Nor is it correct to argue that, just as there is no difference when the Tāṇḍins teach the same thing nine times in the passage "That is the Self; That art thou, Śvetaketu," so too here there is non-difference.
"May the Blessed One inform me further," for it is heard there [in that context] that non-difference is appropriate;
but here it is not so.

Therefore, although the non-difference of the object to be known (*vedya*) is understood here, nevertheless, because in one place there is meditation upon that very same [Self] characterized by the transcendence of hunger and so forth, while in another place there is meditation upon it characterized by the absence of body and organs, it follows that there is indeed a difference between the two knowledges (*vidyā*).

To this, it is replied: This is not intended as an injunction for meditation; rather, through an examination of the questions and answers, it is perceived that its purpose is the exposition of the true nature of reality (*vastu-svarūpa*).
What follows from this if it is so?
This is what follows: since an injunction (*vidhi*) has the purpose of bringing about what has not yet been attained, it is inapplicable when [the object] is already attained.

However, the true nature of a thing (*vastu-svarūpa*), even when stated again and again, does not incur any fault; for authoritative persons (*āpta*) may indeed say what is beneficial (*pathya*) even a hundred times.
In particular, the Veda is even more highly esteemed than one's parents;
yet there is no total redundancy here,
because in one case [the parents] are honored for transcending hunger and other needs, while in the other [the Veda], it is for the dissolution of cause and effect.
Therefore, there is only one knowledge because of recognition.

Against that proponent of a partial prima facie view who maintains that the Self is presented as distinct by both of these two knowledges, the contradiction with its being the innermost of all has been demonstrated. //35//
If it is argued that otherwise the distinction [between the two] would be untenable, we say no; for it is like other instructions.
However, the intention regarding the reality of this prima facie position (*pūrvapakṣa*) has already been shown.
The rest is easy to understand. //36//

There is an exchange [of attributes], for they distinguish [the two] as in other cases.
(BBs 3,3.37) Because there is no assumption of an inferior form on the part of the superior, there is no meditative reflection on both forms in both places.
Rather, it is the contemplation of the identity of the inferior living being with the superior form.
For in this way, it follows that the inferior becomes superior.
This being the position reached, it is said in reply: because the nature of one is enjoined by means of a restatement of the other, the contemplation of both is enjoined in both cases.

Otherwise, however, if it were merely said, "He who am I, he is that," then, having referred back to the individual soul (jīvātman), its state as the Lord (īśvaratva) would be enjoined; but the state of the Lord as the individual soul— expressed as "He who is that, he am I"— would not be established.
As in the case of "That thou art" (*tattvamasi*).
Therefore, both forms are taught for the purpose of meditation in both cases.

Now, it was argued that this would entail the degradation of the superior [Brahman] to the status of the inferior; so, does the inferiority of this [Brahman], which is in reality devoid of qualities (*nirguṇa*), actually occur when Brahman with qualities (*saguṇa*) is being meditated upon?

If it is argued that, for the sake of some specific result, mere meditation is enjoined and this does not imply the inferiority of [the Self], then here too, the contemplation of the exchange is taught merely for the sake of a result and does not imply the inferiority of the superior [Self]. However, we do not disregard the firmness of identity which is established as a secondary injunction (*anvācaya-śiṣṭa*).

It is established that through the instruction on qualities such as "desiring the truth" (satyakāma), the Lord who possesses those qualities is realized; thus, it is proven that in both cases, there is meditation on the dual nature [of the individual self and the Lord]. //37//
