"By 'Brahman' one conquers these worlds; he has conquered," so they say of him who knows this great, first-born Yakṣa as "Brahman is Truth.
For Brahman is indeed Truth. Through this passage, the meditation upon the previously mentioned Brahman called "the Heart" as "Truth" is enjoined.

The word "that" refers here to Brahman, known as the heart; by the phrase "this very [thing]," he refers to another mode of its manifestation which is about to be described. That [Brahman] existed (ās) in that state at the beginning (agre), that is, it came into being (babhūva).
To the question "What is that?", he says: "The Real (Satya) alone.
That which is manifest (sat), having form (mūrta), and that which is unmanifest (tyat), being formless (amūrta), is the Real.
He states the fruit for one who meditates upon it: "He who [meditates] on this... and so forth.
He who knows the first-born Yakṣa as worthy of worship—how he knows it is stated: "Brahman is Truth.
He conquers these worlds.

Furthermore, the word *inu* means "conquered" or "subdued" and functions in the sense of the word *ittham* (thus). It refers to the enemy who is present in the intellect as something to be conquered, [denoted by] "this one" (*asau*).
He would become non-existent; he would perish.
He concludes the stated point with the words, "He who knows this thus.
To the question, "Why does one who knows thus conquer?", he says: "Because Brahman is indeed Truth.
The meaning is that, therefore, the production of the fruit from its meditation is also true.

Now, as for that which is the Truth (*satya*), what is it? Here too, the two words "that" (*tat*) refer back to the two forms previously mentioned. To the question, "Upon what object of focus (*ālambana*) is that to be meditated upon? the answer follows with the passage beginning, "That is the sun, this one which... and so on, concluding with "Its secret name (*upaniṣad*) is 'Aharaham'."
It ends with the words, "He who knows thus slays evil and abandons it.
*Upaniṣad* means a secret doctrine;
its etymological definition is: "it slays evil and it abandons [it]."
Alternatively, this is the meaning of the root *han* (to strike) or *hā* (to abandon).
Thus, providing the etymological derivation (*nirvacana*), he states that the fruit is the destruction of sin. Regarding this subject, the author of the Commentary (*bhāṣyakāra*) says:
"Whoever indeed [knows] this"—that is, the meditation on the syllables of the name "Satya.
And thus says the Śruti: "This is that imperishable reality, 'Sat-ya. 'Sa' is one syllable; 'ti' is one syllable; 'yam' is one syllable."
"The first and last syllables are truth, while that which is in the middle is untruth. This untruth is enclosed on both sides by truth;
thus it becomes essentially truth. Untruth does not harm one who knows this.
Here, the *it* (the *i*-suffix) is for the purpose of pronunciation.
The letter *t* should be seen as unconnected [to the others].
For here, the first and last letters are truth, because they lack the form of death;
in the middle—that is, between them—is falsehood, for falsehood is indeed death.
Because of the similarity of the letter *t* in both "death" (*mṛtyu*) and "untruth" (*anṛta*),
this untruth, which is of the nature of death, is enclosed on both sides by truth;
it is contained within two forms that are of the nature of truth.
Therefore, that abundance of truth, being nothing more than truth itself, is indeed truth in its multiplicity. The remainder has a meaning that is not obscure.
This is the meditation upon the syllables of the name of this very knowledge of truth (*satyavidyā*).

Although non-difference is perceived through the attraction of the subject matter by the phrase "that which is truth," nevertheless, there is a distinction due to the difference in results, just as there is between the two scriptural injunctions regarding the *darśapūrṇamāsa* sacrifices— one being obligatory and the other optional:
"One desiring heaven should sacrifice with the *darśapūrṇamāsa*s" and "One should sacrifice with the *darśapūrṇamāsa*s for as long as one lives."

Although it might be argued that there is a difference [between the two meditations] despite the non-difference of their connection, the following reply is given: this meditation is indeed one, because it is recognized as non-different through the reference to what has been previously introduced in the words "That is the Truth" (*tatsatyam*).
Furthermore, there is no difference in the fruit;

the passage beginning with "Its secret name is *aharaham*" is an explanatory eulogy (*arthavāda*) intended to praise another ancillary part of that very same meditation—the worship under the name "Secret"—and is not an injunction for a separate fruit.

If, however, because there is no hearing of a qualification for the procedure of knowledge (*vidyā*), one were to postulate a qualification by assuming a fruit mentioned in an explanatory passage (*arthavāda*), then—just as in the case of the *jāteṣṭi* sacrifice—a combined qualification would have to be postulated due to the absence of any distinguishing factor.
Consequently, it would be established that meditation is a single entity endowed with all the fruits mentioned in the explanatory passages.
He sets forth the interpretation of another:
Regarding the phrase "others, however":

some hold that because the object of meditation is non-different—since both the Vājasaneyaka and the Chāndogya concern the eye and the sun—there is non-difference [between the two texts], and consequently, there should be a combination (*upasaṃhāra*) of the qualities such as "truth" mentioned in the Vājasaneyaka.
They have thus explained the sūtra, "For that same [meditation] indeed, truth, etc. [BS 3.3.5]. The author now refutes this:
That is not correct.
[The phrase] "connected with the ritual action of the Jyotiṣṭoma and resting upon the udgītha" [is the point].

Even though there is no difference in the adjuncts (anubandha), there is a distinction because of the difference in what is to be accomplished (sādhya); thus, due to the difference between the two knowledges (vidyā), there is no combination [of details]. //38//

"Desire and so forth [are to be combined] elsewhere and there, from the bases and so forth" (BBs 3,3.39).
Although there is a distinction between the Chāndogya and Vājasaneyaka meditations by virtue of being with qualities (*saguṇa*) and without qualities (*nirguṇa*), [the details are to be combined].

For instance, in the Chāndogya Upaniṣad it is heard that "those who depart here having realized the Self and these true desires," whereby the desirables (kāmāḥ), like the Self, are taught as objects of knowledge.

In the Vājasaneyi [Upaniṣad], however, the supreme Brahman devoid of attributes (nirguṇa) alone is taught in the passage, "Speak for the sake of liberation. Nevertheless, there is a mutual combination of qualities between the two.

In the case of the knowledge of the attributeless (nirguṇa-vidyā), the inclusion of qualities associated with the knowledge of the qualified (saguṇa-vidyā) is possible solely for the purpose of praising Brahman.
And although, in the case of the qualified [Brahman], it is not possible to include qualities such as mastery (*vaśitva*) for the sake of meditation—

since these are not enjoined as objects to be meditated upon in the knowledge of the unqualified Brahman, whereby they might be connected here as objects of meditation— but rather their attainment occurs as being inseparable from qualities such as having true desires (*satyakāma*), it is nevertheless said that there is an "inclusion" (*upasaṃhāra*).

Thus established is this summary of the meaning of the section: the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) is that even though there is a similarity in abundance, because in one place the support of space (*ākāśādhāratva*) is heard and in the other the identity with space (*ākāśatādātmya*), there is no mutual inclusion of qualities between the two meditations (*vidyā*). The final conclusion (*rāddhānta*), however, is that there is complete similarity in both cases because of the instruction regarding the Self (*ātman*); for by the word "space" the Self is denoted in one place, and in the other, that very same [Self] is denoted as the support of the small space (*daharākāśa*). Thus, due to complete similarity, [the qualities] apply to Brahman in both places.
There is a collection of all qualities.

However, even though there is a difference between the meditations (vidyās) based on whether they possess qualities or are devoid of qualities, the systematic arrangement regarding the collection of qualities has been shown.
Therefore, everything is clear. //39//
START BsVBh_3,3.26.40:
Non-omission due to reverence.
BBs_3,3.40: In the Vaiśvānara-vidyā, there is indeed the rule that the practitioner of that meditation must eat before his guests.

Therefore, although this reflection does not directly concern the sphere of meditation (*upāsanā*), it is nonetheless connected [to the present topic] because of its connection with the first meal which is related to that [meditation].
He shows the subject of the inquiry: "In the Chāndogya, having introduced the Vaiśvānara-vidyā... and so forth.
He states the doubt that motivates the inquiry:
"Is it the omission of the meal?
Here, he raises an objection to the doubt on the grounds that there is no prima facie position (pūrvapakṣa) against it.
Regarding the phrase "tadyadbhaktam" (that which is the rice-offering), it is because of the scriptural mention of the conjunction with the arrival of the cooked rice.

This has indeed been stated in the very first *tantra* [of the *Mīmāṃsāsūtra*] by the rule: "The action regarding the footstep is not the motive for the leading [of the cow], because the leading is for the sake of another.

Just as the taking of the dust from the seventh footprint of the one-year-old heifer (*ekahāyanī*) being led for the purpose of purchasing *soma* is not the motive, and does not, in turn, motivate the leading of the heifer itself.
For what reason?
Because the bringing [of the Soma] is already enjoined by the purchase of the Soma, and because the taking of the dust from the seventh step depends upon that [purchase].

Likewise here as well, since the offering of the vital breaths (prāṇāhuti) is connected with the arrival of food for the purpose of eating, in the absence of eating, there is no causal efficacy toward the food; thus, the prima facie argument (pūrvapakṣa) does not hold.
Thus, the meaning is that this section (adhikaraṇa) constitutes the prima facie view (pūrvapakṣa).
Having raised an objection against the prima facie view, he provides the resolution:
"This being the case... (evaṃ prāpte).
He says "lest it be lost" (na lupyet); the word "first" (tāvat) is for the purpose of refuting a doubt regarding the established doctrine (siddhānta).
He asks:
Why? The answer is: out of respect. He elucidates that very point:
For it is thus:
the Jābālas indeed transmit [the tradition], "One should eat before the guests";
and the statement "one should eat" is a teaching primarily concerned with the Prāṇāgnihotra.
For, from the scriptural statement, "Just as hungry children wait upon their mother,

so do all beings wait upon the Agnihotra," it is heard that all beings are dependent upon the Agnihotra as its guests; therefore, by virtue of being part of the same context, here too in the phrase "one should eat before the guests," the primary focus is indicated to be the oblation to the vital breaths (prāṇāhuti).

This being the case, the text—by first censuring the priority of feeding guests with the words, "Just as if one were to offer the Agnihotra for another without having offered it oneself, so would that be," and then establishing the master's own eating as the master's Prāṇāgnihotra—demonstrates a regard for the Prāṇāgnihotra. Now, one might object: "Let this scriptural statement be accepted as referring to the offering to the vital breaths; however, does it apply only to the case where the master eats, and not even when he does not eat? To this, the author replies:
For [the scripture] cannot tolerate the omission of even the quality of "priority," much less the omission of the Agnihotra itself which possesses that priority; this is what is intended.
Indeed, such is the regard for the Prāṇāgnihotra that the master’s meal—which was prescribed to occur after the guest’s meal—is drawn forward from its time and prescribed before the guest’s meal.

Thus, when the Śruti does not tolerate even the omission of the property of "priority" belonging to the Agnihotra (the substratum of the property), what need is there to mention its tolerating the omission of the substratum itself? This is the meaning.
Having restated the objection raised by the prima facie position (*pūrvapakṣa*), he refutes it:
"But surely they are for the purpose of eating.
For just as the *agnihotra* belonging to the *kauṇḍapāyināmayana* sacrifice is distinct from the obligatory (*naiyamika*) *agnihotra* due to the difference in context (*prakaraṇāntara*).

Since the Prāṇāgnihotra lacks any other substance or deity by way of a distinct property, it requires them; thus, through the transfer of properties based on the similarity of the goal and the identity of name with the obligatory Agnihotra, the acquisition of those material properties occurs.

In this manner, when the milk and other materials belonging to the obligatory Agnihotra would otherwise apply to the Prāṇāgnihotra, the fact that the substance is the rice-gruel obtained from the meal is specifically enjoined.
Nor does this much establish that eating is the motivator [of the Prāṇāgnihotra].

This has already been stated: just as the Prāṇāgnihotra is not motivated by eating because it occurs after the time for eating has passed, so too is there no lack of motivation for that which employs a portion of a substance, just as in the case of the rule, "one cuts off for the Sviṣṭakṛt from the northern half."
Because it is the motivator (*prayojaka*).

For example, in the injunction "they cause the wives to perform the *patnīsaṃyāja* sacrifices with the tail" (*jāghanyā patnīḥ saṃyājayanti*), the tail is the motivator for the *patnīsaṃyāja* sacrifices which consume a portion of the tail as their substance.
Indeed, that alone is called a non-motivator (*aprayojaka*) whose purpose is not understood without the mention of a motivator.

Just as it is impossible to know the "northern half" without the taking up of the *puroḍāśa* cake by the instigator (*prayojaka*), whereas it is possible to know the "tail" (*jāghanī*) even when it has been divided; therefore, just as in the case of the tail, even without the procurement of a whole animal, the form [of the tail] is taken— like that of a shaven-headed man or others— from a seller of meat who lives off the remnants of animals procured by another and sells them in pieces.
In this way, even cooked food can be taken;
therefore, the proponent of the prima facie view (pūrvapakṣin) maintains that there is no lapse of the Prāṇāgnihotra when the eating of food is omitted.
However, the use of the word "water" by the author of the Bhāṣya is intended merely to indicate the necessity of taking a substitute. //40//
START BsVBh_3,3.26.41:
Because of the statement regarding what is present.
(BBs 3,3.41) For the statement, "This is for the oblation" (*taddhomīyam*), employs some proximate substance in the act of oblation by means of the pronoun *tat*.

Since the denotation [of the injunction] does not reach its completion without the cognition of something proximate, this [injunction] must be fulfilled by depending on what is proximate— namely, "whatever food comes first"— in order to complete its own denotation.

And since that proximate food is for the purpose of eating, one ought not to employ other substances such as water or other items, just as in the case of the rule, "he cuts off from the northern half for the Sviṣṭakṛt."

As for the tail (*jāghanī*), its specific classification as a distinct part is not dependent upon the *agnīṣomīya* animal sacrifice, because it is seen even independently when situated at the slaughter-ground (*sūnā*). Therefore, there is a distinction between this [tail] and the [tail] from that sacrifice.
Furthermore, as for what was stated—that there is an injunction of a different substance (cooked food) by way of subverting the substance obtained through the *codaka*—that is incorrect.

He says that because the name *agnihotra* occurring in the injunctive statement (*vidhyuddeśa*) does not possess that nature [of being a distinct rite], whereas the name occurring in the explanatory passage (*arthavāda*) can be justified as a mere eulogy by taking up some established similarity, it cannot enjoin that very nature; thus he states:

"And here there is no acquisition of the properties of the archetypal *agnihotra*. Furthermore, if the acquisition of properties for the *agnihotra* were admitted through the force of the extended injunction (*codaka*), a much greater number of established [properties] would be sublated.

Furthermore, it is not logical to assume a systematic sublation when such sublation is possible; for it is only in the case of the *kṛṣṇala* oblation that sublation of what has been obtained is accepted due to the lack of any other alternative. Thus he says: "And when the acquisition of those properties is admitted... This supports the absence of a *codaka* (extended application).
And for this very reason, it is said here as well:

"precisely because there is no extension [of the ritual details] according to the sequence already stated, the components of the Agnihotra are merely figurative (sāṃpādika). If that [extension] were to apply, however, their figurative nature would not be tenable."
Indeed, in the case of a beautiful woman, her breasts, face, and so forth are produced as the forms of a ruddy goose (*cakravāka*), a lotus (*nalina*), and so on;

however, it is not the case that actual ruddy geese and the like in a river are produced as ruddy geese and so forth. From this also, we understand that there is no application of the water-rite (*udaka-prāpti*).
As for the observation regarding "respect," that is intended to enjoin priority in the case of feeding [the guests].

The sense is that while the substratum (dharmin) is not necessarily permanent in the same way as the properties (dharmas) whose non-lapse is enjoined in a particular case, its permanence is not thereby established.
Now, one might object: since the time for the master's meal is prescribed as occurring after the feeding of the guests, how can this [priority] be set aside? To this, he says:
There is no excessive burden for a statement; the meaning is that there is no excessive burden for a specific rule when it subverts a general rule. //41//
START BsVBh_3,3.27.42:
There is no restriction regarding the determination of that [result], because it is seen [in scripture]; for it is a separate result, being unobstructed.

Just as the statement, "He whose *juhū* ladle is made of *parṇa-wood hears no evil report," which is studied as an independent injunction (*anārabhyādhīta*) and has an inseparable connection with the sacrifice, [is understood to produce a distinct result].

Just as that which is grasped by the injunction for the performance of a sacrifice through the *juhū* ladle— being for the sake of the sacrifice (*kratvartha*), independent of a fruit, and understood through a statement in the present indicative—

is not accepted as having a fruit of its own (as in the case of the *Rātrisatra*), so too meditation pertaining to the *udgītha*, being invariably connected with the ritual action and grasped by the injunction for the performance of the action, is not capable of being assumed to have a fruit characterized by the attainment of all desires, as understood from a statement in the present indicative.
Because it is for the sake of another.

Thus, there is a Sūtra of the Great Sage: "In the case of substances, purificatory rites, and actions, since they are for the sake of another, the mention of a fruit should be regarded as a mere explanatory eulogy (arthavāda).

This being the case, when it is argued that—just like the rule regarding the *parṇa*-leaf in a sacrifice—the rules concerning meditations (*upāsanā*) must likewise be mandatory, we reply: It is appropriate that the mention of a fruit in the case of the *parṇa*-leaf is merely an explanatory eulogy.
For the state of being made of parṇa-wood cannot, like the sacrifice and so forth, experience a connection with a fruit,
because it is not of the nature of an activity;
and only an activity possesses a fruit.
As they have said: "Because a result is seen for that which has an origin.

Nor is there, as in the case of being made of khadira wood, a sacrificial post (yūpa) connected to the context of the ritual under discussion to serve as the substratum; for the quality of being made of parṇa-wood is taught as an independent injunction (anārabhyādhīta), and thus no such contextual substratum exists.
Therefore, by means of the sentence itself, through the connection with the *juhū* ladle, the sacrifice must be made known as the substratum for the quality of being made of *parṇa* wood.
And since a sentence that is not intent upon [that substratum] cannot make it known, the intention (*tātparya*) of the sentence toward that [substratum] must necessarily be accepted.
Consequently, being intent upon that, it is not capable of establishing even a connection between the *parṇatā* and a fruit.
Because this would result in a split of the sentence (*vākyabheda*).

However, since meditations (*upāsanā*) consist of an activity, it is logically possible for them to be connected to a fruit by their very nature; thus, there is no contradiction in enjoining the meditation as having the *udgītha* and so forth as its basis while prescribing it for a specific fruit, because this constitutes a qualified injunction (*viśiṣṭavidhi*).
Indeed, when a meditation having the *udgītha* as its means is enjoined for the sake of a fruit, it does not entail a split of the sentence.

[Objection: Is it not the case that meditation is a consecration (*saṃskāra*) of the *udgītha*—which is an auxiliary (*aṅga*) of the ritual action—because of the accusative hearing "the *udgītha*" [in the text], just like the act of sprinkling (*prokṣaṇa*) and so forth?
And thus, as with the application of ointment and other such consecrations, the mention of a fruit [for meditation] is merely an explanatory eulogy (*arthavāda*).
[Reply: Not so.
For it has been stated above that here the meditation is not on the *udgītha* itself, but rather on the syllable *oṃ*, which is a part of it;
moreover, the syllable *oṃ* is not a constituent of the ritual action (*karman*) per se, but is a part of the *udgītha*, which is a constituent of the ritual action.
And what is useless is not desired [as an object of meditation].

Therefore, as in the case of "he offers the flour-meal," the connection is that the fruit results from the meditation (upāsana) which has the syllable Om (oṃkāra) as its means, by way of a modification of the application (viniyoga-bhaṅga). Consequently,

it should be understood that just as the godohana vessel and other such items— though based on a sacrifice— are non-obligatory (anitya) due to their connection with a specific fruit, so too are the meditations on the udgītha and the rest.
The remainder has been stated in the Bhāṣya.
Nor is this hearing of the fruit merely an explanatory passage (arthavāda);
for if it were merely an explanatory passage, its function would be entirely indirect, whereas such is not the case when it is intended to convey the fruit.
However, there is no direct cognition of a fruit from a statement in the present tense.
For this very reason, in the case of the *prayāja* offerings and the like, one does not postulate a fruit based on an explanatory passage (*arthavāda*) that is stated in the present tense.
This would only be the case if such a passage were intended to convey a fruit.
It cannot be said that the *prayāja* and other such rites are fruitless because they exist for the sake of another. //42//

It has been stated that this is just like the case of the offering (pradāna). Since the non-difference of the essential nature of Vāyu and Prāṇa is established through a consideration of the meaning of their respective scriptural passages, the meditation upon them is also non-different, as it is defined in dependence upon them. Nor is there a difference [between the two meditations] due to the difference in qualities pertaining to the internal self (ādhyātma) and the divine realm (adhidaiva).
For there is no difference in the possessor of qualities (guṇavat) due to a difference in the qualities themselves.

Indeed, once the Agnihotra has been established by the injunction "one should offer the Agnihotra," there is no differentiation of that Agnihotra based on differences in qualities such as rice and so forth.
For it is only a difference in quality connected with an action at the time of its origination that serves to differentiate the action.
Just as in the case of two rites connected with curd (*āmikṣā*) and whey (*vājina*),
there is no connection with a rite that has already arisen;
likewise, in the instructions concerning the internal (*adhyātma*) and the divine (*adhidaiva*), there is a connection with meditations (*upāsanā*) that have already arisen.

Thus, by considering the opening and the conclusion, there is a determination of the unity of the knowledge; hence, the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) is that there is only a single performance [of the meditation].

The established conclusion (*rāddhānta*), however, is as follows: It is true that the knowledge is one; nevertheless, due to the difference in qualities (*guṇa*), there is a difference in performance.

Just as there is a difference in the performance of the single *Agnihotra* sacrifice because of the difference in qualities such as the evening and morning times, so too here, although the meditation is one, a difference in performance is established due to the difference in qualities pertaining to the internal (*adhyātma*) and the divine (*adhidaiva*). Thus it is proven.
For this instruction on the division between the internal (ādhyātma) and the divine (adhidaiva) is for the purpose of meditation;

it is a separate instruction intended for meditation upon the Agnihotra, just as the rice-grains and other materials are [separately taught] for that same rite. By this, the instruction regarding the vows is also explained.
By this, it is meant through the non-difference of reality (*tattva*).
And the particle *eva* (only/just) is for the purpose of excluding vows such as those regarding speech and so forth.

Now, one might object: "In the phrase 'to this deity' (*etasyai devatāyai*), only a deity in general is heard, not Vāyu; so how can it be said that it teaches the attainment of Vāyu? To this, he says:

Regarding the term "deity," it refers here to Vāyu. Indeed, Vāyu encompasses fire and the other elements; thus, in relation to fire and the rest, he is unconditioned, whereas fire and the others are conditioned by him. Therefore, by virtue of his quality of encompassing them, Vāyu is the unconditioned deity. [The phrase] "causing all to attain" means...

Since there is no distinction in the hearing [of the mantra] for those who have assembled, and since the deity Indra is non-different, there might arise a suspicion that all three *puroḍāśas* are to be offered simultaneously.

However, because the qualities of *rājā*, *adhirāja*, and *svarāj* are distinct even in the original injunction (*utpattivākya*), and because the transposition of the *yājyā* and *anuvākyā* verses is prescribed therein, the offerings must indeed be separate according to the respective order, due to the distinctness of the deities.
For if they were offered together, the prescription of the transposition would be illogical.
In the case of a sequential offering, the rule for transposition is meaningful, because such a sequence is precisely what is intended to be expressed. The rest is easy to understand. //43//

"On account of the abundance of indicatory marks; for that [scriptural statement] is stronger.
(BBs 3,3.44) Here, having begun with the established conclusion (*siddhānta*) and then set forth the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*), he establishes the final conclusion.
In this regard,

although there are many indicative marks (*liṅga*) that suggest the independence of the mind-altars (*manaścit*-) and so forth, nevertheless, they do not establish independence as an independent means of proof;
rather, they merely reinforce the independence already established by a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*).
And there is no means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) here that establishes independence;
nor is this a mark (*liṅga*) characterized by capacity (*sāmarthya*) by which its independence might be established.
For that capacity would have to belong either to the expression or to the meaning.
Likewise, there is the case of the mantra for the consecration of Pūṣan being used for the consecration of Pūṣan;
or, for example, the capacity of the meaning of the singular number in "one should sacrifice with an animal" (paśunā yajeta) to delimit the object to be numbered.
And this is not like the indicative mark (liṅga) characterized by the observation of another's purpose.
Because this [passage] is intended as a praise and thus forms a single syntactical unit with the injunctive statement, it is subordinate to that injunction.

Therefore, in the absence of a contradiction characterized by semantic capacity (sāmarthya) which would obstruct the context, the context leads one to understand that the "mind-altars" (manaścidityādi) are subsidiary to ritual action. Nor does the restrictive scriptural statement, "These indeed are piled by knowledge alone" (vidyācita eva), preclude their entry into the ritual action.
For if there were a contradiction with scripture (*śruti*), the context (*prakaraṇa*) would not prevail,
since the restrictive particle (*avadhāraṇa*) serves the purpose of excluding external means.
Furthermore, the sentence— "By knowledge alone these [fires] become built for one who knows thus"— which establishes a connection with the person, is capable of setting aside the context.
Indeed, this too is merely an observation of something else;
and it has already been stated that such an observation does not, by itself, establish a rule.

Therefore, even that is not sufficient to contradict the context; thus, these fires, though metaphorical, enter into the ritual action precisely because of the context, just like the mental [sacrifice].

Regarding the twelve-day sacrifice (dvādaśāha), it is heard in the scripture: "With this vessel, the sap-filled ocean, I take for you the mental cup belonging to Prajāpati. In this regard, there is a doubt: Is the mental cup a separate rite distinct from the twelve-day sacrifice, or is it a subsidiary part of the tenth day occurring within that [sacrifice]? On this point, because the mental cup is designated as distinct from the twelve-day sacrifice in the statement, "The twelve-day sacrifice is speech; the mental cup is mind," there is a distinction between them, just as there is a distinction between speech and mind.

The twelve-day sacrifice (*dvādaśāha*) has its *chandas* verses shaken off and their essence gone; yet it is said that "they are replenished by the mind alone. Because the twelve-day sacrifice is praised by means of the mind, and because the relationship between the praise and the object of praise is logically possible only when there is a distinction [between them], the day [in question] is a different day from the twelve-day sacrifice and not a part of it.

Furthermore, since the days end with the *patnīsaṃyāja* offerings, and because it is heard [in the scripture] that "having performed the *patnīsaṃyāja*, they proceed toward the mental [rite]" (*mānasa*), the mental rite is situated after the *patnīsaṃyāja*.

It might be argued that even on the thirteenth day, by somehow excluding it from the count through a secondary (jaghanyā) application of the term, there would be no contradiction with the designation "Twelve-Day Sacrifice" (*dvādaśāha*) because the number twelve is still present; to this, we reply: if the thirteenth day were established as such by some other means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), then the term "Twelve-Day Sacrifice" could be applied to it in a secondary sense. However, no such other means of valid cognition exists.
Moreover, a difference in designation does not necessitate the assumption of a distinct ritual act (*ahar*),

since that can be accounted for even by the distinction between a subordinate member (*aṅga*) and its principal (*aṅgin*). For this very reason, the relationship between the object of praise (*stutya*) and the eulogy (*stāvaka*) is also established.
Just as in the case of Devadatta’s long hair;

although the rule that the Patnīsaṃyājas constitute the end is the general one, nevertheless, due to a specific statement regarding the tenth day, the mental acts—such as the taking up, placing, and offering of the cups—will follow after the Patnīsaṃyājas.
For what indeed would a scriptural injunction not cause one to do?

It is established that the *mānasa* (mental cup) is an integral part of the tenth day, not a separate day; for it is understood from the statement "this is indeed the release (*visarga*) of the tenth day" that it is subordinate to the tenth day. Furthermore, since "release" (*visarga*) is the characteristic of that which has an end (*anta-vat*), it is not independent. And because of the designation of the tenth day as its substratum in the passage, "On the tenth day they proceed for the *mānasa*," it is proven that the *mānasa* is an ancillary of the tenth day.
In this regard, the author of the *Dharmamīmāṃsāsūtra* stated that the *mānasa* (mental cup) is an auxiliary (*aṅga*) of the tenth day belonging to the twelve-day sacrifice (*dvādaśāha*).

However, the venerable commentator (*bhāṣyakāra*) maintains that it is also an auxiliary of the tenth day of the ten-night rite (*daśarātra*), citing the authority of another scriptural passage (*śruti*). He says:
Just as in the case of the ten-night sacrifice, there is the "day on which no dispute is permitted" (avivākya) on the tenth day;
"avivākya" is the name of the tenth day. //44//
The previous alternative [of the mental recitation] may apply here because of the context, as in the case of the mental performance of the ritual action. (BBs 3.3.45)
And because of the extension [of the rule] (atideśa):
for there is no similarity whatsoever between the fires that are merely symbolically identified with bricks and the fire built with bricks, except for their entry into the ritual action.
Therefore, when it is argued that [the self] is likewise not independent, the following is stated: //46//
But it is knowledge alone [that is enjoined], because of its definitive determination (nirdhāraṇa).

Let it be that other scriptural injunctions (*vidhi-uddeśa*) which are observations of another purpose (*anyārtha-darśana*) do not have the function of enjoining what has not been previously established; however, in these cases where there is no scriptural statement of an injunction, an injunction must be inferred according to the principle: "The statements are indeed injunctions, because they present something new (*apūrvatvāt*). (Mīmāṃsā-sūtra 1.2.18).
And thus, whatever kind of meaning is understood from these [passages], it becomes exactly according to that;
for from these, there is understood the continuity of the *manascit* and other fires, their definitive nature, their connection with distinct results, and their relation to the person (*puruṣa*).
Nor does this have the character of being dependent on the ritual (*kratvartha*), like the *godohana* vessel and so forth, by which the human purpose would become subordinate to the ritual act.
Nor is the restrictive determination "only that which is piled by knowledge" intended for the purpose of excluding external means;
for it is established by its very nature that knowledge does not depend upon external things.
Therefore, by process of elimination, the restriction is intended to exclude the suspicion that knowledge might enter into ritual action, as occurs in the case of the mental cups (*mānasagraha*).
And since this meaning is possible,
the scriptural mention of the particle (*nipāta*) need not be strained by taking it as a mere indicator (*dyotaka*).

Therefore, it is established that scripture (*śruti*), indicative mark (*liṅga*), and syntactical connection (*vākya*) set aside the context (*prakaraṇa*) and convey the independence of the mental fires (*manaścid-ādi*) and so forth.
This should be understood in the same way on account of the connection, extension, direct scriptural statement, and so forth;
these are indeed clear in the Bhāṣya itself.

As for what was stated by the proponent of the prima facie view—that if they were auxiliary parts of the sacrifice, there would be an option between the previously mentioned altar built with bricks and the mental altars (manaścidityādi)—[that is refuted].

He refutes [the opponent's view] by showing that it would result in an effect identical to that [of the preceding section]: "And there is no connection with ritual action while [knowledge] itself exists.

Furthermore, since the predominance of knowledge is observed in both the preceding and following portions, that which falls in between them is also characterized as having knowledge as its primary focus due to its similarity to them, rather than being a subordinate part of ritual action; thus he says in the Sūtra:
"And because of the subsequent word, it has that same nature; however, due to abundance, there is a connection [with ritual action]."
The commentary on this is clear:

there is the Rājasūya sacrifice, [enjoined by the injunction] "A king desiring self-sovereignty (svārājya) should sacrifice with the Rājasūya. With reference to that [sacrifice], they prescribe an offering named Aveṣṭi.

"An offering on eight potsherds dedicated to Agni, gold as the sacrificial fee," and so forth—this is taught with reference to that [archetypal sacrifice]. It is further taught: "If a Brāhmaṇa should sacrifice, he should place an offering to Bṛhaspati in the middle, and having offered the oblation, he should pour clarified butter over it; if a Vaiśya, [an offering] to the Viśvedevas; if a Rājanya, [an offering] to Indra.
Regarding this, a doubt arises:
Is the mention of the Brahmins and others for the purpose of indicating [their] attainment [of the status], or is this sacrifice enjoined for the Brahmins and others?

In this regard, if "kingship" (*rājya*) refers to the activity of protecting subjects, removing thorns [from the state], and so forth, and the meaning of the word "king" (*rājan*) is "one who performs that [activity]," then the one who performs kingship has the entitlement (*adhikāra*) to the Rājasūya, according to the injunction: "A king should sacrifice with the Rājasūya."

Therefore, it is established that Brāhmaṇas, Kṣatriyas, and Vaiśyas alike can arise as performers of the kingdom; thus, all of these are eligible for the Rājasūya sacrifice. Consequently, scriptural passages such as "If a Brāhmaṇa should sacrifice" are intended to indicate a specific occasion (nimitta).

However, if "rājya" (sovereignty) is understood as the action of a king (*rājñaḥ karma*), such that the action is termed "kingdom" due to its connection with a royal agent, then, upon the inquiry "Who is a king?"—among the Āryas...

Because that [usage] is not established [among the Aryas], just as the usage of Mlecchas is a means for determining the meaning of words such as *pika*, *nema*, and *tāmara* (lotus), so too the usage among the Andhras regarding the word *rājan* in the Kṣatriya caste is the cause for determining its meaning; thus, since only a Kṣatriya is a *rājan*, there is no application [of the term] to Brāhmaṇas or Vaiśyas.
Consequently, breaking through the context (*prakaraṇa*) of the Rājasūya, separate rites performed by Brāhmaṇas and others are obtained.
Thus, they are not occasional.
In this regard, what is first established?
That they are indeed occasional.
That the one who performs the act of ruling is a "king" (rājan) is a point of no dispute among both the Āryas and the Āndhras.

For instance, it is observed that both the Āndhras and the Āryas employ the term *rāja* without disagreement for those who protect the subjects—such as Brāhmaṇas and others—and who bear the insignia of the golden staff, the parasol, and the white chowries.

Therefore, because there is no contradiction [regarding the meaning], even when there is a difference in usage, the usage of the Āryas is more authoritative than that of the Āndhras, according to the maxim of the barley and the boar (*yavavarāhavat*). This is because the usage of the Āryas possesses greater established authority.

However, when there is a conflict with the powerful consensus of the noble ones (*āryaprasiddhi*), the consensus of Pāṇini—which is rooted in that [common usage]—is sublated according to the maxim "In case of conflict, it shall be disregarded" (*virodhe tvanapekṣaṃ syāt*). Alternatively, it may be interpreted as being directed solely toward grammatical derivation (*anvākhyāna*), like the words *nakha* and *nakula*, in a manner consistent with that [consensus].
Thus, since the status of "king" (*rājā*) as the agent of ruling (*rājana*) is established, the scriptural mentions [of the suffix] serve merely to indicate the occasion (*nimitta*).
And thus, it would follow that the word "yadi" (if) would also be used in its primary sense.
This being the position reached, it is said in reply: "There is indeed no difference in form between the usage of the Āryas and the Mlecchas;
however, the distinction in that case is shown by the Vedic supplementary passages."

Thus, regarding the doubt as to whether the word "rājan" (king) is used here in the sense of the agent due to its connection with the action, or in the sense of the object due to its connection with the agent— just like the supplementary Vedic passages— the matter is determined by the traditional authority (*smṛti*) of the venerable Pāṇini, who is more learned in this regard; for the usage among the Andhras is beginningless,
whereas the usage among the Āryas has a beginning, like the words *go* and *gāvī*.

Furthermore, a well-known usage that is subject to the possibility of having a beginning cannot override the traditional authority of Pāṇini’s Smṛti to establish a usage such as "cow" (go) as having a beginning;
for if the usage of words like *gāvī* were [considered] beginningless, it would follow that even the established usage of words like *go* would be subject to having a beginning.
Therefore, since the Andhra usage is stronger when authorized by Pāṇini’s Smṛti, the word "king" (*rājan*) is used in its primary sense for the Kṣatriya caste.

Since the word "rājā" (king) would then be used figuratively for one who performs that [Aveṣṭi] sacrifice or belongs to that caste, the context of the Rājasūya—which pertains specifically to the Kṣatriya—would be set aside by the presence of the suffix *-ākāra*, resulting in the displacement (*utkarṣa*) of the Aveṣṭi.
Furthermore, the word "yadi" (if) conforms to the logical connection [of the sentence]; it cannot alter that connection when an original injunction (*apūrva-vidhi*) is present.
For this very reason, they say: "If there were a rejection of the word 'yadi,' there would be the assumption of an implied verb (*ruci*) and the addition of a word (*adhyāhāra*)."
And this [discussion] is a reflection based on the premise that there is no separate qualification for the Rājasūya such as "one desiring food should cause him to sacrifice with this [offering]";

however, since the three castes are possible for one desiring food under this very qualification, it is unavoidable that the mention of "Brāhmaṇa" and so forth serves merely as a conditional factor (nimitta). //47//
And because it is observed [in scripture]. (BBs 3.48) // 48 //
Furthermore, because of the superior strength of direct scriptural statement (*śruti*) and other means of proof, there is no sublation [of the primary meaning]. (BSBh 3.3.29.49) // 49 //
On account of the [differences in] adjuncts and so forth, [the meditations] are distinct, just as other forms of wisdom are; and this has been seen and stated. (BSBh 3.3.50) 50.
Nor [is there a loss of selfhood] even through similarity, because perception [continues]; for there is no transition to another world, just as in the case of death. (BBs 3.3.51)
And by the subsequent [sūtra], the same nature applies to sound; however, due to its multiplicity, it is a subordinate element (anubandha). (3.3.52)
