For it is not the case that because yeast and other ingredients, whether combined or separate, are not seen to be intoxicating, they fail to intoxicate once they have transformed into the form of wine.
Furthermore, in the experience "I," it is the very body, appearing in forms such as fair-complexioned, that manifests.
But it is not the case that there is something distinct from those [qualities] which serves as their substratum, such that the pot itself is the curd;
for this very reason, the grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) of the "I" with "corpulent," "moving," and so forth is possible.
Sweetness and other qualities are never experienced as being coreferential with the pot in the same way that they are coreferential with the curd—as in "the white, sweet pot."
Furthermore, the reality of the self (*ātmatattva*), which is not perceptible, cannot be inferred by means of inference and other such proofs;
for indeed, there exists no means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) that is non-perceptual.
For it has been said: "Since capacities differ due to differences in place, time, form, and so forth..."
"The establishment of the various states of existence through inference is extremely difficult.

And if this is the case for an inferential mark (*liṅga*) whose existence is invariably concomitant with what is to be proven by perception, then what can be said of verbal testimony, which has been observed to be fallible; or of presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*), which deals with objects entirely beyond the senses; or of comparison (*upamāna*), which is conceptualized as either total or partial similarity?
Because [comparison] would be a reality if there were complete similarity;
and because if there were similarity in only one part, it would lead to an over-extension, whereby everything could be compared with everything.
However, the reason stated in the Sūtra was [explained] by the author of the Bhāṣya.
It has been explained:
"activity" (ceṣṭā) is an exertion for the purpose of attaining the beneficial and avoiding the harmful.

And since that [activity] is observed to be dependent upon the body, it is indeed a property of the body; likewise, the vital breath (prāṇa), consisting of inhalation and exhalation and so forth, is also a property of the body alone.

Although desire, effort, and so forth are internal, nevertheless, because no substratum for them is perceived apart from the body, and because they exist only when the body exists, they must have their locus within the body itself;
otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence of abandoning what is observed and postulating what is unobserved. [This applies] regarding a self distinct from the body.

Since there is no evidence for [the soul] being distinct [from the body], and since desire and other qualities are found to exist in the body, it follows that the body alone is the self possessing desire and so forth; to this, it is replied: //53//
The negative concomitance [is established] because [the cognition] occurs when that [object] exists; it is not like [the case of] perception.
One who asserts that non-perception is not a means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) must be asked: "From what source have you determined the invalidity of inference and the other [means of knowledge]?"
For perception, which grasps only the form of the mark (*liṅga*) and so forth, is not capable of determining the invalidity of these [cognitions].
Indeed, unlike the cognition of smoke, a cognition of invalidity cannot arise for these [cognitions] from the contact of the sense organ with its object;
rather, it arises through the imagination of deviation based on differences in place, time, state, and form.
Furthermore, such an extensive operation is not possible for perception.
As they have said: "This [perception] is not capable of performing so many operations, because it arises by the power of a proximate object and is non-discursive.
Therefore, even if one does not wish it, another means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) must be accepted in this case.
Furthermore, discerning persons, setting aside those who have already adopted [a view], instruct those who have not yet adopted one or who are in doubt;
and such a state of theirs is not within the range of your direct perception (*pratyakṣa*).
Indeed, these states are not objects of direct perception like whiteness and so forth, but are rather to be inferred from signs (*liṅga*) such as speech and behavior.
Nor is inference a valid means of knowledge by which these [entities] could be established.
For one who, without knowing the true nature of men, desires to instruct some random person, cannot be said to possess discernment if his words are not worthy of attention.
Furthermore, even animals, seeking to obtain what is beneficial and avoid what is harmful, proceed upon ground dark with tender grass.
And they avoid ground strewn with withered grass and thorns;
yet the nihilist is a beast even among beasts, for he does not know the means for achieving what is desired or avoiding what is undesired.
Indeed, perception has no power over this domain of activity and cessation, which falls within the scope of inference.
Furthermore, one would not employ speech for the purpose of communicating with others, because the object denoted by words is not perceptible.

Let it be that there is no future birth for the nihilist; even in this very life, he is presented with a great hell consisting of muteness and the absence of both engagement and withdrawal from activity.
And the wise have exerted themselves in refuting this point.
Presumption (*arthāpatti*), although its object is entirely beyond the senses, arises from a fact that cannot otherwise be accounted for.

Furthermore, analogy (*upamāna*) has been established as a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) in the definition of the instruments of knowledge through the application of commonality with what is frequently observed.

Let this aside for now; rather, it is determined through positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*) that the cognition of "I" (*ahaṃpratyaya*) is indeed perception (*pratyakṣa*) and that it takes as its objective support something distinct from the body.

It has been stated that, like a yogi or a tiger, even when there is the conceit of assuming another body during the state of dreaming, that which is the locus of the "I-notion" (ahaṅkāra) is recognized [as the same]. As for the application of the Sūtra: the self is not non-different from the body, but rather different from the body;
why? Because it does not exist merely by the existence of that [body] (tadbhāvābhāvitvāt).
If consciousness and the like were qualities of the body, then they would have to be specific qualities (*viśeṣaguṇa*) of it;
they could not be general qualities (*sāmānyaguṇa*), such as number, dimension, or conjunction.
And thus, those which are specific qualities of the elements are observed to persist as long as the element exists, just like color and so forth.
For it is impossible for something to be both an element (bhūta) and devoid of form and other such qualities.
Therefore, because consciousness possesses characteristics different from those of the specific qualities of the elements—such as form—it is not a quality of the body.
By this, the claim that desire and so forth are specific qualities of the body is also refuted.
Although vital functions such as breathing and movement are indeed attributes of the body, they do not originate from the body alone;
for if that were so, they would also occur in the state of death.
Therefore, he upon whose support these bodily attributes depend is the Self, which is distinct from the body.
If it is admitted that the unseen force (adṛṣṭa) is the cause, then since it too cannot logically have the body as its substratum, the self alone must be accepted [as its substratum].
He states another point of dissimilarity: "And the properties of the body... and so forth.
For bodily attributes, such as form and so forth, are observed to be perceptible both to oneself and to others;
however, desire and the like are perceptible only to oneself. Thus, they possess a dissimilarity to bodily attributes.
For this reason as well, they are attributes distinct from the body.
In that regard, although consciousness is also a specific quality of the elements, it would nevertheless persist as long as the elements exist.
Nor is there a deviation [from this rule] in the case of the power of intoxication,
because that capacity is a general quality.
Furthermore, just as the power of intoxication resides in every part of wine in a certain measure, so too consciousness in the body would exist in a certain measure in each of its parts.
And in that case, many [consciousnesses] would cognize within a single body.

But it is not possible for many conscious beings to conform to one another's intentions; like many birds bound by a single snare, even if they are capable, they would be unable to move even a mere hand’s breadth when directed toward contradictory actions.
They are unable to transcend their own country;
likewise, the body also is unable to do anything at all.
Furthermore, the relationship between property and its possessor does not arise from mere positive concomitance alone.
It can be determined through positive and negative concomitance;
let it not be that every phenomenon belongs to space because it is present in all things.
Rather, [its presence] is established by both anvaya and vyatireka.

Furthermore, the negative concomitance (*vyatireka*) here is doubtful; thus he states that the proving power belongs to the positive concomitance (*anvaya*) alone: "Moreover, for as long as... and so forth.
Desiring to state another refutation, he raises an objection with the words, "And of what nature is it? He then explains this very point in a single passage:
"No," says the nihilist:
"That which is experience."

The meaning is as follows: just as the various transformations of the elements (bhūta), such as form (rūpa) and so forth, are not something other than the four elements themselves, so too consciousness (caitanya) is merely a specific transformation of the elements and not something distinct from them; otherwise, there would be a contradiction of the proposition that "earth, water, fire, and air are the [only] principles" (tattva).

What is being said is this: the entire world is a transformation of these four elements alone, and there exists no other principle whose transformation constitutes form and the like, or any other further transformation.
Although the status [of the self] as a property of the body has been refuted by the arguments stated here, the author says "If [you say] then... with the intention of stating further arguments.
The properties of the elements, such as form and so forth, being insentient, are observed only as objects and not as subjects.
Nor should it be argued that some objects might also possess the status of being subjects;

for that would contradict the principle that something cannot operate upon itself. Furthermore, this contingency does not apply to cognition itself, since it is admitted to be non-inert and self-luminous.
This has already been established previously.
He applies the portion of the sūtra beginning with "upalabdhivat" (like perception), stating: "just as of this... and so forth.
From the very means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) that apprehends perception, the distinctness of the self from the body is also understood;
for by means of that [perception] itself, which is self-luminous, there is a determination of its distinctness through its difference from the insentient properties of the elements (*bhūtadharma*).
If it is argued: "Let it be then that perception is independent of the elements due to this distinctness, yet there is still a lack of proof for the self," to this he says:

Furthermore, the self is not of the very nature of apprehension. For one who understands this, no distinction in apprehension is experienced; therefore, it must be accepted that [the distinction] arises from the distinction of objects.
Moreover, it has been demonstrated that the manifestation of objects as distinct from apprehension is impossible.
Furthermore, we have established in the *Brahmatattvasamīkṣā* that there exists no means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) capable of apprehending a difference between objects.

This being the case, since the very nature of the object and its difference are extremely difficult to establish, the talk of a difference in cognitions based on a difference in objects is cast far aside.
Therefore, even the status of being a cognizer for a cognition is not ultimately real.
However, [this distinction] is constructed by ignorance (avidyā).
He states that even in the state of ignorance there is non-difference because of the perception [of them together], saying: "And [the thought] 'I saw this'."
The meaning of this is that permanence is established not only through real non-difference, but indeed through unreal [non-difference] as well;
for otherwise, the occurrence of memory and so forth would be impossible.
For if there were plurality, memory on the part of one person regarding what was perceived by another would not be possible. This is the meaning.
He restates the point that was already refuted, in order to prevent further objections, saying:
"As for what was said...
This is the refutation directed against one who believes that because perception arises from the activity of the body, it must therefore be a property of the body.
"And it does not belong to the body absolutely.
He concludes the topic under discussion:
"Therefore, [the position] is faultless. //54//
"But those connected with the limbs [of the sacrifice] are not [restricted] to the branches, for they belong to each Veda.
(BBs 3.3.55) Because of differences in accent and so forth, the *udgītha* and other such elements differ according to each Veda.
However, the meditations (pratyayas) connected with those [Udgītha and other elements] are prescribed differently for each Vedic branch.

In this regard, a doubt arises: are the meditations prescribed in a particular Veda intended only for those Udgītha and other elements prescribed in that same Veda, or are they intended for the Udgītha and other elements prescribed even in other Vedas?
What, then, is the prima facie position?

By the hearing of the term "udgītha" in the passage, "One should meditate on the syllable 'Om' as the udgītha," the general category of the udgītha is understood. Since that [general category] cannot exist without specific qualifications, when there is a desire for a specific detail, the requirement is satisfied by the very qualification prescribed in one's own Vedic branch (śākhā) due to its proximity; thus, it does not require another udgītha from a different branch.
Nor does such reliance on proximity cause any contradiction with the direct scriptural statement (śruti).
For if one were to subvert a meaning presented by direct scriptural statement (śruti), one would thereby afflict the scripture itself; yet this is not the case here.

This is because the general and the particular—though denoted or indicated by the scriptural mention of the *udgītha*—are not subverted, since those belonging to one's own recensional branch (*sva-śākhā*) are accepted even when those belonging to other branches are not.
As they have said: "Having grasped both the genus and the individual here, we indeed accept what is both directly stated and indicated by scripture."
"If we were to abandon Kṛṣṇa and the others, what Vedic scripture would be violated therein?"

This being the position reached, it is said in reply: the meditative reflections (*pratyaya*) bound to the *udgītha* and its parts should follow along with each Veda across the various recensions (*śākhā*), rather than being restricted to each individual recension. This is because there is no distinction in the general scriptural mention of the *udgītha* and so forth. What is meant is this: in cases such as "bring the white cloth," although the word "cloth" applies without distinction, the word "white" restricts it by virtue of proximity (*saṃnidhāna*).
Thus [it is said],
because the co-occurrence (*samabhivyāhāra*) of words is for the purpose of conveying a qualified meaning (*viśiṣṭārtha*),
since that [conveying] would otherwise be impossible.

Furthermore, since words do not convey a qualified meaning without first causing the recollection of their own individual meanings, the recollection of their own meanings—being prompted by the qualified meaning—is not capable of setting aside its own prompter.

Nor is it logical that the recollection of one's own meaning should cease simply because its prompter is absent; for even a Vedic revelation (*śruti*) that functions without distinction can be restricted to a single specific instance.
However, in this case, the *udgītha* revelation conveys a qualified meaning without such restriction.
There is no authority whatsoever for such a restriction;
nor can mere proximity serve to set aside [the general rule].
Furthermore, for a scriptural statement that, through a commonality of sound, applies to all specific instances, to be confined to a single instance is indeed a contradiction.
Therefore, all meditative reflections have the entire udgītha as their object. //55//

Alternatively, there is no contradiction, as in the case of mantras and so forth. Our conviction that something is contradictory is based on its not being perceived by a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*).
Furthermore, it is observed that in the case of mantras and other elements belonging to one Vedic branch, there is a connection with rituals belonging to another branch;
since the same is seen here as well, there is no contradiction.
And this has been demonstrated by the Bhāṣya in an easy-to-understand manner. //56//
"The greater importance belongs to the totality, as in the case of a sacrifice; for so [the scripture] shows.
Regarding the Vaiśvānara-vidyā in the Chāndogya Upaniṣad, is there meditation on the parts individually and on the whole together, or is there meditation on the whole alone?

In this regard, because of the scriptural injunction for individual meditations—such as "The heaven alone, O venerable King," he said—and because the attainment of results is recorded for each individual meditation, and because the attainment of results is also recorded for the collective meditation, there is meditation in both ways.

Nor is it the case that, as in the Vaiśvānara sacrifice, statements such as "When it consists of eight potsherds" and so forth are merely explanatory passages (*arthavāda*) despite the hearing of results for each part; rather, [the result belongs] only to the injunction: "One should offer the Vaiśvānara oblation on twelve potsherds."
Thus, even in this case, there ought to be the possession of a fruit;
for in that instance, "one should offer [an oblation] on twelve potsherds" is a scriptural statement of an injunction (*vidhi*),
whereas in passages such as "it becomes [an offering] on eight potsherds," there is a statement in the present tense (*vartamānāpadeśa*).
Nor can there be an assumption of an injunction based on the principle "because of the unprecedented nature" (*apūrvatvāt*) of the statements,
since they are justified even as praise through the method of detached speech (*avayujyavāda*).

However, in this case, because there is no distinction between the statement of the present tense whether it occurs in a collective or a distributive sense, and because no specific qualification is perceived, there is a difference between the two cases regarding both the assumption of an injunction and the assumption of a result.

Since the censure [of the individual meditations] applies equally at the commencement of both collective meditation and individual meditation—just as in the statement, "The dark horse consumes the oblation"—it follows that both types of meditation are valid;
yet, it is said in response: only the collective meditation is superior, not the individual meditation.

Although the status of being a statement in the present tense is common to both cases, nevertheless, through an examination of the preceding and following context, it is understood that the intent is the entirety of the meditations.
For the meaning of a sentence is that toward which it is directed.
To illustrate: Prācīnaśāla and others approached Aśvapati Kaikeya for the sake of determining the Vaiśvānara-vidyā.

And they have set forth the meditation on various individual parts [of the self]. In that context, the descendant of Kekaya, after first censuring those various meditations, concluded by teaching the meditation on the whole through their negation.
Thus, for the sake of achieving syntactic unity and avoiding a split in the sentence, the entire composition is seen to have as its purport the meditation on the whole.
Therefore, the proclamation of manifold fruits is for the purpose of praising the principal [meditation];
it is thus established that only the meditation on the whole possesses fruitfulness.
Having presented the interpretation of a certain partial school (ekadeśin), he refutes it with the words "But some [say] here.
The meaning is that since it is improper to split a sentence when it can be understood as a single syntactical unit, such an explanation of the sūtra is not correct. //57//
Starting from *BsVBh* 3.3.33.58: "Because of the difference in various words and so forth" (*nānāśabdādibhedāt*).
Having taken for granted the distinction between the sciences (*vidyābheda*) as established in the preceding section, the present investigation has been carried out.

Now, however, it must be investigated whether there is non-difference or difference among all the *vidyās* that have Īśvara as their object, and likewise among those that have the vital breath (*prāṇa*) and so forth as their objects. [Objection:

But surely, just as in the case of the unprecedented mental cultivation (*apūrvabhāvanā*) denoted by the suffix, although there is no difference in its essential nature, there is a difference because it is defined by the meaning of the verbal root, and because that [root-meaning]—such as sacrifice and the like—is different; thus, there is a difference due to the difference in the adjuncts (*anubandha*) of the root-meanings such as sacrifice which constitute the meaning of the base (*prakṛti*).
For it is perceived as being colored precisely by that [individual soul].

Likewise, although the Lord—who is the object of knowledge—does not differ in essence from the various forms of knowledge (*vidyā*), there is no room for doubt regarding their non-difference, because the knowledge is differentiated by the distinctions of the limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*) consisting of such qualities as "having true resolve" (*satya-saṃkalpa*).

It is replied: It is logical that there is a distinction among the *apūrva* and the creative mental impressions (*bhāvanā*) in the form of ritual effects, due to the difference in their attendant factors (*anubandha*).

In this context, because Brahman exists as an established reality (*siddharūpa*), its attributes—such as the power of true resolve (*satyasaṃkalpatva*) and so forth—which reside in Him, are likewise established; therefore, there is non-difference [of these attributes] across all meditations (*vidyā*). For instance, when a young Kṣatriya is described in one place as "broad-chested, with eyes like a *cakra* bird, and possessing the nature of Duścyavana," and is described elsewhere as "lion-faced and bull-shouldered," he does not lose his broad-chestedness and other such traits. Indeed, an object does not become different with each individual description.
Because it remains in that same state in all respects;
or, if it were not in that same state, it would simply not be that thing.
For a real entity cannot be conceptualized [into something else].
Therefore, it follows that there is a difference among the meditations (*vidyās*) due to the difference in their objects of knowledge.

This being the position reached, it is said in reply: this would indeed be so if the sentences concerning meditation were established as referring to an existing reality; however, they enjoin the cultivation of meditation directed toward that object, and that [cultivation] is of the nature of an action (*kārya*).

Although the cultivation of meditation (*upāsanā-bhāvanā*) is defined in dependence upon meditation, and meditation is defined in dependence upon the object of meditation (*upāsya*), and that object of meditation— such as the Lord (*īśvara*) and so forth— is of a fixed nature, nevertheless,
its becoming the object of meditation for someone at some time in some particular form remains entirely undetermined.

Just as a single female body becomes an object of perception for someone as food, for another as a partner to be approached, for another as a child, for another as a mother, and for another as something to be disregarded, it is dependent upon the will of the person.
Likewise here as well, the meditations (*upāsanā*) do not transcend the status of being scriptural injunctions (*vidhi*), since they depend upon the will of the person.

Nor are these meditations differentiated merely by the differences in their qualities (*guṇa*), such as [the quality of] truthfulness of resolve (*satya-saṃkalpatva*). Furthermore, it is not the case that after enjoining a meditation—as one does with the *agnihotra* sacrifice—there follows an injunction of qualities such as truthfulness of resolve, similar to the injunction of qualities like curd or rice; if that were so, there would be a single unified scripture (*eka-śāstra*).

Moreover, since the meditations (upāsanās) are understood at the very moment of their origination as being distinguished by their respective qualities, and since no distinction [between them] is perceived therein, the difference between all of them is equal.
Furthermore, the integration of all qualities prescribed in every single recensional branch (śākhā) cannot be practically accomplished; therefore, there is a difference [between the meditations].

And on this view, it is not the case that "Satyakāma and the others are common [to all meditations]. Indeed, certain qualities are common to some meditations; therefore, because they have been stated in one place, they should be repeated [in the others] if the meditations were identical. However, [they are not repeated]. Thus, [the meditations] are distinct.

But in the case of a difference between meditations (*vidyā*), there is no tautology; for since a quality mentioned in one meditation is not mentioned in another, it must be stated [in each] so that the other meditation may also possess that quality, as qualities not explicitly stated would otherwise not be obtained. //58//
There is an option [regarding the performance of meditations] because their fruit is not distinct (BBs 3.3.59).

In the case of the Agnihotra, the Darśapūrṇamāsa, and other such rites, a combination is observed even for those who have separate entitlements, because they are obligatory and thus subject to a rule of necessity; however, meditations (*upāsanā*) are performed for the sake of specific desires and are not obligatory. Therefore, there is no rule of necessity regarding their combination.

The prima facie (pūrva-pakṣa) position is that, because these meditations yield equal fruits—just like the Darśapūrṇamāsa and Jyotiṣṭoma sacrifices—their option is not subject to restrictive rules, since for one who desires an abundance of results, a combination (samuccaya) of them is also possible. However, [the established conclusion is as follows]: since these meditations are accomplished by the direct realization (sākṣātkaraṇa) of the object of meditation, once the realization of the object is achieved through a single meditation, the fruit is obtained from that alone; thus, there is no further need for another meditation.

Moreover, it is impossible for there to be any excellence in the realization itself, as its nature remains constant even with a thousand means, and the attainment of the fruit is accomplished by that realization alone.

Furthermore, since the practice of one form of meditation may be obstructed by the lack of one-pointedness of mind when practicing another, the established conclusion (rāddhānta) is that in this case, optionality (vikalpa) alone is the rule. //59//

But the optional meditations (*kāmyā upāsanā*) may be combined according to one's desire, or not, because the previous reason [for non-combination] is absent. Regarding those meditations in which the means to the desired end is achieved through the unseen merit (*adṛṣṭa*) alone, even without the direct realization of the object of meditation, they depend upon the will of the person, just like the optional *darśapūrṇamāsa* sacrifices and others.
Now, [the categories of] conceptual construction and collection [are to be explained]. //60//
The existence of the [meditations] upon the limbs [of the sacrifice] according to their respective substrata is established;

there is no restriction regarding the determination of those [limbs], because they are seen as distinct, and the fruit is the absence of obstacles— this is because the scriptures proclaim fruits for these meditations (*upāsanā*).

Having raised the objection—based on the *parṇamayī* principle—that because meditations (*upāsanā*) serve the purpose of the sacrifice as mere explanatory passages (*arthavāda*), there must be a rule of mandatory combination, [the author] refutes that rule by showing that since they serve the purpose of the person (*puruṣārtha*), there is no inclusion under a single injunctive statement (*prayogavacana*).

Now, however, [the opponent] objects, challenging the previously stated point: "Even though these meditations serve the purpose of the person, why does a single injunctive statement not apply to them?"
For although these meditations are indeed optional (*kāmyā*), they cannot be independent;
for if they were, it would follow that they could be performed even outside the performance of the sacrifice, since they would not depend on the sacrificial acts.
Yet they are not so performed; what is the reason for this?

This is because those [meditations] which depend on ritual acts are enjoined specifically for the sake of their respective fruits. And thus, since the dependent meditations are governed by the substrate, it is logical that there should be a rule of combination for the meditations as well, based on the rule of combination for the substrates established by the injunction of performance (*prayogavacana*); otherwise, their status as being dependent on those substrates would be untenable. Furthermore, that injunction of performance, while combining the meditations, implies the necessary presence of the desire for their respective fruits, because in the absence of such desire, there would be no rule of combination for them. This is the view of the opponent.
This is the prima facie view (*pakṣa*).

However, the established conclusion (*rāddhānta*) is as follows: the injunction regarding performance (*prayogavacana*), which conforms to the ritual elements (*padārtha*) as they have been prescribed and specified, cannot alter the inherent nature of those ritual elements; rather, it subsists in accordance with them.

In that regard, since those [meditations] subserving the ritual are enjoined as if they were obligatory (*nitya*) and such a status is possible for them, one should necessarily combine them. However, the meditations connected with specific desires (*kāma*) cannot be restricted by way of combination because desires are non-obligatory (*anitya*).
For desires are not enjoined (as ritual duties) such that they might be combined; rather, they are merely mentioned as objects [of the meditation].
A preliminary enunciation follows other means of knowledge and does not alter the object of that enunciation by contradicting them; for if it did, the enunciation itself would be untenable.
Therefore, because desires are impermanent, the meditations bound up with them are also impermanent.

Because of the contradiction in the conjunction of the eternal and the non-eternal, even though their substrata are eternal, this alone constitutes the dependence of the dependent upon the substrate: that they exist only when the substrate exists and not when it does not. It does not mean, however, that they must always exist there and never cease to do so; thus it has been said: "For even those things which are dependent on a substrate... (61).
And because of the conduct of those learned in the scriptures (śiṣṭa). (Sūtra 62)
Because of the restoration:
"For even from the Hotṛ’s seat, he restores a poorly performed udgītha. (BBs 3.3.63)
The word *api* (also/even) has a distributive sense, meaning "even the *durudgītha*.

By the power of the cognition of the identity between the *praṇava* and the *udgītha* taught in the other Veda, the Udgātṛ priest rectifies what arises from the recitation (*śaṃsana*)—the duty of the Hotṛ priest. To the question "What is that?", he says: "Even the *durudgītha*," which is the defect (*kṣata*) produced in the Udgātṛ's ritual action as taught in the other Veda.
Speaking thus, one should apply [the analysis] beginning with "of that which is enjoined in another Veda" (*vedāntaroditasya*) and so forth. //63//
And because of the scriptural teaching regarding the commonality of qualities (guṇa-sādhāraṇya).
This aphorism is explained both by way of positive concomitance (anvaya) and by way of negative concomitance (vyatireka).
The remainder has its meaning not obscured. //64//
Or rather, it is not so, because their coexistence is not taught. (BBs 3.3.65)
And because it is observed [in scripture]. (BBs 3.66) //66//
"Human purpose [arises] from this [knowledge] derived from the Word; thus says Bādarāyaṇa.

Having established that the Upaniṣads are devoted to the knowledge of the Self—which is the means for achieving the human purpose called liberation—and having completed the preceding inquiry into how various forms of meditation serve as means to their respective human purposes, we now deliberate: is the knowledge of the reality of the Self taught in the Upaniṣads a human purpose by virtue of being a means to liberation, or is it a purpose of the ritual (*kratvartha*) by virtue of presenting the agent required for the performance of the sacrifice?

And when [the self] is for the sake of the ritual (*kratvartha*), then only that much is intended in the Upaniṣads: the agency required by the injunctions for the performance of the ritual and the state of being the enjoyer of fruits in the afterlife;

this is not possible if [the self] were non-eternal, because it would entail the loss of what has been done (*kṛtavipraṇāśa*) and the acquisition of what has not been done (*akṛtābhyāgama*); therefore, its eternity as well is intended.
Only that much is intended in the Upaniṣads.
Anything other than this— being unnecessary or contrary— could not be the meaning of the Upaniṣads,
such as [qualities like] purity and so forth. This is because,

although it has been established through an extensive treatise that the Upaniṣads are intent upon demonstrating the Brahman-nature of the individual soul (jīva) by means of restating its existence, [any other interpretation would be inconsistent].

Although this has been established in various places, there is still a purpose for this inquiry: to render that very point immovable—following the maxim of "driving in a pillar"—by refuting certain seeds of doubt raised by opponents.
In this regard, even though the knowledge of the Self is not taught in connection with any specific ritual, as is the case with acts such as sprinkling (prokṣaṇa), [it is nevertheless required].

And although the mere agent (*kartṛmātra*) is not invariably connected with the sacrifice— since the mere agent is seen even in worldly actions, whereby [the agent] would not, like the *parṇatā* (palāśa-wood quality), attain the status of being for the sake of the sacrifice (*kratvartha*) through the sentence alone by way of the *juhū* ladle (which, though taught as an unattached injunction, is invariably connected to the sacrifice)— nevertheless, the kind of self that is the agent, which partakes in the enjoyment of fruits such as heaven in the hereafter and is distinct from the body and so forth, [is what is meant].
That which is propounded by the Vedāntas has no utility in worldly activities;

for those activities whose fruits are experienced in this life can be accomplished by an agent who is not distinct from the body, however he may be. However, since Vedic activities whose fruits are experienced in the hereafter are impossible without such [an agent], it is precisely with them that this Upaniṣadic teaching is connected.

Since the agent is invariably connected with those [actions], the knowledge of that [Self] is brought about by the sentence itself—just as the ladle and other implements—which, like the quality of being made of *parṇa*-wood, attains its purposefulness for the sacrifice;
thus, the mention of a fruit is an *arthavāda*.

As it has been said: "In the case of substances, purificatory acts, and rituals, because they are for the sake of another, the mention of a fruit should be regarded as an *arthavāda*. [The knower] is one whose self-knowledge has been refined by the Upaniṣadic teachings.

For it is the agent who possesses knowledge and faith— thinking, "I am fit to enjoy the fruits in the next world"— who becomes a constituent part of the performance of a sacrifice, and not otherwise, just as rice grains that have been sprinkled with water become a constituent part of the sacrifice.

Furthermore, since it is the transmigrating self alone, indicated by the words "dear" and so forth, that is declared to be the object to be seen, the attributes such as "freedom from evil" (apahatapāpmatva) are merely qualifications intended for its glorification.

But the Upaniṣads do not have that as their primary purpose. Therefore, knowledge of the Self serves only the purpose of the sacrifice by way of purifying the agent, and not for the sake of the person (puruṣārtha).
And to support this point, the conduct and other practices of those who know Brahman, as understood from the Śruti, have been cited.
It is not only from the syntactical connection (*vākya*) that the knowledge of the Self serves the purpose of the sacrifice;
it follows also from the hearing of the instrumental case-ending (*tṛtīyā-śruti*).

Nor, however, does this refer to the Udgītha-knowledge under discussion, because of the attainment of pervasiveness through the two—namely, the pronoun "whatever" (*yat*) and the restrictive particle "by means of" (*eva*).

Just as it is said that "whatever place possesses smoke possesses fire," so too the statement regarding simultaneous undertaking (*samanvārambha*) demonstrates the cooperation of knowledge and action in the commencement of the fruit. And although this [cooperation] might occur through equal primacy— as in the case of the six sacrifices beginning with the Āgneya— nevertheless, by the reasoning already stated, it must be understood that knowledge functions merely as an auxiliary (*aṅga*) to action.

Since ritual injunctions apply to one who possesses knowledge of the meaning of the Veda, the Upaniṣads also constitute the meaning of the Veda; therefore, their knowledge too is an auxiliary to ritual action. //1//

And thus, the scriptural mention of liberation as a fruit is not merely an explanatory eulogy (arthavāda), but rather has the fruit itself as its primary purport.

For this very reason, having begun with the transmigrating self indicated by [the terms] "dear" and so forth, the absolute non-difference of that very self from the Supreme Self is taught for the purpose of instructing him further.
Just as the absolute non-difference of a superimposed snake from the nature of the rope is established by the statement, "That which is this snake is the rope."
Just as the scriptural evidence for knowledge being an auxiliary to ritual action was presented, so too has the scriptural evidence for it not being an auxiliary been stated.

The meaning of this is as follows: with respect to that study which extends up to the comprehension of the meaning and is employed in ritual acts—such as the injunctions for rituals—the qualification for those acts belongs only to one who possesses that [study] alone, and not to one who has studied the Upaniṣads, because the study of those is of no use in ritual acts.

Thinking that by the inclusion of the word "alone" (*mātra*) in the phrase "only to one who possesses the mere study," the knowledge of the meaning is excluded, the deluded person objects: "But if this were so..."

However, their status as belonging to the [four] stages of life (āśramas) is not established merely by a reference to something else;
for there is an absence of an injunction (vidhi).
Furthermore, their establishment through tradition (smṛti) and custom (ācāra) lacks authority because it contradicts direct Vedic revelation (pratyakṣa-śruti).
For direct Vedic revelation (śruti) explicitly censures other stages of life (āśrama), as in the passage beginning, "He is indeed a slayer of the heroes among the gods.

And when there is a conflict with direct revelation, the lack of authority of Smṛti and custom (ācāra) has been stated [in Jaimini-sūtra 1.3.3]: "But in case of conflict, it should be disregarded; for when there is no [conflict], there is inference [of its validity].
All of this he states with the words, "There are three branches of dharma," and so forth.
Or [it means] "having as its object those for whom one is not qualified.

Moreover, it is said that "it sets aside" (the previous rule).

This might be so:

The meaning is that since this passage also has the purpose of teaching the path of the gods (*devapatha*), it does not have the purpose of [establishing] this [other stage of life].
Furthermore, he says, "And because it is doubtful," meaning that even from a passage whose primary intent is something else, there is no very clear cognition of another stage of life.

For in the phrase "tapas alone is the second," there is no word whatsoever that denotes another stage of life (āśrama). Now, one might argue that another stage of life will be established by the statement, "this very [person] is a wandering mendicant" (pravrājin); to this he replies: "In the same way, this very...
This also is intended solely for the purpose of establishing the order of the worlds.

Having raised an objection regarding the commencement of the topic, he provides the resolution by stating that this inquiry is undertaken on the grounds that there is no explicit scriptural statement [to the contrary]: "Now, [the text says] 'from the very time of brahmacarya'... (Sūtra 1.3.18).
Bādarāyaṇa [holds that the stages of life] are to be practiced, because of the scriptural statement regarding their equality.
(BS 3.4.19) Even if the reference [to other stages] has another purpose, nevertheless, the other stages of life which are perceived from this [text] do not deserve to be rejected.
In this way, those [objections] would be refuted if they were not perceived at all,
or if they were perceived but sublated by direct revelation (śruti).
However, they are certainly not unperceived.
For instance, it is declared that "there are three *dharmaskandhas*," thus establishing a triad of *skandhas*.

In this context, if the word *skandha* were not intended to refer to the stages of life (*āśrama*), but rather denoted a mere collection, then with respect to what could the number three be properly established for the individual occurrences of religious duties such as sacrifices? However, if the *skandhas* are understood as being comprised within the stages of life, then because there are three stages of life, it is possible to establish them as three; thus, the declaration of a triad of stages of life is logically consistent.
In this context, one division of dharma is the householder’s stage, characterized by sacrifices and so forth; the second is the student, and the third is austerity.
Since the forest-dweller’s stage consists primarily of austerity, it is not distinct from that [third division].
And as for the term "established in Brahman," the author will later state that, by the method of elimination, this refers to the wandering mendicant.
Therefore, the other stages of life (*āśrama*), which are understood even from a reference (*parāmarśa*) intended for another purpose, cannot be set aside by the logic of the *Devatādhikaraṇa*.

Nor is there a contradiction with direct scriptural statement (*pratyakṣa-śruti*), because passages such as "a slayer of heroes" (*vīrahā vai*) are applicable to one who has entered the householder stage and proceeds to extinguish the sacred fires through negligence or ignorance.
Thus, since there is no contradiction, we shall either accept the references to the other stages as established facts or postulate their establishment in other branches of scripture (*śāstra*).

Just as in the sentence concerning the rule for the sacred thread (upavīta)—"He wears it over the left shoulder; he thereby produces the mark of the gods"—there is a reference to the *nivīta* and the *prācīnāvīta*, which are established by other scriptural authorities as "the *nivīta* for humans" and "the *prācīnāvīta* for the ancestors. //19//

Or rather, it is an injunction, like the rule of wearing [the sacred thread]. (BBs 3,4.20) Although this section is understood as a single syntactical unit because its purpose is the praise of being firmly established in Brahman (*brahmasaṃsthatva*), [it must nevertheless be taken as an injunction].
Furthermore, when a single syntactical unity (*ekavākyatā*) is possible, a split of the sentence (*vākyabheda*) is improper.
Nevertheless, since the other stages of life (*āśrama*) are not previously established, their reference (*parāmarśa*) would be untenable;

and since praise (*stuti*) is impossible without such a reference, what could the purpose of the single syntactical unity be? Thus, it is better to break that unity and treat it as an original injunction (*vidhi*)—just like the rule regarding the carrying of the firewood—because it conveys something not previously known (*apūrvatva*).

Just as in the case of the passage, "Holding the fuel below, he should run after [the fire], for he holds it above for the sake of the gods," where although there is the perception of syntactical unity with the holding below, the holding above is indeed enjoined because it is something not previously established— as it has been said: "But there is an injunction regarding the holding, because it is unprecedented"— so too here, the scriptural reference to another stage of life (āśrama) is to be understood as an injunction itself.

Now, even with regard to the reference [to other stages of life], the state of being "established in Brahman" (brahmasaṃsthatā) for the other āśramas must be enjoined precisely by the force of the praise itself;
for that which is not to be enjoined is not praised, since praise is for the sake of that [injunction]. Thus he says: "Even when...
Here he begins an intermediate inquiry: "And does that [state] exist in all four?"
He states the purpose of this deliberation with the words "yadi ca" (and if).

Now, one might object that a person could simply remain without any stage of life (*anāśramī*) and yet be established in Brahman; to this he replies with "anāśramitvā" (by not being in a stage of life).
Regarding that, he states the prima facie position (*pūrvapakṣa*) with the words "tatra tapaḥśabdena" (there, by the word 'penance').
This is the intended meaning:

if the term *brahmasaṃstha* were a conventional designation (*rūḍha*) for the wandering mendicant (*parivrājaka*), with its etymological components having ceased to function—just like the word *aśvakarṇa* [which denotes a specific tree regardless of its etymology]—then immortality would result merely by attaining that stage of life; consequently, one would not require knowledge of Brahman to achieve that state.
And thus, there would be a contradiction with the scriptural statement: "There is no other path for proceeding.
Furthermore, when the meaning of the individual components is possible, one should not assume a conventional power for the whole word as a collective entity.
Therefore, [the suffix] must reside in Brahman.
"One who is firmly established in Brahman" (*brahmasaṃstha*).

Thus, among the four stages of life (*āśrama*), it is logical that whichever resident of a stage of life has his firm foundation (*niṣṭhā*) in Brahman is "firmly established in Brahman" and attains immortality.

In this context, the student (*brahmacārin*) and the householder (*gṛhastha*) are denoted by their own specific terms, while the mendicant (*bhikṣu*) and the forest-dweller (*vānaprastha*) are presented by the word "austerity" (*tapas*), since austerity is their predominant characteristic.

For even a monk, by virtue of the rule of eating eight mouthfuls and possessing the purity of meditative concentration (*samādhi*), becomes preeminent in austerity like a forest-dweller (*vānaprastha*).
Nor is it impossible for a householder or others who perform ritual action (*karmin*) to be established in Brahman;
if "being a performer of action" (*karmitā*) refers simply to the yoga of action, that exists in the monk as well through body, speech, and mind.
Now, those who do not perform action with the offering to Brahman, but rather out of a desire for rewards, are "doers of action" (karmiṇaḥ).
If that were the case, then householders and others as well, who perform action with the offering to Brahman, would not be "doers of action.
Therefore, what is required is devotion to Brahman and steadfastness in Brahman, but not the abandonment of action.
Because it would contradict the authoritative means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*). Furthermore, by combining the two stages of life through austerity (*tapas*), the number three is established;

thus, even though all three stages of life are "not established in Brahman" (*abrahmasaṃstha*), they partake of the worlds of merit, whereas he who among these is "established in Brahman" (*brahmasaṃstha*) partakes of immortality.
Nor is there a contradiction in the fact that those who possess the state of sharing in the worlds of merit are the very same ones who possess immortality.

Just as Devadatta and Yajñadatta were once of dull intellect, but now, due to the study of the scriptures, Yajñadatta among them possesses sharp intellect—so too here, those who do not abide in Brahman share in the worlds of merit, while those who do abide in Brahman share in immortality; thus, there is no contradiction because of the difference in their respective states.
And thus, the word *brahmasaṃstha* will be a derivative term (*yaugika*) referring to the subject under discussion.

Just as in the case of the injunction "one worships the Āgnīdhra altar with an Āgneyī [verse]," it is the very same *Āgneyī* verse that is understood from the context, even though it has already been employed elsewhere;
nor is there any contradiction in the employment of what has already been employed.
For if it were taught here as something already established (*prāpta*), then it would have to be referred to exactly as it is perceived;
and since its application (*viniyoga*) is already established, there would be a contradiction in applying what has already been applied.
But in this case, that [mantra] is enjoined for the purpose of the *āgnīdhra* worship (*upasthāna*).

But it is not indicated [as such]; for when there is an application by way of being something to be enjoined, since there is a requirement for the referent of the word *āgneyī* (pertaining to Agni), and because there is no authority for deviating from the context (*prakṛta*),
the purpose of the scripture is fulfilled by that much alone, and thus there is no possibility of including even those things outside the context.

Nor is there a lack of application due to their being stale, because all mantras are applied in the Vācastoma sacrifice, which would otherwise entail the consequence that they could not be applied elsewhere.

Likewise here as well, it is only the stages of life already under discussion that are referred to as revolving in the mind, and not the unmentioned wandering mendicant alone; such is the prima facie view (pūrvapakṣa).
He begins the final conclusion: "That is incorrect; for when a [more appropriate] interpretation is possible, it is not right to qualify [the subject] as a forest-dweller (*vānaprastha*).
It is proper to conclude exactly as one began."
It is appropriate that those which are well-known as being of a certain number should be mentioned as being of that very same number;

for when a way [of classification] exists, it is not proper to set aside a general rule with an exception. Since each stage of life (āśrama) was begun to be described by means of its own unique characteristic, it is fitting that the conclusion should be made in that same manner.

However, the commencement and conclusion [of the stages] are not linked by what is common and uncommon; nor is it the case that austerity (*tapas*) is not uncommon to forest-dwellers (*vānaprastha*). Therefore, he says: "And austerity is uncommon.

Indeed, a mendicant (*bhikṣu*), even while observing the restriction of eight mouthfuls and so forth, does not primarily engage in bodily mortification through practices such as *parāka* in the same way as a forest-dweller.

For this very reason, the elders speak of purity and the others as distinct from austerity, stating: "Purity, contentment, austerity, self-study, and devotion to the Lord are the observances (*niyamas*).
