Furthermore, there is a designation of distinction here:
"these three. Does this refer to the monk as well? Or rather, excluding the monk, are there only three?
It is not possible, while including the monk in the number "three," to exclude him in the phrase "these three" by saying "only three."

By the use of the word "these" (*eta*), there is a comprehensive reference to those under discussion; and since the inclusion of the mendicant (*bhikṣu*) does not entail his being established in Brahman (*abrahma-saṃsthātva*), he lacks the state of having a meritorious world (*puṇya-lokatva*).

Therefore, there would be a contradiction [if one were to claim] that for such a person established in Brahman, there is both the constant attainment of a meritorious world and immortality (*amṛtatva*).
Furthermore, in the three instances where the term "established in Brahman" occurs, it must be construed with the word "when" (*yadā*).
Furthermore, there is an inconsistency regarding the phrase "in a monk always.
This is what was stated: "And if [the two were] separate.
He recalls the semblance of an objection: "But how can the word 'established in Brahman' [be used] through etymological derivation (yoga)?"
He refutes that [objection] with the words "To this it is said. This is the intended meaning:

it is true that a word is etymological (yaugika), yet when its primary application is possible, it ought not to function by bypassing that [primary sense] and applying to something other than the primary one.
But since such a possibility does not exist, one must interpret [the term] as referring to something not under discussion, lest there be an erroneous reading;
and this has been demonstrated below regarding the impossibility [of such a case].

For this dharma, characterized by being "established in Brahman" (*brahmasaṃsthatā*), is unique to the mendicant (*bhikṣu*); whereas for the other stages of life (*āśrama*), whether they are established in that [Brahman] or not, the mendicant alone is said to be "established in that."
For being established in that [state] excludes its own inherent nature; due to this contradiction, it applies directly only to that which is established in that state, and not elsewhere.
Since tranquility, self-restraint, and so forth belong to that [state], the meaning is that one's own limb does not constitute an intervention.
The scripture shows that being established in Brahman (*brahmasaṃsthatva*) is the unique duty of the wandering mendicant; thus it says: "Likewise, renunciation (*nyāsa*) is Brahman.
For renunciation is the abandonment of all attachments; why is that [renunciation] Brahman? To this it says: "Brahman is indeed the Supreme (*para*).
Therefore, renunciation, being the Supreme, is Brahman.
With reference to what is this "renunciation" (saṃnyāsa) considered superior? To this he says: "These other austerities, indeed, renunciation (nyāsa) surpasses.
This is what is meant: renunciation, characterized by the abandonment of all desires through devotion to Brahman, is itself Brahman.
Thus, such a state of being established in Brahman, characterized by renunciation, is unique to the mendicant alone and not shared by those in the other stages of life.

The meaning is that renunciation is prescribed as an auxiliary to that maturation of the knowledge of Brahmana produced by scripture—which is direct realization and the means to liberation—but not for one who is ineligible [for it]. //20//
If it be argued that [the mention of the Udgītha] is merely for the sake of praise because it is mentioned [in proximity], we say no, because it conveys something not previously known (*apūrvatva*).

If there were no injunction of meditation (*upāsanā-vidhi*) in this context due to its proximity, then even though it is situated in another place, the Udgītha is brought to mind through its connection with that injunction, owing to its non-deviation from that specific injunction.
This very [Brahman] is praised as having attained the status of a single syntactical unit through this sequence of words beginning with "the most flavorful of flavors.
For there is no restrictive reason why syntactical unity can only exist between those [words] that are explicitly uttered together;

for it is accepted that even explanatory passages (arthavādas) not uttered in conjunction with an injunction—whether obtained through ellipsis (anuṣaṅga) or extension (atideśa)—constitute a single syntactical unit.

If it is argued that— even though the co-occurrence with injunctions such as "one should meditate on the udgītha" or "one should meditate on the sāman" is heard in scripture— this [statement] is nevertheless merely a praise of that very injunction and not intended to provide the object of meditation, since the object of meditation is already provided by the words "the syllable Om is the udgītha," we reply: first of all, there is no possibility of forming a single syntactical unit (ekavākyatā) with a distant injunctive sentence concerning ritual action.
The purpose of the *arthavādas* (explanatory passages) is to serve as praise through syntactic unity with the injunction (*vidhi*), according to the analogy of the "red-clad" (the Buddhist monk).
However, there is no inconsistency in the injunction that cannot be resolved without such praise;
as they say: "But since it exists, this is the rebuttal to the objection."

For this very reason, since there is no need for an injunction (*vidhi*)—which consists essentially in instigation (*pravartanā*)—the claim that the *arthavāda* provides the means of attainment through *anuṣaṅga*, *atideśa*, and so forth, is inconsistent.
Indeed, once the means desired by the agent has been understood, the cognition of excellence (*prāśastya*) serves no purpose whatsoever.
Therefore, the injunction of the ritual act located at a distance would be rendered useless in its praise.

Since syntactical unity with that [injunction] is thus untenable, there arises a doubt regarding the proximate injunction for meditation (*upāsanā-vidhi*): "Is it useful by providing the object [of meditation], or by way of praise? In this dilemma, its utility lies in providing the object, so that it may possess purposeful meaning;
it does not lie in praise, because that is an external factor (*bahiraṅga*). For such praise is resorted to only as a last resort (*agatyā*).
Therefore, it is established that [these passages] are for the purpose of meditation (upāsanā).
"One should do," "it should be done," "it is to be performed," "it would be," and "it may be"— this fivefold form is invariably the characteristic of an injunction (vidhi) in all the Vedas.
Indeed, a positive injunction (vidhi) is that which is conducive to what is desired by the agent, while a prohibition (niṣedha) is that which is conducive to what is harmful to the agent.
As they say: "That which has happiness as its fruit is to be performed; that which has suffering as its fruit is not to be performed.
And this has been established by us in the *Nyāyakaṇikā*.
Action (*kriyā*) is cultivation (*bhāvanā*), and the words expressing it are "to do" (*karoti*) and so forth;
as they say, "the roots *kṛ*, *bhū*, and *as* denote action in general. For this very reason, he has cited *kṛ*, *bhū*, and *as* as examples.

When a general statement is made, its specific instances—such as "one should cook" and so forth—are also understood; thus, in that context, the *bhāvanā* (productive operation) has an implied agent in the form "one should act," and it has an implied object in the form "it should be done.
However, in the form "it must be done" (*kartavyam*), the *bhāvanā* is subordinate to the substance which serves as the object.

In this way, examples of the productive urge (bhāvanā) conditioned by an injunction (*vidhi*) and directed toward the meaning of a single verbal root (*dhātvartha*) should be cited: "one should be a staff-bearer," "one must become a staff-bearer," and "one would be a staff-bearer.

Furthermore, this verb *bhavati* refers to coming into existence (*janman*); for instance, people employ it as in "the jar comes into being from the potter's activity" and "the sprout comes into being from the seed."
And people do not employ the expression "the sprout exists from the seed";
therefore, existence pertains to being, not to arising. //21//
And because of the word "existence" (bhāva), [the suffix -tva is applied]. (BBs 3.4.22) // 22 //
If it be argued that [the narrative tales] have the purpose of the *pāriplava* [recitation], we say no, because they are specified [otherwise].

(BS 3.4.23) Even though the narrative tales known as *upaniṣads* are heard in proximity to [injunctions for] knowledge (*vidyā*), nevertheless, because the weaker factor of proximity (*saṃnidhi*) is set aside by the scriptural statement "all narrative tales [are recited] at the *pāriplava*," which— by virtue of the word "all"— has an exhaustive scope, the narrative tales must indeed serve the purpose of the *pāriplava*.

Nor should it be argued that, just as even when there is an injunction stating "one should recite all the ten mandalas," the individual application of the verses from the ten mandalas to various specific rites is not contradicted by that general injunction, so too here, despite the general application to the *pāriplava*, they will also serve as auxiliary elements (*aṅga*) to the knowledge (*vidyā*) due to their proximity (*saṃnidhāna*). This cannot be maintained.

In the *Daśatayīs*, because the individual applications (*prātisvikaviniyoga*) and the collective application (*samudāyaviniyoga*) possess equal force, whereas here, due to proximity (*saṃnidhāna*), the direct statement (*śruti*) is stronger, it follows that the narrative accounts (*ākhyāna*) are intended solely for the *pāriplava* recitation. To this, it is replied: these narratives are not applied to the *pāriplava*.

Rather, having begun with the injunction "one should recite the *pāriplava*," those [accounts] which are specifically prescribed there—beginning with "Manu Vaivasvata was king"—are alone to be employed therein.
For these very [stories] are specified by the term *pāriplava*;

otherwise, since the requirement would already be fulfilled by the statement "all narratives (*ākhyāna*) in the *pāriplava*," the injunction "he shall recite the *pāriplava*" would be redundant. However, if it serves as a qualifier for "narratives," it becomes purposeful.
Therefore, due to the requirement of specific particulars, the word "all" (sarva) is dependent upon them and does not denote the absolute whole.

Just as in the expression "All Brāhmaṇas should be fed," the word "all" refers to those who have been invited, so too it is established that the proximity of the Upaniṣadic narratives to knowledge (vidyā) indicates their syntactic unity with knowledge, being free from any contradiction; they possess syntactic unity with knowledge just like the passage beginning with "He wept" (so 'rodīt). Thus, it is proven.
"And because practice is made easy; for even children are instructed by means of a narrative, just as in this treatise by means of illustrative stories. //23//
And likewise, because it is connected as a single syntactical unit (ekavākyatā): BBs_3,4.24 // 24 //

For this very reason, there is no dependence on fire, fuel, and so forth. (BBs 3.4.25) If knowledge were for the sake of the sacrifice, then the sacrifice would be required for its own purpose, namely as an auxiliary to the sacrifice.

In the absence of that [human goal], for whose benefit would knowledge exist? But when it serves the human goal, then the ritual act is not required by this [knowledge], because it possesses the capacity to accomplish its own purpose independently.

By the mention of "kindling the fires" and so forth, the duties of the stages of life (*āśrama-karma*) are indicated; thus he says: the duties of the stages of life, such as kindling the fires and so forth, need not be depended upon for the accomplishment of the goal of knowledge itself.
They need not be relied upon for the accomplishment of one's own purpose, but rather for one's own establishment;
this will be explained further below.
And it is with the intention of explaining that [point] that this purpose of the preceding section has been stated. //25//
Regarding what was stated [in the previous sūtra] as "with the intention of expressing something additional," he states that additional point:
"Moreover, there is dependence on all [works], because of the scriptural mention of sacrifice and so forth, as in the case of the horse. (BS 3.4.26)

One might suspect that just as the duties of the stages of life (āśramakarmāṇi) are not required for the attainment of one's own spiritual goal, they would likewise not be required for its origination;
nor, however, is there any contradiction with such passages as "they desire to know through sacrifice" (yajñena vividiṣanti),
for this is not an injunction (vidhi), but rather a statement of an existing fact (vartamānāpadeśa).
And that [realization] is also possible through praise.
Furthermore, there are four modes of realization regarding Brahman.
First, there is that which arises merely from hearing the sentences of the Upaniṣads, which they indeed call "hearing" (śravaṇa).
The second is accompanied by reflection (*mīmāṃsā*), which they call "contemplation" (*manana*) based on those very same Upaniṣadic passages;
the third is "meditation" (*cintā*).
That which consists of a continuous stream is called *nididhyāsana* (contemplation).
The fourth [stage] is of the nature of direct realization (*sākṣātkāra*), for liberation (*kaivalya*) is its inevitable consequence.

Regarding these, first of all, the two initial stages are indeed possible for a person who has understood the words and their meanings, and who knows the logical principles governing the application of sentences; thus, there is no dependence on ritual action (*karman*) in those cases.
And since those two alone give rise to the third practice, which consists of reflection (*cintāmayī*), there too there is no dependence on karma.

And that [reflection], when cultivated with diligence, continuity, and over a long period of time, certainly brings about the fourth practice, which is characterized by direct realization (*sākṣātkāravatī*); thus, there too there is no dependence on karma.
Furthermore, since liberation (*kaivalya*) is inseparable from that [realization], there is no dependence on karma for that either.

Thus, since cognition does not depend upon an object (*karman*) with respect to its means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), its objects of knowledge (*prameya*), its origination (*utpatti*), or its result (*kārya*), this is the seed for doubt.

This being the position reached, it is said: Cognition does indeed depend upon an object at the time of its origination, by way of producing the desire to know (*vividiṣā*), because of the Vedic scripture: "They desire to know through sacrifice" (*yajñena vividiṣanti*).
Nor is this merely a figurative praise (based on a statement of the present), because the matter is something not previously established (*apūrva*).

Just as the injunction "one for whom the *juhū* ladle is made of *parṇa*-wood" is an original prescription (*apūrva*) because it is not a restatement of something already established— and is not a mere description of a present state because a restatement would be untenable—
so too, at the time of its origination, knowledge requires ritual actions, just like tranquility and the other virtues.

In that regard, because they are connected with the very nature of knowledge (*vidyā*), tranquility (*śama*) and the like are "internal" factors for the arising of knowledge; whereas ritual actions (*karman*) are "external" factors because they are connected with the desire to know (*vividiṣā*).
For it is thus: from the performance of the obligatory duties (*nityakarman*) prescribed for one's stage of life (*āśrama*), dharma arises; from that, evil (*pāpman*) is dissolved.

For while saṃsāra is in reality impermanent, impure, suffering, and non-self, it defiles the essence of the mind through the delusion characterized by permanence, purity, happiness, and self, because such delusions are the cause of unrighteousness (*adharma*). Therefore, when evil is destroyed and the doors of perception and reasoning are opened, one unimpededly determines—by means of both perception and reasoning—the true nature of saṃsāra as being impermanent, impure, and suffering;
consequently, detachment (*vairāgya*), known as "disenchantment" (*anabhirati*) toward this [saṃsāra], arises.
Then, the desire to abandon that [world] arises in him;

thereafter, he seeks the means for its abandonment. While seeking it, having heard from the scriptures and the words of the teacher that knowledge of the true nature of the Self (*ātmatattvajñāna*) is the means, he desires to know it. Thus, through the mediation of the offering of the desire to know, there is a utility for ritual actions (*karma*) in the production of self-knowledge.
Indeed, one who desires to know (vividiṣu), being disciplined, is capable of performing hearing and reflection with one-pointed concentration;
from that, there arises in him an indubitable knowledge of the statement "That thou art" (tat tvam asi).
And for one who has ascertained the meaning of the statement "That thou art" beyond doubt, there is no further eligibility for ritual action.
By this, it should be understood that the utility of ritual actions (*karman*) for the direct realization of meditation or its result has been refuted;
by extension, the utility of ritual actions for liberation (*apavarga*), which is the result of the direct realization of the nature of the self, must be considered utterly rejected.

Therefore, the claim that just as tranquility (*śama*), self-control (*dama*), and so forth persist throughout one's life, so too must the duties of the stages of life (*āśrama-karman*) persist, is an unexamined statement.
It has been stated that the learned have no authority in those [Vedic rites].
However, in the case of actions with visible results, even for one who lacks formal authority, spontaneous engagement in the avoidance of what is prohibited is indeed possible;
for in that regard, where the result is to be understood through positive and negative concomitance (anvaya-vyatireka), there is no dependence upon an injunction.
Therefore, the clamor that "if worldly action is performed through delusion, let Vedic action be likewise for you" is mere idle talk.
As for tranquility, self-control, and the like, which are undertaken for the production of knowledge, they continue even when not required because of their inherent nature in the subsequent states;
this has already been established by us in the first Sūtra and is not being restated here again.

Therefore, it is established that the utility of the duties of the stages of life (āśramakarmāṇi) for the arising of knowledge is by way of generating the desire to know (vividiṣā), and not as a direct effect of knowledge itself. The remainder [of the commentary] has its meaning self-evident. //26//

He should be endowed with tranquility, self-control, and so forth; nevertheless, because there is an injunction for those [qualities], they too must necessarily be practiced as auxiliary parts of that [injunction]. (BSBh 3.4.27) // 27 //

And there is no permission for all [actions] except in a life-threatening emergency, because that is seen [in scripture]. (BBs 3,4.28) In the dialogue concerning the vital breaths (*prāṇasaṃvāda*), it is heard regarding all the sense organs: [that they do not eat when the *mukhya-prāṇa* does not eat].

This is indeed the subject of reflection: having conquered all [the senses] beginning with speech, the principal vital breath (prāṇa) said, "What shall be my food? They replied, "Whatever food there is in this world, from dogs down to birds—whatever is the food of all living beings—that shall be your food.
Having thus prescribed the meditation that everything is the food of the vital breath through this context, the Śruti says: "For one who knows this, nothing whatsoever becomes non-food."

"For one who knows thus, everything is food for the vital breath; nothing whatsoever becomes non-food"—regarding this, a doubt arises: is this permission to eat all food enjoined as an auxiliary part of this knowledge, like tranquility (*śama*) and other such qualities, or is it mentioned merely for the sake of praise?
In this regard, although it is not perceived as an injunction because of the use of the present tense in the word "becomes" (*bhavati*), [the following applies].

Nevertheless, just as in the case of the statement "He whose *juhū* ladle is made of *parṇa*-wood," the understanding that it must be made of *palāśa* wood arises from the present-tense indicative— even though this involves the application of the fifth verbal mood (*liṅ*)— so too here, when a specific impetus toward action is obtained, there is the understanding of an injunction (*vidhi*). For in the case of praise, it is merely an explanatory passage (*arthavāda*), and its purpose is not as effective as it is in the case of an injunction.

The general scripture concerning what is fit and unfit to be eaten is set aside by this specific scripture, just as the general scripture distinguishing between those who may and may not be approached is set aside by the specific scripture regarding the avoidance of all women that forms part of the Vāmadeva-vidyā. To this objection, it is replied: [This is not so], because of incapacity, because it would require an unwarranted assumption, and because of contradiction with other scriptures; rather, there is praise for the contemplation that "all this is food for the vital breath" (prāṇa).
It is not possible for a human being to consume, either simultaneously or sequentially, the food that constitutes the diet of a dog,

because even a single item from the food of elephants, young camels, and so forth— such as *śamī* pods, *karīra* shoots, thorns, or wood— is impossible to eat; nor is there here, as in the case of an inferential mark (*liṅga*), a particularly clear understanding of an injunction.
Nor can a rule be inferred, because there is no element of *apūrva* (unprecedented result);
for that [result] is established even through praise (*stuti*).
Furthermore, when another way is available, it is not proper to restrict the scope of a scripture that has already functioned in a general sense.
Therefore, it is appropriate that the statement "all food belongs to the vital breath" (prāṇa) is a praise intended to enjoin the constant reflection [on this truth].
Furthermore, the capacity for performance is what makes an injunction effective by producing specific activity; it is not useful when the injunction is impossible to carry out.
Moreover, the phrase "in case of danger to life" (prāṇātyaye) is intended as a restriction, meaning that the status of being able to eat all kinds of food applies only in cases of danger to life.

In that regard, because of the illustrative narrative (*upākhyāna*) and because the rule is more clearly remembered, and because it is prescribed for both the learned and the unlearned—with the exception of wine—it applies there and not elsewhere.
[The term] *ibhyena* refers to an elephant-keeper; *sāmi-svāditān* means those that have been tasted and half-eaten.
For that Cākrāyaṇa, while eating the remains of boiled grain left over by the elephant-keepers, was addressed by one of the keepers:
"Why do you not drink the water like the boiled grain, as it is my leavings?
Being thus addressed, he rejected that water on account of the fault of being leavings.
And he stated the reason for this:

"I did not eat these sour gruel beans thinking, 'I will not live,' nor did I think, 'I will live. My desire was for the drinking of water—that is, my freedom regarding the drinking of water at rivers, wells, ponds, cisterns, and so forth, according to my wish."
"I shall obtain [it]"—this is not the case when there is no danger to life due to the absence of leftover water; in that situation, there is the fault of eating what is left over.
Thus, when the Kurus were devastated by hailstorms, a sage, emaciated by hunger and devoid of shame, ate half-chewed food from a wealthy man.
And because there is no sublation [of the scripture], [the Veda is authoritative]. (29)
Moreover, it is recorded in the Smṛti: [BBs 3,4.30] // 30 //
And for this reason, there is a scriptural injunction regarding the non-willing of [evil] in the case of sound. (BBs 3.4.31)
And because they are prescribed, the duties of the stages of life (*āśramakarma*) must also be performed.
For the duties of the stages of life are obligatory, since the scriptural injunction "as long as one lives" establishes them as necessary means for attaining the eternal goal.

Furthermore, because they are described as "desiring to know" (*vividiṣanti*), and because there is no necessary rule that knowledge must arise [from such desire], it follows that knowledge would be non-eternal. Moreover, the conjunction of both the eternal and the non-eternal is impossible for a single entity,
due to the contradiction between what is necessarily occurring and what is not necessarily occurring in one and the same thing.
Nor can the actual contradiction resulting from the split of the sentence be removed;
therefore, it follows that this is merely a case of indecision (*anadhyavasāya*).
By this, the principle "when one [thing] has both [functions], there is the separateness of conjunction" (*saṃyogapṛthaktva*) is refuted.
This being the case, it is replied: This contradiction would exist if [the nature] were already established, but not at all while it is yet to be proven;
since its very acquisition of selfhood depends upon the injunction, its status is held to be exactly as prescribed by that injunction.
For an established entity is sublated by its connection with contradictory properties,

but not that which has the nature of a probandum, as in the case of the *ṣoḍaśin* cup, where there is both taking and not taking; for those two, being dependent on injunctions, are indeed subject to option (*vikalpa*).
Furthermore, once [the nature of the act] is established, there can be no room for doubt.

Thus, in this case, the single rite called Agnihotra, being connected with the lifelong injunction (*yāvajjīva-śruti*) as its occasion, has the purpose of destroying the accumulated sins that must necessarily be expiated; it is therefore mandatory.

And while it is not strictly necessary as a subordinate member (*aṅga*) of knowledge (*vidyā*) because knowledge occurs only occasionally, nevertheless—according to the maxim "whether optional or occasional, it enters by modifying the meaning of the obligatory"—even though it enters under an occasional qualification, it remains mandatory.

It does not make the eternal non-eternal, for that [non-eternality] is established by that very [connection]; thus, due to the distinctness of the conjunctions, it is established that there is no contradiction in a single effect being both eternally and non-eternally conjoined.
Furthermore, the cooperation of karmas is not with respect to the result of knowledge, but rather with respect to its arising.
"What is the meaning of the statement that ritual actions are auxiliaries to knowledge?
This is the meaning: when ritual actions exist, knowledge alone operates toward its own effect.
Just as in the expression, "The she-ass carries the load together with her ten sons," even though the ten sons are present, the she-ass alone is the carrier of the load.
"Because it does not have the characteristic of being an injunction.
For that which is enjoined is connected with the subsidiaries of the Darśa-Pūrṇamāsa and other rites, but that which is not enjoined is not;
this is because the status of being a subsidiary is preceded by being grasped by the principal rite, and the injunction is what performs the grasping.
Furthermore, because that [realization] is not possible in the case of what is not enjoined,
and because it has been stated in the first sūtra that an injunction regarding the four modes of practice is impossible with respect to Brahman;
and it has also been stated that the expressions "it is to be seen" and "it is to be meditated upon," though having the form of an injunction, are not actually injunctions.

It has been established above that the causal relationship regarding the arising [of knowledge] occurs through the production of the desire to know (*vividiṣā*) by means of the purification of the inner being (*sattva-śuddhi*).

Furthermore, liberation (*apavarga*), which is the fruit of knowledge, is not something to be accomplished (*asādhya*); for it is characterized as abiding in one's own true nature (*svarūpāvasthāna*).
And the true nature of Brahman is not something to be accomplished, because it is eternal.
The remainder has its meaning not concealed. //32//
And by way of being a cooperative cause. // 33 //
In every respect, it is those very same [acts] because of the twofold characteristic (ubhayaliṅga).

Just as in the case of "they offer the Agnihotra for a month," where a difference of action (*karmabheda*) arises from a different context (*prakaraṇāntara*), so too here [in the passage] "him, this very one, by means of the recitation of the Vedas... [a difference of action is established].

Regarding the statement, "Brāhmaṇas desire to know [Brahman] through sacrifice," since it is heard outside the context of ritual action (*kratuprakaraṇa*), and because the notion of that [context] is interrupted by the presence of a different context (*prakaraṇāntara*), the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) is that this is a different ritual action. To this, it is replied: even though there is a different context, it is indeed the same ritual action;

however, based on scripture (*śruti*) and tradition (*smṛti*), there is merely a difference in connection (*saṃyogabheda*). Just as in the cases, "One desiring heaven should offer the Agnihotra" and "One should offer the Agnihotra as long as one lives"—it is the very same Agnihotra connected with both [injunctions].
A different context (*prakaraṇāntara*) is not directly a differentiator.

Rather, an injunction (*vidhi*), whose natural tendency is to make known what was previously unknown, would abandon its natural tendency through the force of a clearer recognition when the context is identical.
However, when recognition is disrupted by a different context, it abandons its natural tendency and differentiates the ritual action (*karman*).

But here, one who enjoins sacrifices and the like— which already exist as established forms— for the sake of the desire to know (*vividiṣā*) cannot, like the injunction "he does not offer oblations," produce a new form for them that did not previously exist.
Nor is it correct to say that even in that case, the injunction regarding the month refers to the regular *agnihotra* and does not constitute the production of a new *agnihotra*,
because the direct scriptural hearing (*śruti*) of the injunction pertains to the *homa* itself.
Furthermore, because time is not something to be acquired and is not subject to injunction,
the general rule is that the ritual action is enjoined with respect to time, and not time with respect to the action; however, in this case,
the scriptural injunction pertains to the desire to know (*vividiṣā*), not to the sacrifice and so forth.
But since those [details] are merely restated as already established, the principle of "separateness of connection" (saṃyogapṛthaktva) is established through their being part of a single ritual act.
Having stated the traditional authority (smṛti), the observation of indicative marks (liṅgadarśana) has been stated. //34//
And it demonstrates non-overpowering: BBs_3,4.35 // 35 // START BsVBh_3,4.8.35.
But even in the interval [between stages], because that is seen.

(BS 3.4.36) If the duties of the stages of life (*āśramakarma*) were auxiliaries to knowledge (*vidyā*), then alas! those who do not belong to a stage of life, such as widowers and others, would have no qualification for knowledge.

Since there is an absence of the auxiliary factors that are the duties of the stages of life (āśrama-karma), it might be concluded [that they have no qualification]. To this, it is replied: It is not the case that those such as Raikva, Vidhura, and Vācaknavī were entirely devoid of action;
for even while they were not in a formal stage of life, they possessed actions such as recitation (japa), fasting (upavāsa), and the propitiation of deities.

Furthermore, since it was stated that the auxiliary nature of actions refers to the duties of the stages of life by way of illustration (upalakṣaṇa), they do not lack qualification for knowledge (vidyā).
And even regarding [the phrase] "from what was performed in another birth":
indeed, there is no dependence on ritual actions for the effects of knowledge (*vidyā*),
but rather for its arising.
And they produce knowledge through the offering of the desire to know (*vividiṣā*).
For those foremost among men, such as Vidhura, Saṃvarta, and others, for whom the desire to know has already arisen, there is no need for ritual actions.

Even if ritual actions have not been performed in this life, it is understood that they were performed by them in a previous existence, because an excellence of the desire to know is observed in them.

[Objection: Just as only one who has studied the Vedas is qualified for the inquiry into Dharma (dharmajijñāsā) and not one who has not studied them in this life, so too here, only one who has produced the desire to know (vividisā) through the performance of duties belonging to the stages of life (āśrama-karma) in this life is qualified for knowledge (vidyā), and no other; thus, those without a stage of life, such as widowers and the like, would have no qualification. To this, he says: "And because its purpose is seen"—the removal of ignorance is the visible purpose of knowledge.
The meaning is that this [invariable concomitance], established through positive and negative concomitance (anvaya-vyatireka), does not depend on a restrictive rule (niyama).
"Negation" means its non-existence; that is, the absence of such a rule. //36//
Moreover, it is recorded in the Smṛti: [BBs 3,4.37] // 37 //
And there is the special favor [of the Lord]. (38)
"But the other is superior, on account of scriptural indication.

(BS 3.4.39) Anticipating the objection that "if those who do not belong to any stage of life (āśrama) also have the qualification for knowledge, then what is the use of the stages of life which involve such great exertion?", he says: "But the other is superior, on account of scriptural indication."

One should remain a non-ascetic while in good health; however, if by fate one becomes a non-ascetic due to separation from a wife and so forth, there would be eligibility for knowledge (*vidyā*). This is understood from the greater authority of the scriptural and traditional texts, such as "They desire to know through sacrifice" (*yajñena vividiṣanti*), and the indicative mark (*liṅga*) of the Śruti: "By that [path] goes the doer of meritorious deeds."
And such Smṛti indications as "one who does not belong to a stage of life (anāśramī) should not remain [in this world]" are also present. //39//
But for one who has become that [state], there is no returning to what is not that state, even according to Jaimini, because of the restrictive rule and because of the absence of those forms.
(BS 3.4.40) This section is intended to dispel the weak suspicion that, like the ascent, there might occasionally be a descent for those of perpetual celibacy (*ūrdhvaretas*).
Regarding the former dharmas, such as sacrifices and oblations:
out of attachment, one might think, "May I be a householder surrounded by a wife and so forth.
He explains the restrictive rule (*niyama*) as follows: "For thus, [one should] completely [withdraw] oneself... and so on.
He explains the absence of similarity, which consists in the ascent to the state of not having that nature, with the words: "And as when, having completed the period of studentship...
He analyzes the absence of the conduct of the learned with the words: "But such practices do not belong to the learned. The rest has a meaning that is not obscure. //40//

Nor can it be argued that even for one holding an office (an adhikārika), there is no penance because of the inference of a fall from his status; for regarding the lifelong student (naiṣṭhika), there is a traditional rule stating, "I see no penance," which indicates an absence of penance. However, the sacrifice of a donkey to Nirṛti is a penance intended for the student who has completed his initial course (upakurvāṇaka).

Therefore, the prima facie position (*pūrva-pakṣa*) is that, like a man whose head has been severed, there can be no remedial action. As for the interpretation of the Sūtra: the expiation determined in the first section (*kāṇḍa*), which deals with qualifications (*adhikāra-lakṣaṇa*), by the rule "And the animal sacrifice for one who has broken his vow of celibacy (*avakīrṇin*) is likewise, because the time for the consecration (*ādhāna*) has not yet arrived"—that expiation cannot apply to the lifelong student (*naiṣṭhika*).

Why? Because, according to the Smṛti statement "one who has ascended to the lifelong stage," there is an inference from the scriptural texts regarding falling [from that state], and because an expiation for that is impossible. //41//
However, some maintain that even when preceded by the prefix *upa*, it denotes a state (*bhāva*), as in the case of eating (*aśana*); this has been stated [in the following]:

"First, scripture—possessing an unrestricted application (*asaṅkucadvṛtti*)—directly teaches penance for the celibate student (*brahmacārin*) without distinction between the lifelong (*naiṣṭhika*) and the temporary (*upakurvāṇa*)."
The Smṛti states, "I do not see an expiation.
Even in that case, the prohibition of expiation is not understood as meaning that expiation must not be performed directly;
rather, because he says "I do not see," that [prohibition] is to be inferred from his lack of vision [of a remedy].
Thus, having inferred that the Smṛti rule is for the purpose of prohibition, one must infer a corresponding Śruti text;

for a Śruti text, though having a general scope, moves swiftly when it approaches a specific case. As for the non-observation of a penance in the Smṛti, it is intended to indicate the gravity of the effort required [to avoid the transgression].

This is what is meant: even by those who have performed purification, no formal counting (of the offense) should be made. As for the meaning of the Sūtra: even a minor sin (*upapātaka*) consisting of the loss of chastity (*avakīrṇitva*) for one who has taken a lifelong vow (*naiṣṭhika*) is not a mortal sin (*mahāpātaka*); the particle *api* here has the sense of *eva* (only). For this reason, some maintain that there is an absence of expiation (*prāyaścitta*). Since there is no distinction in the disagreement among the teachers, there would be equality [between their views].
Whatever established usage is rooted in the scriptures (śāstra) is to be accepted, because it is based upon the scriptures.
And it has been demonstrated that the established existence of expiatory rites (prāyaścitta) is rooted in the scriptures. The rest is easy to understand. //42//
But regarding those outside [the community], it is in both cases [permissible] because of tradition and custom.
(BBs 3.4.43) If there is atonement for lifelong celibates (*naiṣṭhika*) and others, should one interact with them once they have performed the purification, or not?

In this regard, since non-intercourse with certain persons is caused by their faults, it might be argued that because those faults are removed by penance (*prāyaścitta*), or else because performing penance would otherwise be futile, such persons are indeed fit for social intercourse. To this, it is replied: "But they are excluded from society in both cases, according to Smṛti and custom.

The sin (*enas*) produced by the performance of forbidden acts brings about impurity in both worlds; however, there is a twofold distinction: for some sins, impurity in both worlds is removed by penances through the destruction of that sin.

While some perform expiations that merely remove the impurity pertaining to the next world by destroying the transgression, the impurity pertaining to this world produced by that transgression cannot be removed for those who have killed women,
children, and so forth.

As they have said: "One should not even drink [with] those who are pure in terms of their dharma. Likewise: "The sin that has been committed unintentionally is removed by penances; so too is that which was committed intentionally.
However, one such as a killer of a child, even though he has performed the purification, becomes unfit for social interaction in this world due to the scriptural injunction.
And there is the statement beginning with "and those who kill children," and so forth.
Therefore, everything is clear. //43//
“Because the fruit is declared for the master [of the sacrifice], so says Ātreya” (BBs 3.4.44).

In the first section (*kāṇḍa*), which defines the status of the subsidiary (*śeṣa-lakṣaṇa*), since the connection of the ritual action with the officiating priest (*ṛtvij*) has been established in the rule “likewise [the fruit belongs] to the one who desires,” what then is the purpose of the desire?

Having raised the doubt as to whether [the fruit] belongs to the sacrificer (*yājamāna*) or to the officiating priest (*ārtvijya*), it was determined that even in the case of ritual acts, the desire for the fruit of the subordinate qualities (*guṇaphala*) belongs to the sacrificer alone;

however, here it is deliberated whether meditations (*upāsanā*) of this kind, which are connected with the constituent parts of the rite, belong to the sacrificer or to the officiating priest— and thus it is not a redundant repetition.

In this regard, because the fruits of meditation are heard of as belonging to the *upāsakas*, those who lack the qualification [for such meditation] cannot logically possess them; furthermore, since the fruit produced by ritual action belongs to the patron (*yajamāna*) who enjoys it, and since that [fruit] is not logically applicable to the officiating priests (*ṛtvij*), and because of the scriptural statement—which stands in the place of a royal decree—there are instances where the fruit is heard of as belonging to the priests. However, in the absence of such a specific statement, the meditation results in fruit for the patron, because the fruit is heard of as his; as in the passage beginning, "Baka Dālbhya knew him," which refers to the meditation.

And since there is no capacity for the sublation of the [general] rule due to the fact that [the meditation] has a realized object, it follows that the act of meditation belongs to the sacrificer alone; to this, it is replied: //44//
"Regarding the office of the officiating priest (*ārlijya*), Auḍulomi maintains that it belongs [to the sacrificer], for he is hired for that purpose.
From the introductory narrative (*upākhyāna*), it is understood that the meditation (*upāsana*) pertains to the office of the Udgātṛ priest.
Therefore, since there exists a powerful subverting factor (*bādhaka*), the narrative must be explained otherwise.

It is not impossible for the fruit of the meditation performed by the officiating priests (*ṛtvij*) to accrue to the patron (*yajamāna*); for he has hired them, and thus it is logical that they act for the sake of a fruit that goes to him. Consequently, it is not proper to alter the narrative merely out of a sense of dogmatic attachment; such is the final conclusion (*rāddhānta*). //45//
And because of scripture. (Sūtra 46)
START BsVBh_3,4.14.47:

"The injunction for another auxiliary [is] by way of an alternative; it is the third [kind], like the injunction regarding one who possesses that [knowledge]. (BBs 3,4.47). Therefore, a Brahmin, having thoroughly understood scholarship through certainty...

"Having attained childhood, one should remain in it; having become indifferent to both childhood and panditya (scholarship), one then becomes a muni; and having become indifferent to both non-mauna and mauna, one then becomes a brahmana. For wherever an injunctive suffix is heard, that is what is to be enjoined.
And while that suffix is heard in the phrase "one should remain in childhood," it is not heard in the case of mauna.
Therefore, just as the statement "Then [he becomes] a Brahmin" is not something to be enjoined since no injunction is heard therein, so too is *mauna* (the state of a sage).
Nor is it to be enjoined because it is something previously unknown (*apūrva*).
Consequently, since *mauna* is established by the very injunction of *pāṇḍitya* (scholarship) in the passage "A Brahmin should become disillusioned with scholarship," *pāṇḍitya* itself is *mauna*.
Alternatively, this word "muni" (sage) denotes a *bhikṣu* (mendicant), as seen in the passage: "The householder's life, the teacher's family, the state of a sage (*mauna*), and forest-dwelling.
This [mention of *mauna*] is a restatement of that which has been prescribed elsewhere.
Therefore, it is logical that "childhood" (*bālya*) alone is what is being enjoined here, while "the state of a sage," being already established, is restated for the purpose of praise.
This would be so if the word *muni* were a synonym for "learned" (*paṇḍita*).
However, scholarship is merely knowledge, whereas sagehood (*mauna*) is the perfection of an excellence of knowledge, because that is how it is well-known in that very context.
As for its application to the different stages of life (*āśrama*), this is due to its proximity to terms such as "householder" and so forth.

Therefore, because it is something not previously established (*apūrva*), this third stage of silence (*mauna*), which consists of a preeminent form of knowledge in relation to childhood and scholarship (*bālya-pāṇḍitya*), is enjoined.
And thus, the fact that it is to be "realized" (*nirvedanīya*) would also be directly applicable to the injunction; hence he says: "because of the instruction regarding its being to be realized.

To the question of for whom this silence is enjoined as an auxiliary to knowledge (*vidyā-sahakārin*), he replies: "for one who possesses that—namely, for the mendicant ascetic (*bhikṣu*) who possesses knowledge (*vidyāvat*)."
He asks: "How so?

The meaning is that being possessed of knowledge (*vidyāvattā*) is perceived, but not the state of being a renunciant (*saṃnyāsitā*). The answer is: "Because of his qualification for that," that is, because the mendicant (*bhikṣu*) has the qualification for it.

He shows this with the words "having known the self. He raises an objection in order to apply a portion of the Sūtra with the word "but" (nanu). He resolves it with the words "therefore he says: by way of an alternative" (pakṣeṇa).
By "one who possesses knowledge" (*vidyāvān*), an excellence of knowledge is not intended;
rather, it refers to one who has engaged in practice for the arising of knowledge, but in whom an excellence of arisen knowledge has not yet occurred.
Thus, the meaning is that, according to this view, the possibility [of the error] exists because of the occasional perception of difference.
The "beginning of the injunction" (*vidhyādi*) is that which has the injunction as its primary element—that is, the principal [act].
For this very reason, the "end of the injunction" (*vidhyanta*) consists of the *samit* and other such [subsidiary acts], for they follow after the principal injunction.
The meaning is that, even though no injunction is explicitly heard there, an injunction must be assumed because of the novelty (*apūrvatva*) of the matter. //47//

START BsVBh_3,4.14.48 Now, one might object: "If this stage of life (āśrama) is characterized primarily by childhood, why does [the text] conclude with the householder's stage? Thus he raises the objection: "In this way, distinguished by childhood and so forth. He recites the reply:
"But the conclusion is made by means of the householder because of his all-encompassing nature.

(BBs 3.4.48) This means that in the Chāndogya Upaniṣad, the conclusion is reached through the householder stage because it involves many duties requiring great effort, and because it includes certain duties belonging to the other stages of life, such as non-violence (*ahiṃsā*) and so forth; it is not, however, because the [teaching] is completed by him alone.
(START BsVBh 3.4.14.49)

Thus, by the presentation of these two stages of life (*āśrama*), a person of dull intellect might occasionally suspect the non-existence of the other; therefore, to dispel that [doubt], the Sūtra states:
"As with the vow of silence (*mauna*), so too because there is instruction for the others" (BBs 3.4.49).

Just as the mode of life (*vṛtti*) for forest-dwellers (*vānaprastha*) is of many kinds, so it is for those practicing sacred conduct (*brahmacārin*); thus, either the differences in their modes of life or the persons who perform them are distinguished.
Therefore, even when there is duality, the use of the plural number is not contradictory. //49//
START BsVBh_3,4.15.50:
"By not manifesting [himself], because of the connection" (BBs_3,4.50).

This means by means of childhood; for it is well known that, according to the scriptural account of the conduct of a child, there is the state of acting, speaking, and eating according to one's desire, which constitutes extreme childhood.

Since the general scripture prescribing rules such as purity is set aside by this specific scripture, it might be argued that the entire conduct of a child is enjoined; to this, we reply: because childhood is enjoined as an auxiliary to knowledge (*vidyā*), and because enjoining the entirety of a child's conduct would result in a contradiction with the primary purpose, only that which is conducive to it—such as the non-maturity of the senses and the like, consisting of purity of disposition—is what is actually enjoined.
And thus, since the matter is established even without contradicting other treatises, it would be improper to contradict those other treatises. //50//
START BsVBh_3,4.16.51:
"Even that which pertains to this life [occurs] when there is no obstruction of what is relevant, for that is observed.
(BBs_3,4.51) He states the connection [between the sūtras] with the words: "And [there is] dependence on all" (sarvāpekṣā ca).
Is knowledge accomplished here in this very life through hearing and other means, or is there no fixed rule, such that it may occur either in this life or in the next?
Although rituals such as sacrifices have non-fixed results, and since these are the means for the production of knowledge, it appears that the production of knowledge is itself non-fixed.

Nevertheless, because of the scriptural report of Vāmadeva’s self-realization while still in the womb, and because of the Smṛti statement, "One who has been perfected through many births then goes to the supreme goal," its occurrence in the next world is also understood.

Nevertheless, since sacrifices and the like are objects of knowledge (*prameya*) and are not themselves means of valid cognition (*apramāṇa*), whereas hearing and the like are means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), it is these latter alone that are the direct means for the attainment of knowledge (*vidyā*).

Sacrifices and the like serve as means for the attainment of knowledge either by producing the purification of the mind (*sattva-śuddhi*), or by pacifying the obstacles to the operation of the means of valid cognition—namely, hearing and the like—which give rise to knowledge.
Hearing and the like, however, produce knowledge independently, without requiring anything else.

Furthermore, when engaging in the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), cognizers do not desire the production of a cognition that occurs only after a long time even in this life, much less one pertaining to the next world; rather, they desire only that which is immediate.
For one who desires to see a jar does not open his eyes for the sake of seeing that jar at another time, but rather for its immediate perception.
Therefore, the production of knowledge (*vidyā*) pertains only to this life and is not of indefinite time.
The Śruti and Smṛti declare, by way of praise, that the production of knowledge pertains to the world beyond;
they mean that hearing and the other means, being of such a nature, necessarily bear fruit in that they produce knowledge even at a later time.

This being the position reached, it is said in reply: because here, when the production of knowledge is to be accomplished through hearing and the rest, sacrifices and the like [serve] by way of purifying the internal organ (sattva).

Or rather, their utility lies in the pacification of obstacles; for this very reason, since sacrifices and the like have uncertain results depending on whether they are obstructed by other actions or not, it is logical that hearing (*śravaṇa*) and the other stages—which depend upon them—also have uncertain results.
This is because hearing and the rest do not produce their fruit for those whose obstacles have not been removed, or for a person whose mental essence (*sattva*) has not been purified.

And thus, since those [means] such as sacrifice are dependent [on other factors] and are heard to have uncertain results, it is indeed logical that hearing and the rest also have uncertain results; in this way, the contradiction with Śruti and Smṛti will not have to be explained away as being merely figurative praise. Furthermore, persons seeking knowledge will desire only what corresponds to their capacity for the means; this is what was stated by the phrase "because the intention is unrestrained. //51//
Thus, there is no fixed rule regarding the fruit of liberation, because that state has been determined; because that state has been determined.

Indeed, it has been shown that due to the specific intensity of the effort involved in hearing and other means of acquiring knowledge—which are aided by sacrifices and the like—there is an excellence in the fruit of that knowledge characterized by whether it occurs in this life or the next.

And so, just as the excellence or deficiency of the fruit—namely, knowledge (vidyā)—occurs through the excellence or deficiency of the means, in the same way, excellence or deficiency might be conceived for liberation, which is the fruit of knowledge. However, no distinction characterized by being "of this world" or "of the next world" is possible in liberation; for since liberation occurs while one is still living (jīvanmukti) once knowledge has arisen from the ripening of the meditation on Brahman, it necessarily follows that liberation must occur even while the karma whose fruition has already begun remains unexhausted.
Therefore, any excellence or deficiency in liberation could only pertain to its specific form (rūpa).

Furthermore, since it is observed that the excellence or inferiority of the fruits of knowledge corresponds to the excellence or inferiority of the knowledge itself when it possesses qualities, it might follow that liberation (mukti), being the fruit of knowledge, would likewise possess excellence or inferiority based on its form; to this it is replied:
no, because liberation is of a uniform nature in each instance, as declared by scripture and because it is logically consistent.

For that which is to be accomplished (sādhya) becomes characterized by specific qualities through the excellence of its means of accomplishment (sādhana). Now, liberation—which is defined as the abiding in the eternal nature of Brahman—is eternal; being eternal, it cannot be something to be accomplished.

Nor can the total destruction of the impressions (vāsanā), afflictions (kleśa), and the latencies of karma (karmāśaya) be the means, for the arising of knowledge (vidyā) is itself the destruction of the afflictions and so forth, according to the view that the very emergence of an effect that is opposed [to its cause] constitutes the destruction of the preceding [cause].
[There would be] grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*);
[the liberated one] would possess distinctions, by which liberation would also possess those distinctions.
Furthermore, the destruction of afflictions and so forth that leaves a remainder does not conduce to liberation.
Furthermore, no difference in form is observed even within knowledge (*vidyā*) itself, apart from its being produced sooner or later; for it is heard in scripture (*śruti*) as having a single form.
However, in the case of knowledge associated with qualities (*saguṇavidyā*), the excellence or inferiority of its result—the fruit—is logical through the addition or removal of various qualities.
But here, there is no "knowledge-ness" (*vidyātva*) perceived as a commonality [that would allow for such a distinction].
Because it is sublated by scripture and by the reasoning arising therefrom, [the opponent's position] is "mistimed" (kālātyayāpadiṣṭa).
Therefore, since that state of liberation is determined to be of a single uniform nature, it is logical that there is no difference in the fruit characterized as liberation. //52//
Thus ends the fourth quarter of the third chapter in the *Bhāmatī*, a commentary on the *Śārīrakabhagavatpādabhāṣya* composed by the venerable Vācaspati Miśra.
Thus ends the fourth quarter of the third chapter, titled "An Investigation into the Internal Means for Knowledge Devoid of Attributes."
